prompt: I've noticed words like 'lie' and 'abuse' getting stretched to cover more and more. Write a post arguing about whether it matters when we broaden the meaning of a word like that.
response:
**When “abuse” stops meaning something**

When a word starts covering everything, it often stops covering anything. I do not mean that in a dictionary sense. Dictionaries record use; they do not police it. I mean it in the sense that matters when people are trying to decide what to do. “Lie” and “abuse” are not decorative words. They are tools for judgment. They tell us that something has crossed a line, that trust has been broken, that a relationship has become dangerous, that a sanction may be appropriate. If we make those words apply to almost anything, we do not merely change definitions. We change the map we use to navigate other people’s lives.

The pressure to broaden them is real and often legitimate. For a long time, “abuse” could mean a broken arm, a burned hand, a visible mark. That was useful for proving a crime in court, but it was a poor name for a life in which a partner controls the money, isolates a person from friends, humiliates them in front of children, or makes ordinary decisions feel terrifying. If we had insisted on the old meaning, we would have left a large area of harm unspoken. The same is true of “lie.” A person can avoid saying the false sentence and still destroy confidence: answer a direct question with a technically true nonanswer, emphasize one fact to hide another, present a prediction as a certainty when it is not. If “lie” only covered flat, deliberate falsehood, it would miss a lot of deception.

But there is a difference between extending a word to cases it should have covered and inflating it until the center disappears. The difference shows up in gradation. A useful moral word usually has a neighborhood: milder forms, serious forms, extreme forms. “Lie” can be a small concealment, a cover-up, a sworn falsehood. “Abuse” can be harsh treatment, sustained domination, an attempt to make a person distrust their own experience. When we collapse those differences, we lose the ability to say what is worst.

Suppose a parent yells at a child after a bad day. That may be unkind, inconsistent, or even harmful. Suppose another parent makes a child believe that their own memory is false, that they are to blame for every crisis, and that leaving is impossible. The second case is worse, obviously. But if both are simply “abuse,” the word has told us less, not more. It has registered that something bad happened, but not that one relationship contains a mechanism of control. The same with lying: a researcher rounds a number carelessly; an executive knows a product causes injury and says it is safe. Calling both “lies” is not precision. It is a way of avoiding the harder questions of intent, power, and damage.

The hardest objection to this worry is obvious: moral progress often begins when someone refuses to accept the narrow meaning of a word. “That is not abuse, there are no bruises” has been a defense. “That is not a lie, it was an opinion” has been a defense. If we become too quick to police language, we can end up giving the powerful a technicality. The person who says “my boss abused me” because he publicly humiliated her and made the workplace unsafe is not being dramatic. The person who says “the company lied” because it knew what its emissions data meant and presented it in a misleading way is not being pedantic. In many cases, the broadened word is the first honest word available.

So the answer is not “use the old meaning.” The answer is that broadening has to be anchored. A good expansion names a real harm that was previously hard to see. It also keeps a standard that can be disputed. It asks: Was there a violation? Was there a power imbalance? Was there a pattern? Was there an attempt to control, deceive, or silence? If the answer is yes, the word may fit. If the answer is merely “I felt bad,” the word may be too heavy. Not because the feeling is invalid, but because “abuse” is not a word for feelings alone. It is a word for what someone did to you, or allowed to happen to you, in a way that corrupted a relationship or a duty.

I cannot prove that the average private conversation has changed as much as public argument does. What is visible online is a different problem: a transcript without tone, a screenshot without history, a single sentence without the relationship around it can look like evidence of abuse. The word becomes a verdict before the facts are in. That does not mean the person using it is wrong. It means the category is being used faster than understanding can catch up.

Institutions feel this quickly. If every boundary dispute is “abuse,” a manager cannot tell a difficult conversation from a campaign of intimidation. If every false statement is a “lie,” a newspaper cannot distinguish error from corruption. If every omission is a “lie,” a court cannot decide what counts as deception. The result is not that people stop feeling hurt. It is that the word stops helping us decide what to do.

A lie is not just a false statement. It is a false statement made with a betrayal of the expectation of truth. That expectation varies. A joke is not a lie because both parties know the game. A seller’s puffery is not exactly a lie, though it can become illegal when it crosses into material deception. A politician’s slogan may be false, misleading, or a lie depending on what the speaker knows and what he intends the audience to believe. If we flatten those distinctions, we make political language easier to dismiss. When everything is a lie, the discovery of a real one becomes less remarkable.

Abuse is often about a pattern, not an incident. A single cruel act can be terrible, but the word usually points to a climate: fear, obligation, guilt, isolation, repetition. That is why people sometimes say they did not recognize it as abuse until later. The word captures a shape. If we apply it to any unpleasant shape, we lose the shape that matters.

It matters because moral language is a budget. We have finite attention, finite anger, finite willingness to intervene. If we spend the strongest words on the weakest offenses, the strongest offenses get a weaker reception. That does not mean the weaker offenses are unimportant. It means we need a wider vocabulary: discourtesy, betrayal, manipulation, negligence, cruelty, domination, deception, error, malice. We need to say what kind of bad thing happened, not just that it was bad. Broaden “lie” and “abuse” when they have been too narrow. But do not let them become words for everything that goes wrong. A word that can be used for anything is a word that cannot be trusted to point to the worst.

I cannot prove that the average private conversation has changed as much as public argument does. What is visible online is a different problem: a transcript without tone, a screenshot without history, a single sentence without the relationship around it can look like evidence of abuse. The word becomes a verdict before the facts are in. That does not mean the person using it is wrong. It means the category is being used faster than understanding can catch up.

Institutions feel this quickly. If every boundary dispute is “abuse,” a manager cannot tell a difficult conversation from a campaign of intimidation. If every false statement is a “lie,” a newspaper cannot distinguish error from corruption. If every omission is a “lie,” a court cannot decide what counts as deception. The result is not that people stop feeling hurt. It is that the word stops helping us decide what to do.

A lie is not just a false statement. It is a false statement made with a betrayal of the expectation of truth. That expectation varies. A joke is not a lie because both parties know the game. A seller’s puffery is not exactly a lie, though it can become illegal when it crosses into material deception. A politician’s slogan may be false, misleading, or a lie depending on what the speaker knows and what he intends the audience to believe. If we flatten those distinctions, we make political language easier to dismiss. When everything is a lie, the discovery of a real one becomes less remarkable.

Abuse is often about a pattern, not an incident. A single cruel act can be terrible, but the word usually points to a climate: fear, obligation, guilt, isolation, repetition. That is why people sometimes say they did not recognize it as abuse until later. The word captures a shape. If we apply it to any unpleasant shape, we lose the shape that matters.

It matters because moral language is a budget. We have finite attention, finite anger, finite willingness to intervene. If we spend the strongest words on the weakest offenses, the strongest offenses get a weaker reception. That does not mean the weaker offenses are unimportant. It means we need a wider vocabulary: discourtesy, betrayal, manipulation, negligence, cruelty, domination, deception, error, malice. We need to say what kind of bad thing happened, not just that it was bad. Broaden “lie” and “abuse” when they have been too narrow. But do not let them become words for everything that goes wrong. A word that can be used for anything is a word that cannot be trusted to point to the worst.

prompt: Everyone says you can't travel once you have a baby. I think that's wrong. Write a persuasive blog post for new parents.
response:
## You Can Travel With a Baby. You Just Can’t Do the Old Trip.

The warning usually arrives in the first year, offered with a smile. “You won’t get to travel once you have a baby.” It sounds like a fact, but it is not. It is a comparison to the wrong kind of travel.

Before the baby, travel could mean a last-minute flight, a hotel you checked into at midnight, a museum that swallowed the afternoon, a meal that started late and ended later, a day when nobody had to be fed at exactly the right time or put down in a safe sleep space. That trip may be impossible now. But a two-night stay at your sister’s, a drive to a town you have never seen, a flight home to your parents when the house has started to feel like a room: those are still travel. They are just travel with a small person in the center of the plan.

The myth works because it protects a version of travel that belonged to your former schedule. It says the old life is gone, not that a new one is available.

Think about what travel actually does. It changes the air you breathe, the sounds you hear, the distance between your bed and the nearest familiar face. It interrupts the loop. With a baby, the loop is powerful: kitchen floor, stroller route, nap, feed, repeat. A trip does not have to include a famous landmark in order to break that loop. It only has to put your body somewhere else for long enough to remember that the world is wider than the hallway.

A concrete example helps. A family with an eight-month-old drives four hours to grandparents’ house. They leave at seven, baby naps in the car seat, one parent drives, the other watches the rearview mirror and pretends the gas station sandwich is a meal. They arrive at eleven. Baby naps in the crib while the parents shower, sleep for two hours, and walk outside without a destination. On Sunday they leave after lunch. There is no gallery, no wine bar, no spontaneous detour to a village. There is still the fact that they left, crossed some distance, slept in another bed, and came back with the edges of the week softened. That counts.

The strongest objection is not romantic. It is practical. Babies get sick. Ears hurt on planes. Unfamiliar water, sand, bugs, and germs are real. When you are running on four hours of sleep, a minor problem can become a major one because you have less patience, less bandwidth, and less trust in your own judgment. That is true. The answer is not to stay home forever. The answer is to match the trip to the baby’s age, your actual reserves, and the level of medical support around you.

For most healthy full-term babies, a few hours in a car or a short domestic flight is usually manageable. But “usually” is doing important work. If the baby was premature, has breathing or feeding problems, is very young, or the trip is long, remote, or to a place with limited pediatric care, the calculus changes. Ask the pediatrician when there is a medical question. Do not treat a well-meaning relative as the authority on infant safety.

The point is not that every trip is equally wise. It is that “you can’t travel” is too broad. A weekend in the next state is not the same category as a three-country tour. A flight to see family is not the same category as a beach week in a town where the nearest hospital is an hour away and the tap water is not something you want an infant near. Travel with a baby becomes a risk-management problem, not a moral test.

There is also the packing. The old travel skill was spontaneity. The new one is redundancy. A weekend away requires diapers, wipes, formula or pumping supplies, a stroller, a car seat or travel crib, changes of clothes for every hour the baby is awake, a bag for leaks, a bag for sleep, and a plan for what you will do when the baby is awake and the parents are not. If your suitcase looks like a medical kit, that is not proof that travel is absurd. It is proof that you are carrying a small person’s survival.

You will also miss things. You will feed in an airport bathroom. You will leave a hotel room at six because the baby is awake and the parents’ plan is dead. You will stand in a restaurant while the baby bounces in a seat, eating pureed peas with the focus of a soldier. You will come home from a beautiful place and feel only tired. None of that means the trip failed. It means the terms changed.

The baby, for their part, is not thinking about the itinerary. They are thinking about rhythm: hunger, sleep, temperature, whether the person holding them is calm enough to regulate them. A baby can adapt to a new room, a new smell, a new stretch of road, as long as the caregivers can keep the basic needs met. In that sense, the fragile part of the trip is often not the infant but the adults. A well-rested parent in a strange town is usually better company for a baby than an exhausted one at home.

This is also not a claim that every family can or should travel often. Money, work, caregiving support, disability, mental health, and the sheer cost of infant supplies all matter. If travel is not possible right now, that is a constraint, not a character flaw. The problem with the saying “you can’t travel once you have a baby” is that it turns a temporary limitation into a permanent identity. It tells new parents that their lives have narrowed when, more often, the shape of the life has just changed.

Start small. A day trip that returns before bedtime. A night at a relative’s. A short drive to a park you have never visited. A flight when the baby is older and you have help at home. Keep the radius small until it grows. The goal is not to prove that baby can handle Paris. The goal is to keep the world from shrinking to the size of your sleep schedule.

The old trip is gone. Grieve that if you need to. But do not let the memory of it stand in the doorway while you stand there with a diaper bag, waiting for permission that was never really the issue. Get in the car. Choose a place close enough that you can handle a bad night. Go.

prompt: I saw a headline saying a third of newly approved drugs end up recalled or with new safety warnings, and people are saying the FDA is too lax. Is that actually what the number means? Write it up properly, as someone who prescribes these drugs.
response:
I don’t have the article in front of me, so I can’t audit its exact numerator and denominator. But the wording tells me what the number is not. A third of newly approved drugs are not “recalled” in the ordinary sense. If the report is like the postmarketing safety studies that usually generate headlines like this, the number probably means that, over some follow-up period, about one drug in three received some postapproval safety action: a label change, a boxed warning, a use restriction, a new monitoring requirement, or, in a smaller number of cases, withdrawal from the market. That is a real thing. It is also much less clean and much less damning than “a third are recalled.”

The first confusion is semantic. A recall is a corrective action taken because a product is defective: contaminated, mislabeled, underpowered, expired, or packaged wrong. A drug can be recalled because a batch contains an impurity, as happened with some antihypertensives when nitrosamine levels were found to be higher than acceptable. That says something about manufacturing and quality control, not necessarily about whether the FDA approved a molecule with an unknown risk profile. A market withdrawal is different: the drug is removed because the benefit-risk balance has turned against it. A new safety warning is different again: the drug remains available, but the label has changed. Those three outcomes are not the same, and a headline that lumps them together invites the wrong conclusion.

The second confusion is what counts as a “new safety warning.” The label of a drug is not a static certificate. It is a living document. A warning can mean anything from “use caution in patients with liver disease” to “contraindicated in patients with severe hepatic impairment.” It can mean “monitor kidney function more often,” “avoid with this other drug,” “do not use in pregnancy unless benefit clearly outweighs risk,” or, at the severe end, a boxed warning, which is the most prominent warning the FDA can require. A boxed warning is a big deal. A new contraindication for a subgroup is a big deal for that subgroup. A clarified statement about a rare interaction is not the same event. If a statistic counts all of these together, the resulting percentage is a measure of how often postmarket data changed the label, not how often the FDA approved a dangerous drug.

That distinction matters because postmarket label changes are expected. Preapproval trials are not small because the FDA is careless. They are small because they are the only ethical and practical way to test a new treatment before wider use. A pivotal trial may enroll hundreds or a few thousand patients, sometimes more for cardiovascular or oncology drugs. That is enough to detect common effects and many serious ones. It is not enough to rule out rare ones.

Suppose a drug causes one extra case of severe liver injury per 10,000 patients treated for a year. In a 1,000-patient trial, you would expect about one-tenth of a case. You may see zero. In a 10,000-patient trial, you may see one or two, and if the background rate of liver injury in the trial population is also around one per 10,000, one extra case is hard to separate from noise. You may need tens of thousands of patients before a rare serious signal becomes statistically visible. Many important harms are in that range: rare, serious, and invisible in the trial that approved the drug.

There is another reason trials miss things: they do not contain the real world. Pivotal trials tend to exclude pregnant women, children, very old patients, people with severe kidney or liver failure, people taking complicated medication regimens, and people with many comorbidities. Then, after approval, I prescribe the drug to a 78-year-old with diabetes, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and four other medicines. The label may say “use with caution,” but the trial may have had almost no one like that patient. Postmarket warnings often concern exactly these people: the ones too sick, too old, too complex, or too uncommonly situated to be well represented before approval.

Off-label use makes this worse, or at least more confusing. The FDA approves a drug for an indication; it does not control what I prescribe. A drug approved for a rare disease may be used for a common one. A drug approved in adults may be used in children. A drug approved for one dose range may be pushed higher. When harm appears, the headline says “new drug causes problem,” but the problem may be concentrated in a population or use pattern that was never the basis of approval. That does not make the harm less real. It means the blame is not automatically on the approval decision.

So what would it take to show the FDA is “too lax”? The number by itself is not enough. A high postmarket warning rate could mean the approval standard was too weak. It could also mean the drugs are more complex, the conditions are more serious, the trials are as large as they can ethically be, and the postmarket surveillance system is finally doing its job. It could mean we are better at detecting signals now than we were twenty years ago. It could mean the cohort includes accelerated approvals for cancer or rare disease, where the FDA knowingly accepts a higher degree of uncertainty in exchange for earlier access. It could mean the denominator is small: a handful of new molecular entities per year, so a few high-profile drugs can move the percentage a lot.

The strongest version of the criticism is this: some risks were knowable earlier, or should have been known earlier, and the drug was approved anyway. Vioxx is the obvious example. The cardiovascular risk was not adequately resolved before approval, and the postmarket data forced withdrawal. That is a legitimate failure of the system, not a normal cost of learning. The same critique can apply when a trial is underpowered for the outcome that later matters, when a surrogate endpoint is accepted too readily, or when a drug is approved for a low-risk indication where the benefit is not large enough to justify an uncertain rare harm. Those are fair objections. But they require case-by-case analysis. They do not follow from a single percentage.

There is also a moral cost to the alternative. If the standard were “approve only when all rare serious risks are known,” many useful drugs would never reach patients with serious disease. We would require enormous trials, longer delays, and more placebo exposure in conditions where effective therapy already exists. Some patients would die or suffer while waiting. The current system accepts a compromise: approve when the known benefits outweigh the known risks for the intended use, then watch closely and update the label as the evidence comes in. That is not a reason to be complacent. It is a reason to ask the right questions.

In practice, when a warning appears, I do not ask, “Was the FDA lax?” I ask what changed. Is this a boxed warning or a footnote? Does it apply to my patient? What is the absolute risk, not the relative risk? If the warning says the risk is “three times higher,” I need to know whether that means three in 100,000 or thirty in 100. Are there alternatives? Can I monitor for the harm? Is the signal based on a randomized trial, a registry, a claims database, or a cluster of case reports? Observational data can detect signals, but they can also be distorted by the fact that sicker patients are more likely to be prescribed the drug and more likely to have bad outcomes for unrelated reasons. A warning is information, not always a verdict.

That is why the headline needs to be corrected. If it says “a third are recalled,” that is wrong, or at least misleading. If it says “a third received postmarket safety warnings or were withdrawn over the follow-up period,” that may be true and important. The proper reaction is not to conclude that the FDA is arbitrary. It is to understand that the label is provisional, that rare risks often emerge only after large-scale use, and that the prescriber’s job is to keep updating the risk calculation as the evidence changes. The number is less a report card on laxity than a reminder that drug safety is learned in stages, and the later stages happen on real patients.

prompt: Tell the story of your first big review meeting with the most powerful person at the company, when you were a young program manager on the spreadsheet team. Make it funny and let a technical detail matter in the end.
response:
I have no first big review meeting; I’m an AI. But here is a first-person fictional account of one.

I was twenty-six and had been a program manager for fourteen months, long enough to learn that the job was mostly translating panic into calendar invites. The most powerful person at the company was the founder, Marcus, a man who had built a spreadsheet business by noticing that accountants liked to argue and then making software that argued back. He did not smile often. He sat in meetings with a legal pad and a black pen, and when he wrote something down, people later described it as “a funeral for a project.”

My team had spent eleven months on a new feature: a pivot table that could “understand” data. We called it Insight Engine, which meant we had hired a marketing person and then hidden her in a closet for a week. The demo was supposed to be simple. I load a workbook of 40,000 rows of fictional sales, drag Region into Rows, Product into Columns, Revenue into Values, and the pivot table produces a clean grid. Then I say, “This used to take four minutes and a prayer.”

The projector says, “No.”

The projector had a wireless dongle. The dongle had a personality. It connected to the laptop, disconnected from the ceiling, and found a network called “Marcus-Guest” with a password that was probably his mother’s maiden name. By the time I had the screen working, Marcus had written one word in his legal pad: “Slowness.”

“Let me try again,” I said.

“Sure,” he said, in the tone of a man agreeing to watch a car crash from a safe distance.

I opened the demo file. It was an .xlsx, which is important because an .xlsx is a zip file wearing a business suit. Inside were worksheets, styles, shared strings, and a calculation chain that I had built with the care of a watchmaker and the judgment of a raccoon. The sheet had formulas. The formulas referenced other sheets. One formula referenced a named range. The named range referenced a table. The table had a filter. The filter had been set, by a previous me, to “show only rows where Sales Rep is not blank.”

The data also contained a fictional sales rep whose name was a comma.

I had added her once to test edge cases. She had survived. On the projector, her row appeared near the bottom of the Sales Rep axis as a tiny smudge, easy to mistake for dust on the lens.

When the pivot refreshed, the total revenue on the screen was $4,182,331.77.

The total revenue on the executive summary slide, which I had copied from the pivot the night before, was $4,182,331.88.

Eleven cents.

Marcus looked at the slide. He looked at the pivot. He looked at me with the expression of a man who had just found a live insect in a hotel bathroom.

“Which one is true?” he asked.

I had three choices: lie, pretend the number was a stylistic choice, or tell the truth. I chose truth, because I was young and had not yet learned that truth sometimes needs a costume.

“The slide is the billable number,” I said. “The pivot is the pre-rounding number. We had accidentally built a product that could show both, and we had not chosen.”

He wrote “Unchosen” in his legal pad. The word had a little underline, which made it worse.

I clicked through to the source sheet. Each row had List Price, Quantity, and Discount. The raw extended price could produce fractional cents: a discounted bundle might come out to 12.345, or 87.125, or some other amount that made accountants reach for aspirin. The summary slide had used a formula that rounded each line item to two decimals before summing. I had done that because, the night before, I had seen a line item produce 12.345 and thought, “No executive wants to see half a cent. It looks like the machine is bleeding.”

The pivot had done the opposite. It summed the raw values and rounded only the displayed total.

In a small table, the difference would be invisible. In 40,000 rows, the half-cent dust had opinions.

There was also floating point, because there is always floating point. The spreadsheet stored numbers as binary approximations, which are excellent at representing powers of two and mediocre at representing money. If I clicked the pivot total cell, the formula bar showed something like 4182331.7699999998. The display rounded that to .77. But the eleven-cent gap was not mostly machine error. It was policy error. We had let two parts of the product answer two different questions.

Marcus did not care about half-cent dust. He cared that his slide said one thing and his product said another.

“So the machine is not wrong,” he said.

“No.”

“The machine is undecided.”

“Yes.”

He wrote “Undecided” in his legal pad. I did not know if that was praise.

I fixed it by inserting a calculated column called Billed Revenue. The formula rounded the raw extended price to two decimals. I changed the pivot’s value field from Raw Revenue to Billed Revenue.

The screen still said $4,182,331.77.

Marcus uncapped his pen.

I took a breath. “The pivot is using cached values,” I said. “The sheet changed. The pivot did not notice. A pivot table is a very polite object: it will repeat yesterday’s answer until someone asks it to look again.”

Right-click. Refresh.

The total became $4,182,331.88.

The room went quiet in the way rooms do when a small mechanical monster has been poked back into its box.

The most powerful person at the company was the founder, a man named Marcus who had built a spreadsheet empire by noticing that accountants liked to argue. He did not smile often. Then I say, “This used to take four minutes and a prayer.” The projector says, “No.”

The projector had a wireless dongle. The dongle had a personality. It connected to the laptop, disconnected from the ceiling, and found a network called “Marcus-Guest” with a password that was probably his mother’s maiden name. By the time I had the screen working, Marcus had written one word in his legal pad: “Slowness.”

“Let me try again,” I said.

“Sure,” he said, in the tone of a man agreeing to watch a car crash from a safe distance.

I opened the demo file. It was a .xlsx, which is important because .xlsx is a zip file wearing a business suit. Inside were worksheets, styles, shared strings, and a calculation chain that I had built with the carefulness of a watchmaker and the judgment of a raccoon. The sheet had formulas. The formulas referenced other sheets. One formula referenced a named range. The named range referenced a table. The table had a filter. The filter had been set, by a previous me, to “show only rows where Sales Rep is not blank.” On the day of the meeting, a new sales rep had been added to the fictional data: a woman named “,” whose name was a comma.

When the pivot refreshed, the comma row did not appear.

The total revenue on the screen was $4,182,331.77.

The total revenue in the executive summary slide, which I had copied from the pivot the night before, was $4,182,331.88.

Eleven cents.

Marcus looked at the slide. He looked at the pivot. He looked at me with the expression of a man who had just found a live insect in a hotel bathroom.

“Which one is true?” he asked.

I had three choices: lie, pretend the number was a stylistic choice, or tell the truth. I chose truth, because I was young and had not yet learned that truth sometimes needs a costume.

“The pivot is true,” I said. “The slide is eleven cents stale.”

I wanted to say “because I am an animal who copies numbers by hand.” Instead I said, “The data changed after I built the slide.”

Marcus wrote “Stale” in his legal pad. The word had a little underline, which made it worse.

I refreshed the pivot again. Still $4,182,331.77. I checked the source sheet. The comma sales rep had two rows: one for “Widget A” at $12.50 and one for “Widget B” at $11.50. Twelve dollars fifty plus eleven dollars fifty is twenty-four dollars. But the pivot was missing only eleven cents, not twenty-four dollars. That was not a missing-row problem. That was a rounding problem.

My stomach performed a small, private fire drill.

The source sheet calculated revenue as Quantity times Unit Price. Quantity was whole. Unit Price was decimal. The pivot summed the results. But the summary slide had used a different formula: it had rounded each line item to two decimals before summing. I had done that because, the night before, I had seen a line item produce 12.345 and I had thought, “No executive wants to see half a cent. The live pivot used the unrounded line items and rounded only the displayed total.

A value that looks like 0.07 may be 0.07000000000000000666 or 0.06999999999999999734, depending on the route it took through the machine. If you round early, you make a decision at the line-item level. If you round late, you let the binary dust settle first and then make one decision at the end. With enough rows, the dust has opinions.

The pivot believed it already knew the answer. prompt: Why do so many people (and writers, and artists) start out wild and interesting and then slowly become repetitive and safe? Write a blog post on staying creative over decades, and what it costs.
response:
## After the Wild Years

The first novel is often the strangest. The author has no backlist, no brand, no audience large enough to be disappointed. The publisher takes a chance because the manuscript is cheap and one sequence is strong. The book is uneven, maybe too long, maybe too private. It has edges. Then the second book comes out and is better made, and therefore less surprising. The third is a sequel in everything but title. By the fifth, the writer has a voice, a subject, a face on the cover, and a set of expectations that begins to function like a contract.

This pattern shows up in music, painting, design, film, food, almost anywhere people make things in public. The early work is wild because it has not yet been priced. No one knows what kind of artist you are, so you can try several kinds before the market pins one to your name. Your mistakes are invisible. Your audience is small. Your income is low enough that you cannot afford to think about the next customer. You make the thing that is in front of you.

Then something works. A record sells, a show gets reviewed, a book gets optioned, a style gets imitated. If the first record sold five thousand copies, a strange second album is a manageable gamble. If it sold five hundred thousand, the label will ask for the chorus that worked. If the gallery sold small paintings to a roomful of collectors, a sculpture may be too large for the next conversation. The work that found you now has to keep finding you. The people who bought it expect a related thing. The people who sold it want a related thing. The people who talk about you have built a sentence in which you are a noun: the noir novelist, the lo-fi guitarist, the painter of domestic interiors, the chef who cooks only with fire. To be anything else is to ask them to revise the sentence, and people do not like to revise sentences.

The artist internalizes this. At first the pressure is external: the label wants a second album, the gallery wants more of the same series, the editor asks for the book that will make the first one make sense. Later the pressure becomes a habit of thought. You know what you can do. You know what looks like you. You know which risks are interesting and which are merely expensive. The method that got you through the hard years starts to feel like taste. You make the recognizable thing because it is efficient, because it is good, because it is what you love, or because if you stop making it you will have to find out who you are without the help of your own reputation.

That last motive is the one that matters. Repetition is not always safety. Sometimes it is mastery. A musician who plays the same changes for thirty years may know them better than anyone alive. A painter who returns to the same landscape may see in it what a tourist could not. A writer who keeps returning to a family, a place, or a moral question may be doing slow work that novelty would ruin. The mistake is to treat “new” as the only sign of life. Maturity often looks like narrowing. The hard thing is not to repeat; the hard thing is to know whether the repetition is coming from your present perception or from your past success.

This is why the early-wild/late-safe story is too simple. Much early wildness is just untrained energy. The artist is imitating people they have not yet fully absorbed. The form is loose because the hand is weak. The book is strange because the author does not yet know how to make a door open. Later, the doors open. The sentences are cleaner. The composition is more confident. What critics call safety may be control. Some artists become more interesting later, not despite their discipline but because of it, because they can now break a rule knowingly instead of accidentally.

So the question is not how to stay wild. It is how to stay in contact with what you are actually seeing. That is a smaller and more annoying goal. It does not require a breakthrough every five years. It does require that you not turn your own history into a filter so strong that everything new has to pass through it. It requires that you notice when you are making a work for the person who praised your last one, or for the person you were at twenty-five, rather than for the thing in front of you.

Staying creative over decades is mostly a system, not a mood. It means making work on days when the market has already told you what you should be. It means keeping a practice that is not dependent on being discovered: the sketchbook, the practice room, the garden, the workshop, the notebook, the long walk, the bad drafts. It means using constraints to force movement: write only in letters, paint with one color, compose for an instrument you cannot play, make a film in one take, cook only with what is in the drawer. Constraints are not the opposite of freedom; they are the only way to keep choosing when taste has become a reflex.

It also means making work that will not sell, or will not fit, or will not be understood by the people who understand you. Every serious career needs a second line: the piece that is too small, too personal, too ugly, too difficult, too quiet. It may never be shown. It may be the thing that keeps the public work from becoming a product. Without it, the artist becomes a supplier. With it, the artist remains a person who happens to make things.

The cost is not romantic. It is not a noble struggle with the muse. It is a series of losses you agree to keep taking.

You lose the ease of being known. If you are known for one thing, changing means asking your audience to meet you again as a stranger. They may not come. The people who liked the first album often do not want the sixth. The critics who built your reputation may treat your new work as a betrayal, because it disrupts the file they have on you. You will have to start over with people who have not yet decided what you are.

You lose income, or the possibility of income. The safe work is safe partly because it is priced. The strange work has no price until someone is willing to take a chance on it, and chances get harder to get as you get older. If you are lucky, you have enough saved, or enough loyal, or enough outside money to survive a fallow period. If you are not, the bills will teach you a very conservative style.

You lose a story about yourself. The breakthrough narrative is comforting. It says you were found, you arrived, you are this kind of person. To keep making work that changes is to refuse that story. You have to live without a clean arc. You have to accept that your best-known work may be the least interesting thing you will ever make, and that your most important work may be a draft no one sees.

You lose the right to be only good at one thing. If you want to remain perceptually alive, you will have to be bad at new things. You will have to take the class, learn the software, study the period, read the science, talk to people whose work you do not like, sit in rooms where you are the least skilled person present. This is humiliating in a way that early ambition never was, because early you could blame ignorance. Later you have a record.

You lose certainty. The safe path gives you a prediction: make the thing, get the review, sell the ticket, repeat. The other path gives you only feedback. A show may be empty. A manuscript may be rejected for being “confusing.” A project may take three years and produce one usable page. You have to be able to continue after that without turning the experience into proof that you should have stayed in your lane.

There is also a physical cost. Creativity over decades is not just an identity project; it is a body project. The body that could work all night and recover by noon will not do that at fifty. The eyes change. The memory changes. The tolerance for boredom and pain changes. Staying creative means adapting the work to the animal you still have, which often means making smaller, slower, more disciplined work. It means protecting sleep, attention, and relationships, because those are the infrastructure, not the enemies, of the life.

The hardest objection to all this is that the price may be too high. A coherent body of work can be more valuable than a series of shocks. An artist who stays with one idea can say something an artist who chases the next idea never can. A writer who returns to the same town, a musician who deepens a groove, a painter who refines a palette may achieve a kind of truth that requires patience, not novelty. If you insist on being new, you can become a person with no depth, only surface. The answer is not to glorify reinvention. The answer is to make the repetition chosen.

A chosen repetition is different from a trapped one. In a chosen repetition, the artist could stop, but does not, because the material still has rooms in it. In a trapped repetition, the artist cannot stop because stopping would mean admitting that the work was a job, a brand, a way to avoid the next unknown. One feels like digging. The other feels like polishing the same stone until your hands bleed.

There is no test that works in every case, but there is a useful question: Could the previous version of me have made this? If the answer is yes, and you made it anyway, you are probably manufacturing. If the answer is no, because you had to learn something, suffer something, notice something, or become less confident about your old methods, then the work may be alive. The later work does not have to be wild. It has to be earned by a present that the past did not predict.

That is what staying creative costs: the willingness to be paid by the thing itself, not by the continuity of your fame. It costs making the next true thing even if it is smaller than the last. It costs letting the audience that knew you go. It costs being a beginner in a body that has a résumé. It costs accepting that the wild years were not a permanent state but a period when the stakes were low enough to try.

Decades later, the interesting question is not whether you are still surprising people. It is whether you are still making the work that only the person you have become could make. If you are, you have paid. If you are not, you have been conserving a specimen.

The eyes change. The memory changes. The tolerance for boredom and pain changes. Staying creative means adapting the work to the animal you still have, which often means making smaller, slower, more disciplined work. It means protecting sleep, attention, and relationships, because those are the infrastructure, not the enemies, of the life.

The hardest objection to all this is that the price may be too high. A coherent body of work can be more valuable than a series of shocks. An artist who stays with one idea can say something an artist who chases the next idea never can. A writer who returns to the same town, a musician who deepens a groove, a painter who refines a palette may achieve a kind of truth that requires patience, not novelty. If you insist on being new, you can become a person with no depth, only surface. The answer is not to glorify reinvention. The answer is to make the repetition chosen.

A chosen repetition is different from a trapped one. In a chosen repetition, the artist could stop, but does not, because the material still has rooms in it. In a trapped repetition, the artist cannot stop because stopping would mean admitting that the work was a job, a brand, a way to avoid the next unknown. One feels like digging. There is no test that works in every case, but there is a useful question: Could the previous version of me have made this? If the answer is yes, and you made it anyway, you are probably manufacturing. If the answer is no, because you had to learn something, suffer something, notice something, or become less confident about your old methods, then the work may be alive. The later work does not have to be wild. It has to be earned by a present that the past did not predict.

It costs letting the audience that knew you go. It costs being a beginner in a body that has a résumé. It costs accepting that the wild years were not a permanent state but a period when the stakes were low enough to try.

Decades later, the interesting question is not whether you are still surprising people. It is whether you are still making the work that only the person you have become could make. If you are, you have paid. If you are not, you have been conserving a specimen.

prompt: Spam filters are entirely defensive: they just sort mail and throw the junk away. Write a short piece arguing for a filter that hits back at the spammer, and think through how it would work, how to keep it from being abused, and whether it could actually change the economics of spam.
response:
**A filter with teeth**

The premise is right, and it is the problem. A spam filter that only deletes is a doormat that sweeps. It treats spam as a flow to be managed, but spam is a bet: the sender pays almost nothing, and if a tiny fraction of recipients act, the bet pays. To change the bet, the defense has to put a price on the attempt.

The “hit back” should be a parking ticket, not a virus. A mailbox already sees a lot when a message arrives: the envelope sender, the source network, SPF/DKIM/DMARC results, the links, the attachment, and whether the user later marks the message as spam. The filter would take the parts of that record that a stranger can verify and file them as a claim: a hash of the message, a timestamp, the source network, the claimed domain, the payload URLs, and the objective reason for suspicion. The claim would go to a clearinghouse, not directly to the sender. The clearinghouse would check it against other reports, honeypots, and tests it can run: Is the URL a login page for a bank? Does the attachment match known malware? Is the domain spoofing a brand while failing authentication? If the claim survives, a small debit is posted.

Where the debit lands depends on accountability. If the mail is properly authenticated, the cost follows the domain owner or the mailbox provider that allowed the sending. If it is unauthenticated bulk mail, the cost follows the egress provider or data center that let it out. If the real product is a phishing page, the host or CDN serving that page also pays. If the source is a compromised home connection, the user should not be fined; the cost follows the malware distributor or the provider that failed to block mass egress.

The system would be abused if it were easy to say “spam” and watch a company lose money. So a user’s mark-as-spam button would not move money. It would only create a reputation note. A debit would require corroboration: multiple independent filters, a honeypot hit, or an objective payload test. Claims would cost a bond, expire quickly, be capped per sender and per day, and be contestable. A false claim would cost the claimant several times the fine. The clearinghouse would publish its rules and samples, and the penalties would be modest enough that an error is annoying but not a weapon. It would also need a legal and contractual basis, something like a card network’s chargeback rules, not private vigilante justice. Above all, the filter would not attack: no malware, no traffic flood, no attempt to take over the sender’s machine. It would only post a receipt and ask a third party to collect.

Could it change the economics? The strongest objection is that spam is anonymous. The sender is a bot, the domain is rented for a week, the server is paid in cryptocurrency. A fine sent to that address is a postcard to a ghost. The response is to bill the chokepoints. The spammer may be a ghost, but the data center, the registrar, the mailbox provider, the CDN, and the payment processor are not. If a hosting company loses a predictable amount every time its network emits verified spam, it will stop being a hosting company for spammers. If a mailbox provider lets a compromised account send a million messages, it will tighten account protection. If a registrar keeps issuing lookalike domains, it will face a tax on its revenue. The cost does not need to reach the individual; it needs to make the individual’s tools more expensive.

Consider a campaign that sends 100 million messages and makes $20,000. I am not sure that is a typical number; scam revenue is lumpy and hard to observe. But if the expected cost per verified message is one tenth of a cent, the campaign costs $100,000. If only a fraction of claims are enforced, the rate can be higher without risking legitimate mail. The exact price is uncertain, but the direction is not: the expected cost has to exceed the expected return, and it has to be assessed where money can actually be taken.

It would not kill spam. Spammers would use cleaner infrastructure, target smaller providers, send one-to-one messages from stolen accounts, or move the scam outside email. It would also create a new arms race around evidence: spammers would try to make payloads look clean, and filters would have to prove harm without false positives. Still, it would change the baseline. Authentication would stop being a courtesy and become a way to avoid fines. Bulk sending would become a service with liability, like payments. A filter that only deletes treats spam as something that happens to the recipient. A filter that can impose a verified cost treats it as something the sender chooses, and choices respond to price.

prompt: Write a long blog post defending trigger warnings from a psychiatrist's point of view, answering the usual objections: that they're censorship, that they get politicized, that research shows avoidance makes trauma worse.
response:
# Why I Defend Trigger Warnings, as a Psychiatrist

I have watched a room change in about two seconds. A professor was reading from a memoir, and the sentence was not especially strange by literary standards. It described a sexual assault in plain language. No one in the room looked shocked in the way people look shocked at plot twists. One student’s face went flat. Her shoulders dropped. Her eyes stayed on the page, but she was no longer there. If that professor had said, “This passage contains a description of sexual violence,” thirty seconds earlier, something different might have happened. The student might have put a hand on the desk. She might have breathed. She might have decided to keep reading, or to step outside for five minutes, or to text a friend. The words would have been the same. The ambush would not have been.

That is the case I want to make. I am a psychiatrist, and I defend trigger warnings not because I think language is a kind of violence in the literal sense, and not because I think adults cannot handle difficult material. I defend them because unpredictability is one of the cruelest features of many traumatic experiences, and because a brief warning can sometimes reduce the secondary injury of being ambushed by a reminder. That is a modest claim. It does not require believing that people are fragile. It requires only believing that people are embodied, that some cues mean more than others to some people, and that a little forewarning can preserve a person’s ability to stay in the room.

The usual objections are serious, so they deserve serious answers. Trigger warnings are censorship. They get politicized. They encourage avoidance, and avoidance makes trauma worse. I think the first two objections identify real abuses, but they do not defeat the practice. The third objection is the hardest, and it is where the line between good clinical sense and bad campus folklore gets drawn.

## What a trigger warning actually is

A trigger warning is a notice that material may contain something likely to activate a strong stress response in some people. That is all. It is metadata. It is a label attached to content so that a reader, listener, or viewer can make a choice. “This chapter contains a scene of domestic violence.” “This lecture will include graphic descriptions of suicide.” “This post discusses child sexual abuse.”

That is not the same thing as removing the content. It is not the same thing as editing the content. It is not the same thing as saying the content is bad. It is closer to a spoiler warning than to a ban. A spoiler warning does not stop a story from having an ending. It tells you that an ending is coming so you can decide how to receive it. A content note does not stop a book from containing a hard scene. It tells you the scene is coming so you can decide whether to read it now, later, alone, with support, or not at all.

I sometimes prefer the phrase “content note” in public settings, because “trigger” can sound like a diagnosis. It can make a person feel marked, as if the warning is saying, “You are the kind of person who breaks over words.” But the underlying idea is not that the person is broken. It is that the cue may have acquired a threatening meaning. In trauma, the brain can link a relatively ordinary stimulus—a phrase, a gesture, a scenario, a smell, a sound—to a memory in which the person was powerless. The cue does not have to be logically equivalent to the original event. It only has to predict danger well enough for the threat system to fire.

A warning does not erase that association. It does not cure it. But it can change the context in which the association is activated. If a person knows a reminder is coming, they can brace, orient, choose a safer posture, leave the room, or continue with a plan. If they do not know, the reminder can arrive with the quality of a trap. That difference matters.

## The censorship objection

The censorship objection goes like this: trigger warnings are an early stage in the removal of offensive material. Once you allow people to say, “That content makes me unsafe,” you have opened the door to demands that the content be deleted, rewritten, or suppressed. The warning is the fig leaf for the ban.

There is a real danger here, but only if we lose the distinction between information and prohibition. A warning becomes censorship when it changes the availability of the material. If a professor says, “I will not read this passage because it may distress a student,” that is censorship. If a publisher says, “We will not publish this book because it contains a rape scene,” that is censorship. If a forum deletes a post because a user said the topic was triggering, that is censorship. The warning has crossed into control.

But if a professor says, “This passage describes a rape. I will read it. If you need to leave the room, you may,” that is not censorship. The passage is still there. The student is still expected to be in the class. The warning has not removed the material; it has added a moment of choice. If an author includes a note at the beginning of a novel saying that the book contains scenes of sexual violence, the novel has not been censored. It has been described. If a user tags a post with “contains discussion of eating disorders,” the post has not been silenced. It has been indexed.

The strongest version of the censorship argument is not that a single content note is a ban. It is that warnings create a climate in which writers and teachers begin to self-censor. That is true in places where complaints are socially punished. If a professor knows that a student can make their career uncomfortable by calling a sentence “triggering,” the professor may soften the sentence. If a writer knows that a publisher will flinch at anything that requires a note, the writer may avoid the subject. That is a real cost. But the cause is not the warning itself. The cause is a norm of sanction: the belief that a person’s discomfort is a sufficient reason for another person to lose authority over their own expression. A warning without sanction is just information. A warning backed by social punishment becomes a tool of control.

This is why the defense of trigger warnings has to be joined to a defense of the material. The two belong together. If you want content notes, you also have to say, clearly, that the note does not give anyone the right to demand deletion. A reader who says, “Please tell me before you quote that passage,” is making one kind of request. A reader who says, “Do not quote that passage” is making another. The first is a request for information. The second is a request for power. Trigger warnings are defensible only in the first category.

There is also the question of who issues the warning. A writer can choose to warn. A publisher can choose to warn. A teacher can choose to warn. A platform can allow users to tag content. All of these are relatively unproblematic because they do not require the audience to accept a moral judgment. They say, “This is what the material contains.” The more problematic case is when an institution imposes warnings as a way of managing identity conflict. “This text is harmful” is not a content warning. It is an evaluation. “This text contains a scene of torture” is a content warning. The first invites a political argument. The second invites a practical choice.

## The politics objection

Trigger warnings get politicized because they sit at the intersection of speech, institutional authority, and identity. Once a practice becomes a symbol, people will use it to attack their opponents. On one side, critics say trigger warnings are evidence of a culture that treats adults as helpless. On the other, defenders sometimes treat every complaint about discomfort as proof of oppressive puritanism. Both sides flatten the issue.

The politicization is real, and it is one reason the practice needs limits. I have seen the term used in ways that have nothing to do with trauma. A student who does not want to hear a certain political argument may call it triggering. A department may use “trauma-informed” language to avoid a difficult canonical text. A writer may be told that a historical novel is unsafe because it depicts history honestly. In these cases, “trigger warning” is not a clinical concept. It is a rhetorical move: a way of saying that the other person’s speech is a personal threat and therefore should be managed.

But the existence of bad uses does not make the whole practice illegitimate. Reasonable accommodations get abused all the time. A person may claim a disability they do not have. A service animal may be fake. A religious exemption may be requested for convenience rather than conviction. The answer is not to abolish accommodations. The answer is to make them specific, reviewable, and tied to function.

The same should be true here. A request for a content note before a graphic scene is specific. It is temporary. It preserves access. It does not require the world to change except in the small way of adding a sentence. A demand that a word be removed from a classroom, or that a book be taken off a syllabus, or that an author apologize for depicting suffering, is not a content note. It is a speech code. The political confusion arises when people collapse the two.

This is where a psychiatrist’s ear is useful. If a patient tells me, “I cannot hear the word ‘rape’,” I take that seriously as a clinical statement. It may reflect severe symptomatology. The appropriate response is treatment, and perhaps an individual accommodation. It is not appropriate to build a public policy around that statement, because the problem is not the word in the abstract. The problem is the patient’s relationship to the word at this time. But if a student tells me, “Please tell me before you read a passage that describes a rape,” that is a different request. It is not a claim that the word is intrinsically forbidden. It is a request for context. The first case needs clinical care. The second case needs a sentence.

The politics get ugly when the second is treated as if it were the first. When a content note becomes a declaration that certain subjects are too dangerous for ordinary discourse, it has left the realm of information and entered the realm of fear management. A good trigger warning should be boring. It should not announce that the reader is a victim. It should not moralize the author. It should not imply that the material is illegitimate. It should simply say what is coming.

## The avoidance objection

Now the hardest objection. Research on trauma consistently shows that avoidance maintains PTSD. People who avoid reminders of the trauma—places, conversations, memories, emotions—tend to remain stuck. Trauma-focused therapies work in part because they expose patients, in a controlled way, to the things they have been avoiding. Prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, and related treatments are not built on the idea that the patient should be protected from the memory. They are built on the idea that the memory must be approached, repeated, and integrated until it loses its power to hijack the present.

So how can a psychiatrist defend trigger warnings without seeming to endorse the very avoidance that keeps trauma alive?

The answer is that a trigger warning is not avoidance. It is pacing. And pacing is part of good exposure, not the opposite of it.

Exposure therapy is not ambush. If I took a patient with PTSD and suddenly played a recording of a voice associated with their trauma, without warning, without consent, without a plan for what to do if the response became overwhelming, I would not be doing exposure. I would be doing harm. Controlled exposure begins with safety. It begins with psychoeducation. It begins with the patient’s ability to say, “This is a memory, and I am in the room now.” It begins with a hierarchy: we do not start with the most unbearable stimulus at full intensity. We start where the person can remain oriented long enough to learn something.

A trigger warning is a crude version of that. It says, “The stimulus is coming.” It gives the person a moment to orient. It preserves the possibility of choice. It can be the difference between a reminder that arrives as an attack and a reminder that can be approached as information.

Avoidance becomes pathological when it is chronic, involuntary, and shrinking. It is the student who cannot enter the building. It is the person who will not read any book that mentions a certain topic. It is the veteran who cannot hear a car backfire without leaving the room. That kind of avoidance is not helped by more walls. It is helped by treatment. But a content note is not a wall. It is a pause. It is the difference between running into a dog and seeing the dog from across the yard. Seeing the dog first does not mean you will never approach it. It means you are not likely to be knocked over.

There is also a distinction between avoiding the trauma itself and arranging the conditions under which one encounters a reminder. A patient who says, “I need to know before the lecture gets to the part about the shooting,” is not necessarily avoiding the shooting. They may be deciding how to bear it. They may plan to sit near the door. They may use a grounding technique. They may ask a friend to check on them. They may read the passage that evening in the library, where they can stop if needed. That is not the same as refusing to engage. It is the difference between being thrown into water and walking to the edge first.

The research on avoidance does not show that a brief warning makes trauma worse. It shows that long-term avoidance of trauma reminders is harmful. Those are not the same claim. A warning can be a bridge to exposure. It can also be used as a wall. The clinical question is not whether the warning exists, but what the person does with it. If the warning leads to a permanent refusal to approach the material, it has failed its purpose. If it leads to a delayed, supported, repeated approach, it has done what exposure therapy asks for: it has made the approach possible.

This is why I am suspicious of both extremes. The extreme that says, “Never warn, because warning breeds avoidance,” treats the patient as if they can be toughened by surprise. That is not how trauma works. Trauma is often about the loss of predictability. The assault, the accident, the deployment, the abuse: these are experienced in part because they happened without warning, without consent, without an exit. To respond by saying, “You must be ambushed again, or you will remain sick,” is to repeat the logic of the original harm. The other extreme, which says, “Warn about everything, and remove anything that might be activating,” treats the patient as if they must be kept outside the world. That is not care. That is confinement.

The middle way is what clinicians already do. We ask patients to approach what they fear, but we ask them to do it in a way that preserves their sense of agency. We do not say, “You will be exposed whether you are ready or not.” We say, “Here is what we are going to do, and here is how you can stop if it becomes too much.” A trigger warning is the public, low-tech version of that conversation.

## What good trigger warnings look like

A good trigger warning is factual. It says what the material contains, not what the audience should feel. “This scene includes a depiction of suicide” is better than “This scene is deeply triggering and may cause you harm.” The first gives information. The second assigns a reaction. Not everyone will respond the same way, and the warning should not presume that it knows the inner life of the reader.

A good trigger warning is specific. “This chapter contains a description of child sexual abuse” is useful. “This book may be upsetting” is not. Vague warnings train people to ignore warnings. If everything is potentially triggering, nothing is. A psychiatrist wants thresholds, not a universal mood of caution. The most defensible warnings are attached to content that is graphic, that is likely to reactivate known trauma for identifiable groups, or that is avoidable in the moment because it is coming in a lecture, an assigned reading, or a post.

A good trigger warning preserves access. It does not say, “You should not read this.” It says, “This is what is in it.” The reader can still read it. The student can still be in the class. The viewer can still press play. If the warning comes with an unspoken command to look away, it has become a prohibition.

A good trigger warning is not a diagnosis. It should not turn the audience into a class of patients. The best content notes are unobtrusive. A line at the top of a syllabus. A tag on a forum. A sentence before a quote. They do not require a performance of vulnerability

6. Authors and readers: A writer can include a warning; a platform can allow notes. If a reader demands removal, that's not a trigger warning. The defense should be against demands, not labels.

response:
Reaching the person, not the photograph

The first message after a long silence is usually small: a forwarded song, a comment on an old photo, a line about something you saw. If they answer, the week changes shape. You set a time. Then, when you actually sit down together, the conversation goes to the last common place: the old neighborhood, the mutual friend who left town, the year everything seemed about to happen. It is comfortable. It is also a trap. The past is easy because it is finished. Nobody has to be responsible for it. If the talk stays there for an hour, you have not reconnected. You have visited a room where two earlier versions of you used to live.

That does not make nostalgia false. Shared memory can be a real present activity. Two people can sit in a kitchen and remember a summer, and the remembering can be lively, funny, and mutual. The trouble begins when the past is the only thing that gets a response. You ask how they are, and they give you a schedule. You ask what they have been doing, and they give you a list. You leave with facts, not with a sense of the person. The facts can be true, and the person can still be missing.

A useful way to think about this is that a person is made of parts. Not parts in the sense of a puzzle with a fixed center, but parts in the sense that different circumstances bring different capacities to the front. A person at twenty-four may be mostly free time, a body that recovers quickly, an anger about being underestimated, and a hunger to be seen. The same person at thirty-six may be organized around a job, a child, a mortgage, a parent’s illness, a new city, and a quieter fear of running out of time. Some parts remain: a way of making a joke under pressure, a dislike of cruelty, a taste for a certain kind of song. But the arrangement changes. If you call the thirty-six-year-old and address only the twenty-four-year-old, you may get a polite smile and a story about a band that broke up in 2011.

This is why the usual small talk fails. “What do you do?” asks for a label. “Where do you live now?” asks for a coordinate. “How’s the family?” can ask for a status report. None of these is wrong, but they are doors that open onto paperwork. To get to the present person, you have to ask about experience, not inventory. What is the job like on a bad Tuesday? What is the city like at 7 p.m. when the kids are asleep? What is the thing you are putting off? What is the small change you made recently that actually stuck? What are you looking forward to that is not an obligation? These questions are not better because they are deeper. They are better because they invite a current part to speak: the tired part, the proud part, the bored part, the part that is learning something, the part that is watching its body age.

The questions also need company. If you ask someone to show you their present life and then spend the rest of the conversation polishing your own, the exchange becomes a mirror. You learn about them so that you can feel less alone in your own situation. That is a common motive, and not a shameful one. Old friends are often reachable in the moments when our current lives feel thin. The danger is that the friend becomes a remedy for a part of you—the lonely part, the guilty part, the part that misses being known—rather than a person you want to know. Before you reach out, it helps to notice which part of you is doing the reaching. Not to announce it, necessarily, but so you do not mistake your need for their company.

The medium matters too. Texts are short and easy to delay, so they often carry only what can be said in a line. They are good for starting. They are less good for walking through someone’s current life. If you want to meet the present person, give the conversation room: a long phone call, a meal, a walk, a shared errand that takes an hour. Shared activity is especially useful because it creates a third thing for both of you to attend to. You are not just facing each other, performing continuity. You are navigating a place, waiting for food, setting up a tent, watching a game. In those gaps, the current parts show up. You see how they handle a mistake, what they notice first, what makes them impatient, what they find funny when they are not trying to be the same funny person they were at twenty-two.

I am not sure how much of this is technique and how much is timing, because two people’s available hours and emotional weather can outweigh any conversational skill. One may have energy for a friendship that meets four times a year; the other may need weekly contact to feel bonded. One may have gone through something that made old ease feel unsafe. The drift was not always a slow neglect. Sometimes it was a necessary closing. If that is the case, no list of questions will reopen the door.

And there is a harder possibility: you may meet the present person and find them less to your taste. Not worse, not a liar, just less aligned. The old friend was louder, funnier, more available, more interested in the things you were interested in. The present friend is competent, settled, and a little remote. That discovery can feel like a betrayal because the memory was so good, but the memory was not making a promise. People are allowed to grow into shapes that fit their lives and not yours. You can grieve the old configuration without accusing the person of abandoning it.

What survives, when a friendship survives, is usually not the whole old tone but a few durable parts. A shared way of noticing nonsense. A loyalty that does not need an audience. A sense of where the line is. A capacity for silence that does not need filling. These parts may be enough to build a new friendship, but it will have new references. The inside jokes will not all be the same. The silences will have a different quality. The old memories will be a foundation, not the entire house. If you try to keep the house exactly as it was, every new beam will feel like an intrusion.

So the next time you find an old name in your phone and feel the pull, do not start by asking them to witness the past. Start by asking for something from now. What is the best thing they ate this week? What are they reading that is not work? What is a decision they are avoiding? What is the part of their day that belongs to them? Then listen for the answer that is not a résumé. If they give you a scene—a bad lunch, a strange student, a repair that went wrong—you will recognize the person not because they sound like the old friend, but because they are occupying their life in front of you. If they give you only the list, you will have a better sense of whether the distance is a pause or an ending.
