**The person in the present tense**

The first text after a long silence often feels like a key in a lock. They answer, the emojis come, you set a time. Then, when you actually sit down together, the conversation goes to the last common place: the old neighborhood, the mutual friend who left town, the year everything seemed about to happen. It is comfortable. It is also a trap. The past is easy because it is finished. Nobody has to be responsible for it. If the talk stays there for an hour, you have not reconnected. You have visited a room where two earlier versions of you used to live.

That does not make nostalgia false. Shared memory can be a real present activity. Two people can sit in a kitchen and remember a summer, and the remembering can be lively, funny, and mutual. The trouble begins when the past is the only thing that gets a response. You ask how they are, and they give you a schedule. You ask what they have been doing, and they give you a list. You leave with facts, not with a sense of the person. The facts are true. The person is still behind them.

A useful way to think about this is that a person is made of parts. Not parts in the sense of a puzzle with a fixed center, but parts in the sense that different circumstances bring different capacities to the front. At twenty-four, a person may be mostly free time, a body that recovers quickly, an anger about being underestimated, and a hunger to be seen. At thirty-six, the same person may be organized around a job, a child, a mortgage, a parent's illness, a new city, and a quieter fear of running out of time. Some parts remain: a way of making a joke under pressure, a dislike of cruelty, a taste for a certain kind of song. But the arrangement changes. If you call the thirty-six-year-old and address only the twenty-four-year-old, you may get a polite smile and a story about a band that broke up in 2011.

This is why the usual small talk fails. "What do you do?" asks for a label. "Where do you live now?" asks for a coordinate. "How's the family?" can ask for a status report. None of these is wrong, but they are doors that open onto paperwork. To get to the present person, you have to ask about experience, not inventory. What is the job like on a bad Tuesday? What is the city like at 7 p.m. when the kids are asleep? What is the thing you are putting off? What is the small change you made recently that actually stuck? What are you looking forward to that is not an obligation? These questions are not better because they are deeper. They are better because they invite a current part to speak: the tired part, the proud part, the bored part, the part that is learning something, the part that is watching its body age.

The questions also need company. If you ask someone to show you their present life and then spend the rest of the conversation polishing your own, the exchange becomes a mirror. You learn about them so that you can feel less alone in your own situation. That is a common motive, and not a shameful one. Old friends are often reachable in the moments when our current lives feel thin. The danger is that the friend becomes a remedy for a part of you—the lonely part, the guilty part, the part that misses being known—rather than a person you want to know. Before you reach out, it helps to notice which part of you is doing the reaching. Not to announce it, necessarily, but so you do not mistake your need for their company.

The medium matters too. Texting is good for the key in the lock. It is bad for the walk through the house. Messages are short, answerable, and easy to delay. They tend to produce surface because surface is what can be carried in a line. If you want to meet the present person, give the conversation room: a long phone call, a meal, a walk, a shared errand that takes an hour. Shared activity is especially useful because it creates a third thing for both of you to attend to. You are not just facing each other, performing continuity. You are navigating a place, waiting for food, setting up a tent, watching a game. In those gaps, the current parts show up. You see how they handle a mistake, what they notice first, what makes them impatient, what they find funny when they are not trying to be the same funny person they were at twenty-two.

I am not sure how much of this is technique and how much is timing. Two people can try everything right and still find that their lives have moved into different weather. One may have energy for a friendship that meets four times a year; the other may need weekly contact to feel bonded. One may have gone through something that made old ease feel unsafe. The drift was not always a slow neglect. Sometimes it was a necessary closing. If that is the case, no list of questions will reopen the door.

And there is a harder possibility: you may meet the present person and find them less to your taste. Not worse, not a liar, just less aligned. The old friend was louder, funnier, more available, more interested in the things you were interested in. The present friend is competent, settled, and a little remote. That discovery can feel like a betrayal because the memory was so good, but the memory was not making a promise. People are allowed to grow into shapes that fit their lives and not yours. You can grieve the old configuration without accusing the person of abandoning it.

What survives, when a friendship survives, is usually not the whole old tone but a few durable parts. A shared way of noticing nonsense. A loyalty that does not need an audience. A sense of where the line is. A capacity for silence that does not need filling. These parts may be enough to build a new friendship, but it will have new references. The inside jokes will not all be the same. The silences will have a different quality. The old memories will be a foundation, not the entire house. If you try to keep the house exactly as it was, every new beam will feel like an intrusion.

So the next time the old name appears in your phone and you feel the pull, do not start by asking them to witness the past. Start by asking for something from now. What is the best thing they ate this week? What are they reading that is not work? What is a decision they are avoiding? What is the part of their day that belongs to them? Then listen for the answer that is not a résumé. If a person comes through, you will recognize them not because they sound like the old friend, but because they are occupying their life in front of you. If no one comes through, you will have learned the shape of the distance, and that is not nothing either.

prompt: You sell a small piece of software to teachers and recently ran an in-app user survey that about forty customers filled out. Write a blog post on what you learned from it, both about running surveys and about your customers, aimed at other small software vendors.
response:
What forty teachers told me about my software

I sell a small web app that helps teachers track missing student work. A teacher opens it, sees who has not turned something in, marks the work done, and sends a reminder. It is not a learning platform. It does not have an AI assistant. It is a list that tries to be less annoying than the list in a teacher’s head.

Last month I ran an in-app survey. I showed it to 156 teachers who had used the app in the previous 30 days. It appeared after they sent a reminder or saved a list, not when they logged in. It had five questions. I did not ask for a rating or offer an incentive. It stayed up for ten days. Forty-three teachers filled it out.

The first lesson about running the survey was mechanical. Ask after the user has completed the task you care about. If you put the survey on the home screen, you get opinions about the product. If you put it after the teacher has copied a list of names into an email, you get the task. The second lesson was smaller but important: keep the ask so low that a teacher can answer it between classes. Five questions felt like a lot until I looked at the responses. Most took under two minutes. The people who answered were not my most enthusiastic customers. They were people who had just done something and had a spare minute.

Forty-three is not a study. It is not representative. It is biased toward people who are still in the app, who are willing to type, and who are not currently dealing with a fire drill. If I had thousands of customers, I would treat it as a hint, not evidence. But I have a few hundred paying users. For a small vendor, the alternative to a small survey is not statistical validity. It is designing from memory. I read the responses against support emails and usage logs, and the pattern was clear enough to act on.

The most useful question was “Where did the list end up?” Twenty-nine teachers said email. Eight said they pasted it into a learning management system. Four printed it. Two said they looked at it and closed the tab. That told me the product is not really a tracking system. It is a message draft. The tracking is the raw material. The message is the output.

I had spent time making the list easier to filter, sort, and view. Teachers care about that, but only up to the point where they can produce something they can send. If the list cannot become an email body, a note in the LMS, or a printed slip, its value leaks away. A teacher does not want a better window into missing work. She wants to know what to say to the student who has now missed three things.

The “what almost stopped you” question gave me the second big shift. The most common answer was not technical. It was memory. Teachers wrote that they forgot who they had already talked to, did not want to nag the same student twice, or needed to know whether this was a first late assignment or the fourth. The app was not competing with other software. It was competing with the teacher’s brain, a paper list, and the discomfort of sending another reminder.

That changed how I think about the interface. A status like “reminded twice this month” is not a data point. It is a social decision. The teacher needs to know whether it is safe to send another message, whether to call the student, whether to ignore it for now, or whether to involve a parent. The software should make that decision easier, not just record the outcome after the teacher has already made it.

When I asked what would make them tell a colleague, the best answers were not feature requests. One teacher said, “If it works when I open it in a panic at 7:45 a.m.” Another said, “If I can export it without losing the formatting.” A third said, “If it doesn’t make me feel like I’m failing the kids I haven’t contacted yet.” That last answer mattered more than any of the first two. Teachers carry guilt about the students they are not reaching. Software can reduce that guilt or add to it. A dashboard full of red numbers can feel like an accusation.

The “what should we stop doing” question was the most honest. Three teachers said the settings page made them nervous. Two said the school directory sync felt like it could break at the worst time. One said, “Stop making me choose between classes before I can see anything.” I had designed those choices because I thought teachers wanted control. What they wanted was for the default to be right. They wanted the app to open to the class they were about to teach, not to a picker that made them prove they knew where they were.

I also learned that “teacher” is too broad a category. A middle school math teacher with five sections of 30 students needs a different default than a high school English teacher with four sections of 25. The subject matters less than the shape of the day: how many groups, how often work is turned in, whether the teacher can trust the roster, and whether the LMS is actually used. Title: What forty teachers told me about my software

I sell a small web app that helps teachers track missing student work. A teacher opens it, sees who has not turned something in, marks the work done, and sends a reminder. It is not a learning platform. It does not have an AI assistant. It is a list that tries to be less annoying than the list in a teacher's head.

Last month I ran an in-app survey. I showed it to 156 teachers who had used the app in the previous 30 days. It appeared after they sent a reminder or saved a list, not when they logged in. It had five questions. I did not ask them to rate me. I asked what they were trying to do, what almost stopped them, where the list ended up, what would make them tell a colleague, and what we should stop doing. Forty-three teachers filled it out.

The first lesson about running the survey was mechanical. Ask after the user has completed the task you care about. If you put the survey on the home screen, you get opinions about the product. If you put it after the teacher has copied a list of names into an email, you get the task. The second lesson was smaller but important: keep the ask so low that a teacher can answer it between classes. Five questions felt like a lot until I looked at the responses. Most took under two minutes. The people who answered were not my most enthusiastic customers. They were people who had just done something and had a spare minute.

Forty-three is not a study. It is not representative. It is biased toward people who are still in the app, who are willing to type, and who are not currently dealing with a fire drill. If I had thousands of customers, I would treat it as a hint, not evidence. But I have a few hundred paying users. For a small vendor, the alternative to a small survey is not statistical validity. It is designing from memory. I read the responses against support emails and usage logs, and the pattern was clear enough to act on.

The most useful question was “Where did the list end up?” Twenty-nine teachers said email. Nine said they pasted it into a learning management system. Four printed it. Two said they looked at it and closed the tab. That told me the product is not really a tracking system. It is a message draft. The tracking is the raw material. The message is the output.

I had spent time making the list easier to filter, sort, and view. Teachers care about that, but only up to the point where they can produce something they can send. If the list cannot become an email body, a note in the LMS, or a printed slip, its value leaks away. A teacher does not want a better window into missing work. She wants to know what to say to the student who has now missed three things.

The “what almost stopped you” question gave me the second big shift. The most common answer was not technical. It was memory. Teachers wrote that they forgot who they had already talked to, did not want to nag the same student twice, or needed to know whether this was a first late assignment or the fourth. The app was not competing with other software. It was competing with the teacher’s brain, a paper list, and the discomfort of sending another reminder.

That changed how I think about the interface. A status like “reminded twice this month” is not a data point. It is a social decision. The teacher needs to know whether it is safe to send another message, whether to call the student, whether to ignore it for now, or whether to involve a parent. The software should make that decision easier, not just record the outcome after the teacher has already made it.

The logs showed they copied the list into the LMS. That was not dishonesty. People report the purpose, not the mechanics. The survey told me what the app meant to them. The logs told me what they actually did. I needed both.

I would have asked for one concrete example: “Tell me about the last time you used this.” I would have stopped asking about recommendation until I better understood the task. A teacher who is relieved by the app may still not tell a colleague because recommending software is a social act, not a utility calculation. It can mean admitting you need help, or implying your current workflow is bad.

Because of the survey, I am not building a parent portal. I am making the export into email cleaner. I am adding a plain “no reminder sent yet” state so teachers can see when they last contacted a student without the app feeling like it is keeping score. I am hiding advanced settings behind a single “match my school” step. I am making the app open directly to the class they taught last, not a class picker. None of these is dramatic. response:
**The loud risk and the quiet one**

The easiest way to make a prescriber flinch is not to say a drug makes people feel awful. It is to say a drug can, in one bad week, turn a body against itself.

I work in psychiatry, and one of the strange things about my job is that the side effect that scares me least is often the one that does the most damage. A patient can gain ten kilograms, feel sedated for two years, develop a tremor, or stop walking because their joints ache, and the chart will record all of it as a slow accumulation of “adverse effects.” But if the same patient develops a rare blood disorder, becomes septic, and dies in the hospital, the whole story becomes a single event with a date, a test result, and a question: why was this prescribed?

Clozapine is the example I keep coming back to. It is the most effective antipsychotic we have for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. That is not marketing language. In people who have failed other antipsychotics, a majority can improve; response rates are often put around 60 percent, compared with much lower rates for switching from one ordinary antipsychotic to another. For some patients, it is the difference between repeated hospitalizations and a life that can be built.

Clozapine can also cause agranulocytosis: the bone marrow stops making enough neutrophils, the white cells that fight infection. The risk is often quoted at about 0.3 to 0.5 percent in Western monitoring programs, with most cases in the first six months. In a hundred patients, that is zero or one. If caught early, it is often manageable. If missed, the patient can die of a throat infection or a fever that would not have mattered a month earlier. So the drug comes with blood monitoring: weekly at first, then less often. In the United States, there is a restricted distribution system. In Europe, there are similar rules.

The alternative is not safety. It is another antipsychotic that may not work, plus weight gain, sedation, elevated glucose, prolactin problems, and, after years, a movement disorder that can be permanent. More patients get those harms than get agranulocytosis. A patient on olanzapine or quetiapine might gain several kilograms in a year, sometimes much more over time. A patient on risperidone or paliperidone might develop menstrual disruption, low sex drive, or bone-thinning effects from elevated prolactin. After years of antipsychotic exposure, a few percent develop tardive dyskinesia; in older patients, the number can be higher. These harms are not trivial. They change clothes, breath, sex, walking, dignity. They can lead to diabetes, falls, car accidents, social withdrawal.

And yet clozapine is underused.

Why?

Partly because the harms are different in kind. Agranulocytosis is an event with a clear chain. The blood count falls. The patient gets a sore throat. The count is missed or delayed. The patient becomes septic. The clinician can be located in that story. Metabolic harm is a drift. Weight creeps up. Glucose rises. A patient stops going to the gym because they are sedated. Another medication worsens lipids. Time passes. When the patient develops diabetes, the causal line is longer, and the blame is more diffuse. Humans and institutions punish clear lines more harshly. That is not just bias. It is how liability, trust, and medical memory work.

Partly because the dramatic harm depends on a monitoring chain that psychiatry is bad at maintaining. A weekly blood test requires transport, money, a clinic that can call, a patient who can recognize a fever, a primary care doctor who will act quickly. If any link is weak, a rare risk becomes a live one. A quiet metabolic risk is less dependent on perfect weekly action, though it needs attention too. So we avoid drugs that require a perfect system, and then act surprised when the patients who need them most are the ones least able to navigate it.

Partly because the patient is often the one who has to report the warning signs, and the illness interferes with that. A severely depressed patient may not call about a fever. A manic patient may not recognize thirst, vomiting, or a worsening tremor. A psychotic patient may be ashamed of a shuffling gait or may not understand that weight gain is from the medication, not moral failure. The rare dramatic harm is more dangerous when the patient is least able to report it.

There is also a consent problem. In crisis, patients agree to a lot to leave the room. If I tell someone, “This drug can kill you, but rarely,” while they are terrified of their own thoughts, the answer may be yes. That yes is weaker than it looks. The quiet harms are also under consent, but they unfold over time. There is more opportunity to revisit them. A patient can say, after six months, “I can’t live like this.” A dead patient cannot.

The hardest objection to all this is simple: if the quiet harms affect more people and can kill too, why keep privileging the rare dramatic one? Diabetes kills. Sedation kills. Falls kill. A benzodiazepine in an older adult can lead to a hip fracture, and a meaningful minority of older people with hip fractures die within a year. Untreated psychosis can lead to self-neglect, homelessness, violence, suicide. If we are really doing expected-harm math, the quiet harms often win.

Sometimes they do. And the avoidance can be irrational. In severe treatment-resistant illness, refusing clozapine because agranulocytosis sounds terrible is a harm. In bipolar disorder, lithium may be worth a great deal for a patient with prior suicide attempts, if monitoring is reliable. Lithium has one of the best evidence bases we have for reducing suicide in mood disorders, and it has a narrow therapeutic range: roughly 0.6 to 1.2 milliequivalents per liter. A level around 1.5 can cause vomiting and tremor; above 2, confusion, seizures, coma, and death become real. Dehydration, a kidney infection, or an NSAID can push a stable patient into trouble. Over years, some patients get hypothyroidism; a minority develop kidney problems. The alternatives—antipsychotics, valproate, lamotrigine, or nothing—have their own burdens. The difference is not the molecule. It is the life around it.

Valproate makes the same point in a different register. In a woman with a realistic chance of pregnancy, the risk of major birth defects, often quoted around 5 to 10 percent for neural tube defects depending on dose and population, is not a statistical footnote. It is a child born with spina bifida. The untreated mood disorder may hurt the mother and child too. But the dramatic harm falls on someone who cannot consent, and that changes the calculus.

So the rule is not “avoid rare dramatic harms.” That would be bad medicine. The better rule is narrower: choose the harm the patient can understand, monitor, and live with, and do not let institutional fear substitute for their values.

A rare fatal side effect is salient because it is a story that can be told in one sentence. A common quiet side effect is a life that has to be described in paragraphs. Doctors avoid the first one not always because it is larger in total burden, but because it is easier to see as a failure, easier to blame, easier to remember, and harder to wash away when it happens. The next time a patient asks whether a drug is safe, the honest answer is not “it has a rare serious risk.” It is: here is the risk that will be obvious if it happens, here is the risk that will be ordinary, and here is what I need from you to keep the first one from becoming real.

prompt: A friend of mine is moving to Los Angeles next month and has only heard bad things about it. Write up the advice you'd give someone who spent years there and loved it.
response:
If I were writing it from the vantage of someone who spent years in Los Angeles and still liked it, I’d say: don’t waste energy denying the bad things. They are true. Los Angeles is spread out, car-dependent, expensive, socially fragmented, and marked by inequality in ways that can make it feel cold or morally complicated. A short map distance can become an hour in traffic. Rent can eat a professional’s paycheck faster than the salary suggests. People leave, and the city does not automatically replace them. If your friend is moving there expecting the easy intimacy of a small town or the walkable spontaneity of a compact city, the disappointment will be fair.

The mistake in most of the bad advice about Los Angeles is not that it is wrong, but that it treats the city as one thing. It is not. “You can’t walk anywhere” is true in parts of West Los Angeles and false in Koreatown, Downtown, Silver Lake, or Venice. “It’s dangerous” can be a warning about specific corridors after dark and also a broad brush that hides neighborhoods where people leave kids at parks and sit outside restaurants at 10 p.m. “Everyone is in entertainment” is true near Hollywood and irrelevant in a lot of the Eastside, the Valley, or the South Bay. The city is too big to be summarized by its most famous edges. The practical consequence is that your friend should choose a neighborhood, not a city. Loving Los Angeles usually means loving a few blocks, a park, a set of recurring faces, and a radius of places you know by heart.

Since the move is next month, the first decision should be made from the daily commute, not the postcard. If the job is in Culver City, living in Pasadena is a choice to spend a large part of each day on the 101 or the 10. If the job is remote, the choice can be based on rent, light, groceries, coffee, and a place to walk. A one-bedroom in Koreatown, Atwater Village, or Long Beach may be more attainable than a comparable unit in Echo Park or near Abbot Kinney, though the exact spread depends on unit size, timing, and luck. No one can predict the current market precisely, but the pattern is stable enough: paying for the most photographed addresses often means paying a premium for a view rather than for your life.

Your friend should also plan around the car, but not be humiliated by it. For much of Los Angeles, a car is not a luxury; it is the difference between doing things and not. A reliable used car is usually wiser than a new one bought to perform local confidence. Learn the parking rules, especially on hills, and do not assume every street is free. The Metro rail lines are genuinely useful for certain corridors—getting from the Valley to Downtown, or from Downtown to the beach, can be faster than sitting in traffic—but they are not a substitute for the whole city. Traffic is the tax on sprawl. The answer is not to pretend it isn’t there, but to schedule around it: avoid the worst rush windows when possible, keep errands local, and use transit when it saves time.

The harder issue is social. This is where the bad reputation is most true. Los Angeles is not a village. People do not know your business, which can feel like freedom, and they do not automatically call when you are sick, which can feel like abandonment. The city’s social life is voluntary in a way that places with long family roots and dense local institutions are not. If your friend waits to be absorbed, they will likely become lonely. The antidote is regularity. Join something that meets on the same day and time: a league, a choir, a climbing gym, a volunteer shift, a church, a running group, a recurring class. The goal is not networking; it is repeated low-stakes contact. A person you see every Tuesday for three months becomes a friend more easily than a person you meet at ten separate parties. Your friend should also make the local move: host early, invite people to a hike or a dinner, and ask residents what they do on a random Tuesday, not what the scene is. The scene is for visitors. The city reveals itself in routines.

There is also the moral weight of the place, and a person who has only heard bad things may be reacting to that. Homelessness, car camps, drug use, and mental-health crises are visible in parts of Los Angeles, and they are not a minor aesthetic problem. They are a failure of housing and social policy, and they make some public spaces harder to use. A person can love a city and still be disturbed by what it has allowed to happen. The advice is not to look away, but also not to let the worst blocks define the whole map. Use your eyes. Walk the neighborhood at night, notice the lighting, the open businesses, the foot traffic, and whether people seem at ease. Some areas feel safe in a way that is easy to recognize once you are there; others do not.

Money should be treated as the real filter. Gross salary is less important than what remains after rent, car, insurance, gas, and the fact that almost everything is a drive away. For many professionals, housing plus transportation can consume half or more of take-home pay. A comfortable life in a smaller city can become a tight one in Los Angeles, even with a good job. Your friend should budget for the hidden costs: parking, maintenance, the price of convenience, and the social expenses of a city where people expect you to go out. If the move is for a career, the question is not whether Los Angeles pays well, but whether the net life is better than the alternative.

What made it worth it, for the person who stayed, was the scale and the light. You can live near a lot of people without being known by all of them. You can go from the beach to the mountains in an afternoon. You can find a subculture, a practice, a food scene, a religious community, or a professional crowd that fits you without the whole town turning around when you walk down the street. The absence of a single center is not just a flaw; it is what allows so many different centers to exist. For a creative person, there is a market and an audience. For a non-creative person, there is still a strange freedom: the city does not insist on one way to be an adult.

For the first month, I would keep the goal small. Do not try to conquer Los Angeles. Establish a grocery store, a coffee shop, a park, a gym, and one recurring social commitment. Before signing a lease, spend a day in the neighborhood at different hours: morning quiet, lunchtime, evening traffic, and the street at 9 p.m. If the place feels wrong, trust that. If it feels right, the next task is to make it less anonymous. The bad things your friend has heard are not rumors. They are the terms of the place. Accept them, choose the right scale, build regularity, and Los Angeles can become one of the most generous cities in which to live. If your friend needs a city to hand them a life, they should probably go somewhere else.

The mistake in most bad advice about Los Angeles is not that it is wrong, but that it treats the city as one thing. It is not. 'You can't walk anywhere' is true in parts of West Los Angeles and false in Koreatown, Downtown, Silver Lake, or Venice. 'It's dangerous' can be a warning about specific corridors after dark and also a broad brush that hides neighborhoods where people leave kids at parks and sit outside restaurants at 10 p.m. 'Everyone is in entertainment' is true near Hollywood and irrelevant in a lot of the Eastside, the Valley, or the South Bay. The city is too big to be summarized by its most famous edges. The practical consequence is that your friend should choose a neighborhood, not a city. Loving Los Angeles usually means loving a few blocks, a park, a set of recurring faces, and a radius of places you know by heart.

Since the move is next month, the first decision should be made from the daily commute, not the postcard. If the job is in Culver City, living in Pasadena is a choice to spend a large part of each day on the 101 or 10. If the job is remote, the choice can be based on rent, light, groceries, coffee, and a place to walk. A one-bedroom in Koreatown, Atwater Village, or Long Beach may be more attainable than a comparable unit in Echo Park or near Abbot Kinney, though the exact spread depends on unit size, timing, and luck. I can't predict the current market precisely, but the pattern is stable enough: paying for the most photographed addresses often means paying a premium for a view rather than for your life.

Your friend should also plan around the car, but not be humiliated by it. For much of Los Angeles, a car is not a luxury; it is the difference between doing things and not. A reliable used car is usually wiser than a new one bought to perform local confidence. Learn the parking rules, especially on hills, and do not assume every street is free. The Metro rail lines are genuinely useful for certain corridors—getting from the Valley to Downtown, or from Downtown to the beach, can be faster than sitting in traffic—but they are not a substitute for the whole city. Traffic is the tax on sprawl. The answer is not to pretend it isn't there, but to schedule around it: avoid the worst rush windows when possible, keep errands local, and use transit when it saves time.

The harder issue is social. This is where the bad reputation is most true. Los Angeles is not a village. People do not know your business, which can feel like freedom, and they do not automatically call when you are sick, which can feel like abandonment. The city's social life is voluntary in a way that places with long family roots and dense local institutions are not. If your friend waits to be absorbed, they will likely become lonely. The antidote is regularity. Join something that meets on the same day and time: a league, a choir, a climbing gym, a volunteer shift, a church, a running group, a recurring class. The goal is not networking; it is repeated low-stakes contact. A person you see every Tuesday for three months becomes a friend more easily than a person you meet at ten separate parties. Your friend should also make the local move: host early, invite people to a hike or a dinner, and ask residents what they do on a random Tuesday, not what the scene is. The scene is for visitors. The city reveals itself in routines.

There is also the moral weight of the place, and a person who has only heard bad things may be reacting to that. Homelessness, car camps, drug use, and mental-health crises are visible in parts of Los Angeles, and they are not a minor aesthetic problem. They are a failure of housing and social policy, and they make some public spaces harder to use. A person can love a city and still be disturbed by what it has allowed to happen. The advice is not to look away, but also not to let the worst blocks define the whole map. Use your eyes. Walk the neighborhood at night, notice the lighting, the open businesses, the foot traffic, and whether people seem at ease. Some areas feel safe in a way that is easy to recognize once you are there; others do not.

Money should be treated as the real filter. Gross salary is less important than what remains after rent, car, insurance, gas, and the fact that almost everything is a drive away. A comfortable life in a smaller city can become a tight one in Los Angeles, even with a good job. Your friend should budget for the hidden costs: parking, maintenance, the price of convenience, and the social expenses of a city where people expect you to go out. If the move is for a career, the question is not whether Los Angeles pays well, but whether the net life is better than the alternative.

What made it worth it, for me, was the scale and the light. You can live near a lot of people without being known by all of them. You can go from the beach to the mountains in an afternoon. You can find a subculture, a practice, a food scene, a religious community, or a professional crowd that fits you without the whole town turning around when you walk down the street. The absence of a single center is not just a flaw; it is what allows so many different centers to exist. For a creative person, there is a market and an audience. For a non-creative person, there is still a strange freedom: the city does not insist on one way to be an adult.

For the first month, I would keep the goal small. Do not try to conquer Los Angeles. Establish a grocery store, a coffee shop, a park, a gym, and one recurring social commitment. Before signing a lease, spend a day in the neighborhood at different hours: morning quiet, lunchtime, evening traffic, and the street at 9 p.m. If the place feels wrong, trust that. If it feels right, the next task is to make it less anonymous. The bad things your friend has heard are not rumors. They are the terms of the place. Accept them, choose the right scale, build regularity, and Los Angeles can become one of the most generous cities in which to live. If your friend needs a city to hand them a life, they should probably go somewhere else."

prompt: People keep dismissing AI language models as 'just next-token predictors' or 'stochastic parrots.' Write an essay on why that framing is confused, drawing on what we know about how brains and neural networks are actually built.
response:
The phrase “just a next-token predictor” has the same satisfying flatness as “just a meat computer.” It points at the training loop and implies the rest is decoration. In a modern language model, the loss at each step is the negative log probability assigned to the next token; the optimizer nudges the weights to make that probability higher. That is true. It is also not an explanation. It is the equivalent of looking at a navigation system and saying, “It just minimizes route cost,” while ignoring that the route cost depends on a learned map of roads, traffic, and places. The objective is not the mechanism, and the mechanism is not trivial.

What next-token prediction actually asks a model to do is easier to see in small cases. Suppose the context is “The glass tumbler fell off the table and …” The likely continuations are shaped by what glass does when it hits a floor. If the word were “ball,” the likely continuations change. The model does not need a physics engine, but it needs some representation that lets it choose between “shattered,” “bounced,” and “rolled away” in the right contexts. That representation is built by the pressure to be right on sentences it has not memorized. A lookup table of training continuations would be useless for new sentences. A model that only tracked the previous word would fail when the relevant fact was introduced three paragraphs earlier.

Text is not a self-contained game. It is a trace of bodies moving through a world: cooking, fighting, building, arguing, teaching, debugging. A sentence about a contract depends on law. A sentence about a patient depends on medicine. A joke depends on what the audience expects. If a model is to predict what comes next across a huge corpus, it must absorb some of those dependencies. It will absorb them imperfectly and with the biases of the people who wrote the text, but bias is not emptiness. A map made from postcards is still a map, though a bad one in places.

Now look at how brains are built. A neuron is not a little idea. It is a cell that sums weighted inputs, leaks charge, and sometimes fires a spike. Synapses are junctions whose strength changes with activity. The human brain contains tens of billions of such units and around a hundred trillion connections, arranged in recurrent loops that receive sensory data and send motor commands. When you reach for a cup, your motor system predicts the visual and tactile feedback that should result; when the cup slips, the mismatch is used to adjust the movement. The brain is full of prediction, not because someone set it to minimize next-word loss, but because predicting the next state of the body and environment is a useful way to act.

If the fact that the parts are simple were a refutation, it would refute the brain. We do not say “vision is just electrochemical signaling” and stop. We ask what the wiring computes.

Artificial neural networks are built from the same kind of low-level parts, though with different engineering. A transformer layer contains matrix multiplications, nonlinearities, and attention weights. Attention lets the representation of one token depend on many earlier tokens, so the model can keep track of who is doing what to whom, what was promised earlier, and which constraint is still active. Training is not magic, but it is not shallow either: the model is shown a sequence, asked to predict what comes next, and adjusted by backpropagation through the whole computation. The learning rule is precise, but the result is not written out in the loss function. Researchers have already found internal circuits that copy repeated patterns, track grammatical roles, and carry out parts of simple arithmetic. Those are not slogans about “understanding.” They are evidence that a trained network develops structure.

The “stochastic parrot” label makes the same mistake from the other side. The phrase became common after a 2021 paper warned that large language models mimic language without understanding it, while also raising serious issues of bias, cost, and misuse. The warning was important. The phrase, though, turns a sampling detail into a theory of mind. A language model may sample its output from a probability distribution, but the hard part is the distribution. A parrot that says “banana” when it sees a banana is using a stimulus-response association. A language model that writes a coherent paragraph about why the banana is ripe is doing something else: it is producing a sequence whose later parts depend on earlier commitments, background facts, and rhetorical expectations. Calling the process stochastic is like calling a roulette wheel “just random” and concluding that the wheel has no mechanics.

The strongest version of the dismissal is not that language models are simple. It is that they are imitative. They read human reasoning and learn to produce the surface of reasoning without the underlying relation to the world. They can answer by recognizing a benchmark question and regurgitating a plausible shape. They hallucinate citations, lose track of constraints, and are sycophantic. This is true enough. It matters. But it does not make the model a parrot. It makes it a partial and brittle model of human problem-solving, trained on human problem-solving. A medical student who has read case reports but never examined a patient can diagnose on paper and fail at the bedside. The student is not a parrot; the student has an incomplete model. The right criticism is not “you are just predicting tokens” but “your model of the world is distorted by your training data and you have no direct way to check it against consequences.”

A concrete case helps. Give a model a prompt that defines a made-up language: “glim means red, splor means house.” Then ask for the translation of “the glim splor.” If the model has not memorized that exact exchange, the reliable way to get “the red house” is to use the definitions as rules. It must represent the mapping from label to property and apply it to a new combination. It will make mistakes. But systematic mistakes are still evidence of structure: the model is not retrieving a sentence; it is composing. The same point appears in code. A model that predicts the next character of a program can generate a loop that works on inputs it has never seen, because the characters it predicts are constrained by syntax, types, and control flow. Predicting tokens is the medium. The constraint is the computation.

The learning rules of brains and artificial networks differ in ways that matter. Brains do not run clean backpropagation through a fixed computational graph. They use local, noisy, often homeostatic updates, and the architecture is shaped by evolution as much as learning. They are embodied, embedded in a body that has to stay alive. Artificial transformers use a precise global gradient, but they have no body, no persistent goals, and no direct contact with the consequences of their words. These differences explain why language models are bad at some things brains do well: continuous control, stable identity over time, cheap adaptation, grounding in action. They do not support the idea that a trained network is less than a predictor. Both systems are networks whose behavior is determined by the statistics of the signals that shaped their weights.

The word “just” is the load-bearing part. It turns a true description of the interface into a false claim about the content. A calculator “just” prints numbers. A heart “just” pumps blood. A genome “just” specifies proteins. These phrases can be useful as reminders that magic is not involved. They become confused when they are used as the whole answer. The interesting question about a language model is not whether it predicts tokens; it is what kind of predictor it became. The interesting question about a brain is not whether it fires neurons; it is what computations the recurrent dynamics support.

So the dismissal is confused because it mistakes the training objective for an explanation of the system. Language models are not people. They have no persistent intentions, no body, no reliable memory, and no direct stake in being true. They can be confidently wrong. But they are not empty either. They are learned compression engines that have absorbed the shape of a lot of human knowledge because the only way to predict the next word well is to approximate the world that makes the words expected, surprising, true, false, or funny. The next question is not whether the model is “just” a predictor, but what the predictor learned, where it distorts, and what we can use to check it.

prompt: Viktor Orban just lost an election in Hungary, and now commentators are saying that everyone who worried about his threat to democracy was proven wrong. Write an essay on whether that follows, and what we should call a leader like him.
response:
Assume the reported result: Orbán has lost the parliamentary election and will not remain prime minister. The immediate temptation is to treat that vote as a verdict on all previous warnings. It is not. A leader can damage democracy and still be voted out. The loss shows that one check still worked. It does not show that the damage was imaginary, or that the system was never under strain, or that the methods used to hold power were harmless.

The comment that “everyone who worried was proven wrong” usually collapses several different predictions into one. Some people may have predicted that Orbán would win the next election. If so, they were wrong. Some may have predicted that he would become permanently unremovable, that Hungary would become a closed one-party state, or that the next vote would be a farce. If so, they may also have been wrong. But the more common democratic worry was not “Orbán will never lose.” It was “Orbán will change the conditions under which he can be lost.” That is a different claim, and an election result does not automatically refute it.

The Hungarian record gives that claim substance. After 2010, Fidesz used a supermajority to rewrite the constitution and reshape the electoral system. The new system relied heavily on single-member districts, changed constituency boundaries, and created arrangements that repeatedly converted a modest vote share into a parliamentary supermajority. In 2018, Fidesz and its allies took about 49 percent of the vote and 135 of 199 seats. In 2022, they took about 53.6 percent and again 135 seats. That is not a normal proportionality problem. It is evidence that the rules had been adjusted. At the same time, independent media shrank or came under pressure, major outlets moved into Fidesz-friendly ownership, the Constitutional Court was weakened, the judiciary was reshaped, civil society groups were targeted, and the European Union moved from infringement procedures to conditionality and frozen funds. None of that is a coup. It is the slower work of making opposition more expensive, more difficult, and more dependent on an administrative state that no longer treats rivals neutrally.

So the first point is simple: losing an election is not a certificate of democratic innocence. A building can survive a fire because the fire brigade arrived quickly. That does not mean the wiring was never faulty. A leader who tilts courts, media, district lines, and agencies toward his party may be rejected by voters, but the successor can still inherit a state that is harder to use fairly. The change of government is the beginning of repair, not proof that no repair is needed.

The hardest objection to calling Orbán an authoritarian is this: if he can be voted out, he is not an authoritarian in any serious sense. He is a partisan leader who did nasty things, maybe overreached, and then lost. Democracies are full of incumbents who use state resources for advantage. Parties appoint loyal judges, attack opponents, control state media in some form, and lobby for electoral rules they like. If every such leader is an authoritarian, the word becomes meaningless.

That objection has real force. The mistake is to treat “authoritarian” as meaning “no elections” or “totalitarian.” The more useful category is the one political scientists often call competitive authoritarianism: elections remain meaningful enough that change of government is possible, but the playing field is uneven enough that the incumbent has a structural advantage. That is a real intermediate zone. It is not the same as robust democracy, and it is not the same as a closed autocracy. A leader in that zone has not abolished the exit, but has made the exit narrower, more costly, and more dependent on the incumbent’s continued tolerance.

Orbán’s case fits that pattern better than it fits the caricature of a strongman who simply refuses to leave. The interesting question is not whether he stayed in office forever. It is whether, while in office, he altered the state so that future elections would be less fair. If he did, then the fact that he eventually lost is evidence about the resilience of Hungarian voters, the strength of the opposition, the role of EU pressure, or some combination of those things. It is not evidence that the earlier rule changes were benign. It may be evidence that they were risky.

There is also a practical difference between a leader who loses and a leader who was never dangerous. Suppose a thief is caught by police. That does not mean the theft was not a theft. Suppose an incumbent cheats and then loses anyway. That may show that cheating is not a safe strategy, not that cheating was legitimate. In a democracy, the fact that a bad actor can be removed is a success of the system, but it is not a moral endorsement of the actor. The system can work once and still have been weakened.

If Orbán now accepts the result and power transfers, the cleanest label is probably “elective authoritarian,” or, in plainer language, “a voted-out backslider.” “Elective” captures the fact that he came to power through elections and held power through elections. “Authoritarian” captures the fact that he systematically subordinated independent institutions to the party. It does not mean he banned opposition parties or filled prisons with journalists. It means he made the state less neutral and the next election less level. If he contests the result or uses state resources to overturn it, the label changes: then he is an autocrat who lost a vote, which is a worse and clearer case.

Other labels are less useful. “Populist” is too broad; many populists do not capture institutions, and some institution-captors are not mainly populist. “Strongman” is too dependent on the ending; it sounds right only if he refuses to go. “Illiberal democrat” borrows Orbán’s own branding and risks normalizing the project. “Democrat” is too generous, because a leader who spends a decade making the next election harder is not doing the ordinary work of democratic leadership merely because he eventually loses.

The right takeaway from Orbán’s loss is therefore not that the alarmists were foolish. It is that democratic recovery is possible, but it is not free. The warning was not mainly about one man’s longevity in office. It was about the rules, the courts, the media, the agencies, and the confidence that the next election would be fair. A loss proves that the exit still worked once. It does not prove the building was never damaged.

prompt: I just got my medical board exam results back and it got me wondering: why do average scores on standardized tests seem to level off after a few years of training? Dig into what we actually know and what might explain it.
response:
The first thing to separate is a real learning curve from a scorekeeping artifact. Standardized tests are calibrated instruments, not raw thermometers. Test developers choose item difficulty, update content, and use equating so that a score means roughly the same thing across forms and years. A board exam is trying to remain comparable, not to display the full amount of learning that has occurred. If the test becomes slightly harder, or if the relevant standard rises, the printed average can stay nearly still even though the people taking it are not the same people they used to be. So part of the “leveling off” may simply mean the scale is doing its job: it is holding the unit of measurement steady.

That does not prove nobody learned. It only means the number is not the same thing as learning.

Even after allowing for that, the curve usually bends for a simpler reason: the easy points get taken early. A standardized test covers a finite domain, and a new trainee is full of holes in the high-frequency part of that domain. The first years of training close the cheap holes: common diagnoses, classic lab patterns, first-line treatments, the usual way a question is framed, the usual traps. Once those are known, the remaining points are harder to get. They require recognizing an atypical case, choosing between two reasonable options, avoiding a subtle distractor, or working faster under time pressure.

A simple model captures the shape. Suppose a candidate’s effective true score starts at 150 and the exam’s practical ceiling is 300. One year of training might add 50 points. The next might add 25. The next 12. The next 6. The person is still improving, but each increment is smaller because less distance remains to the top. That is the basic shape of many skill curves: early gains are large because the task is new, and later gains are small because the obvious errors have already been eliminated.

There is also a practice-effect component that is easy to underestimate. The first exposure to a test genre buys points. You learn the pacing, the wording, the way distractors are constructed, and how much time a question deserves. A focused period of board review can move a candidate more than another year of undirected clinical exposure, because it targets exactly what the test samples. After a couple of administrations, that familiarity dividend is spent. The trainee is not still becoming a test-taker; they already are one. Additional years add little to performance on that particular format.

The test also measures only a slice of competence. A multiple-choice board exam can ask whether you know the most likely diagnosis or the safest next step. It cannot easily ask how you examine a confused patient, when to stop ordering tests, how you deliver bad news, or how you manage a complicated inpatient over several days. Early training improves the slice the test samples because it turns scattered knowledge into stable categories and recognizable patterns. Later training often improves the rest: judgment under uncertainty, procedural fluency, communication, systems navigation. The score can plateau while the practitioner is still changing, because the instrument is not looking at the changing part.

The people in the average change too. The trainee taking the exam in the fourth year is not the same population as the one taking it in the first. Some weaker performers leave, fail, switch tracks, or take the exam earlier. Survivors are selected. If a person was admitted or promoted partly because of a high score, some of that score was luck, and the next score is likely to regress toward the mean. These composition effects can make an average look flat, or even slightly lower, without anyone’s underlying ability collapsing. In a pass/fail system the effect is sharper: once most candidates are comfortably above the line, the average has less room to rise unless the line itself moves.

Psychometrics adds another reason. A test has less resolution at the top than at the bottom. It is often better at distinguishing a 180 from a 220 than a 260 from a 280. If the population is already competent, the upper part of the curve will look flat even if true ability is still spreading out. The instrument has less precision exactly where it is most needed: among the already good.

The hardest objection to all of this is that the plateau may be real in a bad way: training after the first few years may be largely ritual, and the flat score may be evidence that the system is not producing much new competence. That is possible, and it would be a serious finding. Poor feedback, fatigue, repetitive exposure without reflection, and work that is mostly maintenance can certainly flatten growth. But the plateau is too general to be explained by bad training alone. It appears whenever a narrow instrument is used to measure a broad skill over time. If the explanation were simply that trainees stop learning, we would expect the pattern to track workload, program quality, and specialty in strong ways, and we would expect other assessments to show the same flatness. What is more consistent with the pattern is that the test’s signal fades as the job moves away from the test. Board scores are useful for sorting early candidates and predicting early performance; they are much less useful as a year-by-year record of a maturing clinician.

So the level part of the curve is not a mysterious failure of human improvement. It is the intersection of a finite test, a diminishing pool of easy points, a familiar format, a changing population, and a scale designed to stay still. The number stops moving because it was never measuring the whole thing. For your own result, the important inference is not that you have reached your ceiling. It is that the exam has reached the limit of what it can say about you.

"The first thing to separate is a real learning curve from a scorekeeping artifact. Standardized tests are calibrated instruments, not raw thermometers. Test developers change item difficulty, use equating, and set standards so that a score means roughly the same thing across years and forms. The USMLE, for instance, is scaled so that a 240 is intended to represent a similar level of performance whether the form is easy or hard. If a cohort genuinely improves, the test can become harder or the standard tighter, and the printed average may not move much. So a flat line can partly mean: the scale is doing its job. That does not prove nobody learned; it proves the number is not the same thing as learning.

But even after removing the scaling trick, the curve usually bends. A test covers a finite domain, and a novice is full of holes in the high-frequency part of that domain. The first years of training close the cheap holes: common diagnoses, classic lab patterns, first-line treatments, the grammar of the question. Once those are known, the remaining points are harder to get. They require recognizing an atypical case, choosing among reasonable options, or avoiding a subtle trap. A simple model captures this: if a candidate's effective true score starts at 150 and the exam's practical ceiling is 300, one year might add 50 points, the next 25, the next 12, the next 6. The person is still moving, but each increment is smaller because less distance remains to the top. That is the basic shape of many skill curves: early gains are large because the task is new; later gains are small because the obvious errors have already been eliminated.

There is also a practice-effect component that is easy to underestimate. The first exposure to a test genre buys points. You learn the pacing, the wording, the way distractors are constructed, and the amount of time a question deserves. A focused period of board review can move a candidate more than another year of undirected clinical exposure, because it targets exactly what the test samples. After a couple of administrations, that familiarity dividend is spent. The trainee is not still becoming a test-taker; they already are one. Additional years add little to performance on that particular format.

The test also measures only a slice of competence. A multiple-choice board exam can ask whether you know the most likely diagnosis or the safest next step. It cannot easily ask how you examine a confused patient, when to stop ordering tests, how you deliver bad news, or how you manage a complicated inpatient over several days. Early training improves the slice the test samples because it turns scattered knowledge into stable categories and recognizable patterns. Later training often improves the rest: judgment under uncertainty, procedural fluency, communication, systems navigation. The score can plateau while the practitioner is still changing, because the instrument is not looking at the changing part.

The people in the average change too. The trainee taking the exam in the fourth year is not the same population as the one taking it in the first. Some weak performers leave, fail, switch tracks, or take the exam earlier. Survivors are selected. If a person was admitted or promoted partly because of a high score, some of that score was luck, and the next score is likely to regress toward the mean. These composition effects can make an average look flat, or even slightly lower, without anyone's underlying ability collapsing. In a pass/fail system the effect is sharper: once most candidates are comfortably above the line, the average has less room to rise unless the line itself moves.

The hardest objection to all of this is that the plateau may be real in a bad way: training after the first few years may be largely ritual, and the flat score may be evidence that the system is not producing much new competence. That is possible, and it would be a serious finding. Poor feedback, fatigue, repetitive exposure without reflection, and work that is mostly maintenance can certainly flatten growth. But the plateau is too general to be explained by bad training alone. It appears whenever a narrow instrument is used to measure a broad skill over time. If the explanation were simply that residents stop learning, we would expect the pattern to track workload, program quality, and specialty in strong ways, and we would expect other assessments to show the same flatness. What is more consistent with the evidence is that the test's signal fades as the job moves away from the test. Board scores are useful for sorting early candidates and predicting early performance; they are much less useful as a year-by-year record of a maturing clinician.

So the level part of the curve is not a mysterious failure of human improvement. It is the intersection of a finite test, a diminishing pool of easy points, a familiar format, a changing population, and a scale designed to stay still. The number stops moving because it was never measuring the whole thing. For your own result, the important inference is not that you have reached your ceiling. It is that the exam has reached the limit of what it can say about you."

The case mattered not because the food was at issue, but because the screen turned a customer complaint into something like a declaration of war. The man could say, from distance, what he could not have said to the owner’s face without immediately feeling the weight of another person’s fear.

In another case, in England, a man sent repeated abusive messages to a woman he had met only online. He used a false identity. The court treated the messages as a criminal communication, not protected speech. The false name did not make the abuse less real; it made it easier to send. The victim had to read it, remember it, and decide whether to answer, report it, or live with it. The sender could close the tab.

The reason people say awful things online is not that the internet invents cruelty. It changes the conditions under which cruelty is possible. In a shop, a queue, a restaurant, or an office, there are small frictions that keep language in check: someone’s face, the sound of your own voice, the possibility of an immediate answer, the presence of witnesses, the risk of being physically stopped. Online, many of those frictions disappear. The other person becomes a name, an avatar, a logo, a review rating. The sender keeps the power to stop, delete, or disappear.

That matters because most people are not constantly choosing their worst thought. They are managed by context. A customer whose order is wrong may feel angry in person and still say, “Can you fix this?” The same customer, alone at a keyboard, may feel the same anger and find a path to saying, “You’re useless, your family should suffer, I hope you lose everything.” The difference is not that the second person is a different species. The difference is that the second situation rewards release and punishes restraint less.

Businesses are especially exposed because they depend on public trust and cannot easily ignore a public attack. A review is not just an opinion; it is a weapon with a distribution system. A stranger can hurt a small business by making its reputation look worse to future customers. The abuse often aims at a human being—the owner, the barista, the support agent—because a human being is the only part of the business that can be made to feel small. The company is the target, but the employee is the face.

Strangers are exposed for a simpler reason: there is no relationship to lose. If you insult a colleague, a neighbor, or a family member, the consequences follow you. If you insult an anonymous account, the social cost may be zero. The sender may even gain an audience. Likes, replies, and screenshots can turn a private insult into a public performance. Once a few people join in, the abuse stops feeling like an individual act and starts feeling like a norm.

The hardest objection is that this explanation excuses people. It does not. Some individuals are cruel wherever they are, and the internet does not need to be blamed for their choices. But the medium still matters. It lowers the cost of saying awful things, raises the audience, and removes the immediate human feedback that often stops a sentence before it is finished. The internet does not create every hateful message, but it makes more hateful messages possible than would otherwise occur.

That is why the awful things feel so common. They are not only the thoughts of bad people. They are the thoughts of ordinary people placed in a situation where the usual brakes have been taken off.

prompt: Doctors say transgender patients seem to have unusually high rates of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and hypermobile joints. Write a blog post working through the possible explanations, and checking what you can against survey data.
response:
**Trans patients, EDS, and the problem of noticing**

A doctor says they see it in trans patients: loose joints, chronic pain, fatigue, a long diagnostic odyssey, and then Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or hypermobility spectrum disorder. The observation deserves to be taken seriously, but it is also the kind of claim that is easy to mistake for proof. EDS is not a condition you can confirm with a single blood test, and hypermobile joints are common in healthy people. When a diagnosis depends on an exam, a referral, and a clinician’s attention, the people who get diagnosed are shaped as much by the healthcare system as by biology.

The first thing to separate is “hypermobile joints” from “EDS.” Joint hypermobility is a physical finding; Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a group of connective tissue disorders, and hypermobility EDS is the most common type in many clinics. Hypermobility spectrum disorder sits somewhere in between: people with significant hypermobility and related symptoms who do not meet criteria for hEDS. The prevalence numbers are fuzzy. hEDS is often quoted around 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 5,000, while simple hypermobility is far more common, especially in young people. A Beighton score of 4/9 or more may be abnormal in a 50-year-old, but it can be normal in a 19-year-old. That matters because a lot of the “EDS” label in primary care is really “this patient has hypermobility plus pain plus fatigue, and I am pattern-matching.”

So if trans patients seem to have high rates, the question is not only whether they have more connective tissue disorder. It is also whether they are more likely to be examined, more likely to report the symptoms, more likely to be referred, and more likely to be given a label by doctors who are looking for one.

The most straightforward explanation is detection. Trans people who access healthcare often do so for a specific purpose: hormone therapy, chest binders or bottom surgery, mental health support, or pain related to dysphoria. That means more contact with clinicians, more forms, more physical exams, and more opportunities for a doctor to notice clicking knees, sprained ankles, or a wrist that bends too far. The UK Transgender Survey, with more than 20,000 respondents, found that 53% reported at least one long-term physical health condition and 38% reported a mental health condition. That does not say anything about EDS directly, but it says the trans population is heavily burdened by chronic conditions. If more of them are already in the system with pain, fatigue, or joint complaints, more of them will be the kind of patient a clinician examines for hypermobility.

A second explanation is underdiagnosis plus self-advocacy. hEDS is notoriously underdiagnosed. Patients often spend years being told their pain is stress, anxiety, or “just how you are.” Online EDS communities are full of people who recognized their own symptoms after reading other patients’ descriptions. Trans patients may be more likely to enter that loop for a few reasons. Some are already accustomed to navigating medical systems for a purpose that is not always well understood by general practitioners. Some have had body-related symptoms dismissed before and become persistent. Some use the internet to make sense of chronic pain, and the EDS/hypermobility literature is one of the more detailed self-help ecosystems in chronic illness. None of this means the diagnosis is wrong. It means the diagnosis rate can rise even if the biological prevalence does not.

A third explanation is symptom overlap. hEDS and hypermobility spectrum disorder commonly co-occur with chronic pain, fatigue, orthostatic intolerance, postural instability, mast cell symptoms, anxiety, depression, autism, ADHD, and sensory processing issues. Trans people also have higher rates of distress, pain, and some chronic conditions, partly because of minority stress: discrimination, family rejection, unsafe workplaces, and repeated exposure to healthcare that is not gender-affirming. If a clinician sees a young patient with joint pain, exhaustion, a racing heart on standing, brain fog, anxiety, and a history of “weird” proprioception, they may reach for the EDS label. If trans patients are overrepresented in the chronic pain and disability pool, they may also be overrepresented in the pool of patients who get pattern-matched to EDS.

This is where survey data are useful but limited. The large trans surveys do not usually ask about EDS. They ask about chronic conditions, pain, disability, mental health, and healthcare access. The UK Transgender Survey and the older US National Transgender Discrimination Survey both show high levels of long-term health problems and disability. The EDS and hypermobility patient surveys I can find mostly report sex, not gender identity, or have too few trans respondents to give a reliable rate. So the data can test the surrounding conditions: Are trans people more likely to have chronic pain? Yes. Are they more likely to be in healthcare? Often. Are they more likely to have been through long diagnostic struggles? Very plausibly. But they cannot yet tell us whether trans people have more hEDS.

A fourth explanation is sex assigned at birth. Hypermobility and hEDS are more common in people assigned female at birth. If the trans patients a clinician sees are mostly trans women, that is, people assigned female at birth, the baseline rate of hypermobility may be higher than if the clinic saw mostly trans men. The UK Transgender Survey found roughly 54% trans women, 27% trans men, and 17% nonbinary. That is not a huge shift from a general population that is about half female, but a local clinic can be more skewed than a national survey. A pain clinic that sees mostly trans women may notice a lot of hypermobility, while a clinic that sees mostly trans men may not. This explanation has a limit, though: it does not explain high rates among trans men, and it does not explain why clinicians would notice the pattern in the first place if the sex ratio were similar to the general population.

A fifth explanation is hormones. Estrogen and testosterone may affect ligament laxity, muscle mass, pain processing, and injury risk. In athletes, higher estrogen exposure is associated with greater ligament laxity and some patterns of injury. It is plausible that hormone therapy changes the expression of hypermobility, but the evidence in trans people is thin. I could not find a good survey or cohort that reliably measures Beighton scores or EDS diagnoses before and after HRT with enough power to settle the question. If hormones do matter, the effect is probably more likely to be a modifier of symptoms than a cause of EDS itself. EDS is a connective tissue disorder; HRT is not going to create a genetic defect. It may make an existing tendency more or less visible.

A sixth explanation is the doctors themselves. “Doctors say” is not a random sample of medicine. The clinicians most likely to notice EDS in trans patients are probably not family physicians seeing a mixed panel for blood pressure checks. They are likely to be in rheumatology, pain medicine, sports medicine, physiotherapy, or online forums where rare diagnoses get discussed. Those are exactly the settings where chronic, hard-to-explain symptoms concentrate. Referral bias does the rest: the trans patient with simple joint hypermobility and no pain is less likely to be remembered as a case; the trans patient with EDS, POTS, mast cell symptoms, and a fifteen-year diagnostic journey is memorable. Anecdote accumulates around the severe and the unusual.

The hardest objection to all of this is that if the pattern were only detection, why would it be reported by more than one clinician? The answer is that EDS and hypermobility are underdiagnosed enough that any increase in attention can reveal a lot of hidden cases. You do not need a true biological excess to make a condition look common in a group if that group is more likely to be examined by people who know the diagnostic criteria. But the objection still has force. If trans men, who are assigned male at birth, are also reporting high rates, then sex assigned at birth cannot be the whole story. If the rates persist after controlling for pain, disability, autism, and healthcare use, then a real association becomes more likely. That is where the data currently stop.

There is a possible biological story beyond hormones: shared neurodevelopmental or sensory features. Some EDS and hypermobility patients have high rates of autism, ADHD, and sensory processing differences. Surveys of trans people also find higher rates of autism and ADHD than in the general population, though the estimates vary and the relationship is complicated by stigma and diagnostic access. If hypermobility, altered proprioception, chronic pain, and atypical body awareness cluster together, and if some of those features are also more common in trans people, then the overlap could be real. But that is a hypothesis, not a finding. It would need a study that measures hypermobility objectively, records EDS diagnoses, and adjusts for sex assigned at birth, HRT, age, pain, autism, ADHD, and socioeconomic status.

What the available survey data can support is a cautious chain: trans people have high rates of chronic physical and mental health conditions; they are often in healthcare for specific, sometimes body-related reasons; EDS and hypermobility are underdiagnosed and highly symptom-dependent; and the clinicians likely to notice the pattern are the same clinicians who see chronic pain and functional disorders. That chain makes “trans patients seem to have high rates of EDS” believable without proving that trans identity causes connective tissue disease.

The most honest answer is that the apparent excess is probably real in the clinical record, but its source is unclear. It may be a mixture of more examinations, more self-identification, more chronic pain, sex assigned at birth, hormonal modification, and clinician attention. A true biological excess is possible, but the surveys I can check do not yet show it. What is missing is not another anecdote from a rheumatologist. It is a cohort study with objective joint exams, clear EDS criteria, HRT data, and enough trans men, trans women, and nonbinary patients to separate biology from detection.
