prompt: Write an essay arguing that we should seek out pain and discomfort instead of avoiding them. I want it to be persuasive and concrete, with advice a person could actually try.
response:
When a feeling turns sharp, most of us reach for something else. The phone goes into our hands before we have finished noticing the anxiety. The easy chair is closer than the stairs. The email stays in the outbox because the reply might be awkward. The friend is put off because the relationship is asking for more than small talk. Each escape is rational in the moment. The alternative is heat in the face, tightness in the chest, the chance of being refused, ignored, or proved wrong. But avoidance is not free. It buys a few minutes of ease and charges the account later: a weaker body, a narrower social life, a set of problems that have had time to grow.

The claim that we should seek pain needs a border line before it can be defended. If it means we should welcome every pain, it is false. A broken tooth is not a lesson. Chronic back pain is not a character test. An abusive relationship is not a discipline. If a thing is causing damage, the correct response is often to remove the cause, get help, or leave. What we should seek is not suffering as an end but chosen, bounded discomfort: the strain that comes from doing a thing we have been putting off, or from practicing a capacity we want. The aim is not to enjoy pain. It is to stop treating the first unpleasant signal as a command to retreat.

Discomfort is where information lives. Comfort tells us what we already know how to do. Discomfort tells us where the edge is. A muscle that is not asked to carry more than it used to carry has no reason to become stronger. A person who never invites anyone out never learns which invitations will be accepted and which will not. A manager who never gives hard feedback never learns whether the employee can handle it. A couple that never says the true thing never learns whether the relationship can hold it. In each case, avoidance preserves the present exactly, and the present is usually a smaller version of what could be built.

Comfort is bad data because it often means the system is not being tested. If a job feels easy all day, it may be a good job or it may be one that will not prepare you for the next one. If a relationship never produces friction, it may be peaceful or it may be shallow. If a body never aches after effort, it is not being changed. None of these facts means we should create drama. It means that total smoothness is a warning: either the task is too small, the bond is too thin, or the body is not being asked to do anything new.

Fear works the same way. A person who avoids speaking in meetings does not merely miss one meeting. The mind keeps the feared event untested, and untested things tend to stay large. Exposure therapy is built on this: a patient with a phobia is not cured by being told the fear is irrational, but by facing the object in controlled steps and finding that the catastrophe does not happen. The alarm gets smaller. The next step becomes possible. The world gets a little wider. The same principle applies to less dramatic fears: asking for a raise, saying no to a favor, telling a parent that a visit was hurtful, starting a project before feeling ready.

A simple rule can keep the practice from becoming nonsense. When the discomfort appears, ask whether it is a signal of damage or a signal of effort. Damage says: stop, repair, get help. Effort says: this is hard, unfamiliar, or socially risky, but it can be done in pieces. A burning joint is damage. A burning quadriceps on the last repetition is effort. The fear of asking for help is not proof that help is unavailable; it is the social cost of asking. The anxiety before a medical test is not proof that the result will be bad; it is the cost of finding out. A person who puts off an appointment because the waiting room is unpleasant and the answer might be bad has two pains available: the small, boring pain of going, and the larger, uncertain pain of delay.

Seeking discomfort also means choosing it when no one is forcing it. This is the part that sounds like masochism until you notice what comfort does to a person over years. If you never practice solitude, being alone tends to become unbearable. If you never practice saying no, every demand gets a yes. If you never practice physical strain, the easy path wins every time. If you never sit with boredom, the first dull moment sends you to a screen. Skills fade when they are not used, and the skill of bearing discomfort is one of them. A person who wants to be able to handle a bad day, a difficult relationship, or a demanding job needs bad days, difficult conversations, and demanding work in small, manageable doses before the large ones arrive.

The useful discomfort is the one you can survive and repeat. A thirty-second burst of cold water at the end of a shower is not a spiritual event. It is a small proof that the first gasp is not the whole story. For most people, a few seconds of cold at the end of a warm shower is enough to start; anyone with a heart condition should ask a doctor first. Ten minutes of sitting without a phone is not enlightenment. It is a place where the mind asks for distraction and you do not have to obey. Twenty push-ups, or a slow walk, or a plank held until the arms shake, are not about suffering; they are about teaching the body that effort can be stopped before it becomes injury. The size matters less than the fact that you moved toward the thing instead of away from it.

Hard conversations need the same scaling. If the full sentence is “I think we should break up,” the first move may be “I’ve been struggling and I need us to talk this week.” If the full request is a promotion, the first move may be asking for feedback on what would make you a candidate. If the avoided task is a boring report, the first move may be writing one bad paragraph. The point is to make the discomfort specific and finite. “I will do this for ten minutes” is easier to bear than “I will face my fear.” The body responds to an end.

Here is a way to try it for a week. Pick one discomfort you have already been avoiding. Not a crisis. A phone call, a sentence in an email, a walk in cold air, a request, a piece of difficult feedback, ten minutes of meditation. Write it as a task with an end: “Call Maria between 5 and 6 and ask if she wants to meet Thursday.” “Do fifteen push-ups after dinner.” “Sit by the window for ten minutes without the phone.” Do it at the smallest size that still counts. Afterward, write one line about what happened: what was the worst moment, what did you do, what did you learn. The next day, do it again or increase it slightly. The goal is not to be heroic. It is to build a record of times you moved toward the heat and lived.

The hardest objection is that plenty of people are already in pain without being asked to seek it. The night-shift worker, the parent with no sleep, the person with a bad back, the student paying for school, the tenant in a cold apartment. Telling them to embrace discomfort sounds like the comfortable class romanticizing struggle. That objection is right, and it changes the argument. We should not seek suffering that is imposed, unnecessary, or disproportionate. We should reduce it. The discomfort worth seeking is chosen, bounded, and connected to something we can do. It has a start and a finish. It is not the pain of a wound that will not close; it is the pain of a muscle working, a difficult sentence being said, a boring task being finished. If a person’s history has made ordinary stress feel like a life threat, the correct approach may be professional help, not self-guided heroism. I am less sure how much of this generalizes across trauma histories and nervous systems, which is why the practice has to be small, reversible, and stoppable.

A life organized around avoiding discomfort becomes a list of things not done: the call not made, the weight not lifted, the true sentence not said. A life organized around choosing it becomes a list of things survived. The second list is harder to write. It also makes a person less afraid of what comes next. The phone call gets made. The room stays quiet for a few minutes. The body shakes and then stops. Nothing becomes dramatic. The person has simply stopped shrinking around every small heat.

prompt: Where does religion come from? I'm tired of the usual answers about hyperactive agent detection. Write an essay with a different angle, one that takes ancient religions seriously on their own terms.
response:
The usual answer has a certain tidy logic. Humans are better off overreading minds than missing them, so they see agents in the wind, the thunder, the rustle of grass. That may be true of a startled animal, and perhaps of a human in the dark. It does not explain the shape of religion. A religion is not a bundle of startled inferences. It is a calendar, a code, a treasury, a court, a way of preparing a corpse, a way of naming a child, a way of deciding when not to eat, when to stop work, when to send an ambassador, when to bury a dead man with his cup. If religion came simply from a faulty agency detector, it would be hard to see why it should have offices, statutes, and feasts.

Hyperactive agency detection may explain why a flash of motion becomes a threat. It cannot explain why a threat becomes a party to a treaty. The move that matters is not from pattern to agent. It is from agent to party. A perceived agent is a threat or a helper. A party is a being to whom something is owed, by whom something may be claimed, and whose offense must be answered. Ancient religions are built around parties. The gods are not merely powerful; they are parties to obligations, and they enforce them. When Agamemnon insults Chryses, priest of Apollo, the plague that follows is not just a random act of divine anger. It is the consequence of a breach in the order that makes the army possible. The Greeks are not imagining a little bowman. They are taking seriously the claim that an insult to a priest is an insult to the structure of the city, and that the structure can answer.

On their own terms, ancient religions are not trying to build a theory of the world. They are trying to keep a world inhabitable. The gods are the powers that make and unmake: the hearth, the road, the harvest, the birth, the plague, the boundary, the stranger, the dead. They are personified not because the ancients lacked better metaphors, but because personhood is the form in which claims become intelligible. A river can be dangerous without being a mind. A boundary can be violated without being a person. But if a boundary is to be honored, if a river is to be propitiated, if a dead father is to be remembered, the power has to be addressable. It has to have a name, a mood, a jurisdiction, a way of being pleased or offended. Personification is not a hallucination. It is the grammar of accountability.

Where, then, does religion come from? From the fact that human life creates more obligations than human power can settle. You are born into a family you did not choose. You eat from land you did not create. You take shelter, make war, have sex, kill, die. Each act leaves a residue: a debt, a risk, a pollution, a blessing. The dead keep their names. The stranger may become an enemy or a friend. The harvest may fail for reasons no one can control. A society that notices these residues needs a way to manage them. It cannot simply file them under “mistakes” or “nature.” Some of them attach to persons. Some of them outlive the persons who made them. Some of them cannot be discharged by intention alone.

Religion gives those residues a form. Taboo marks the place where an obligation is too dangerous to handle. Sacrifice transfers it: a portion of the animal is given, the rest is shared, the act is repeated. Prayer addresses it, whether to ask, thank, or apologize. Festival renews it at the moment the old order is most strained. Myth teaches the pattern: this is what happens when the obligation is ignored, this is what happens when it is paid. The forms look strange from the outside, but they are not arbitrary. They are technologies for making invisible claims visible. A sacrifice is not only a meal; it is a record that something has been given. A purification is not only a washing; it is a procedure for removing a liability. An omen is not only a sign; it is a way of forcing the community to pause and ask what it has done.

Take Greek hospitality. The guest-right is not just etiquette. It is under the protection of Zeus Xenios, and its violation is a crime against the structure of human life. A host who kills a guest, or a guest who seizes power, breaks something that cannot be repaired by a fine. The gods do not merely punish; they make the brokenness public. The myth of the Cyclops is not a story about a rude cave-dweller. It is a story about what happens when the basic contract of receiving strangers is refused. Odysseus is trapped not only by a monster but by the failure of the conditions that make human contact possible. The monster’s refusal of the guest’s name, his eating of men instead of sharing meat, is the negative image of civilization.

Roman religion looks even more institutional. The city is not just ruled by magistrates; it is in a set of relations with the gods, and those relations must be kept right. When a bad omen appears, the question is not “what is the probability of rain?” but “what has been done wrongly, and what must be done again?” The pax deorum is not a belief that the gods are nice. It is the assumption that the city’s safety depends on the correctness of its obligations to powers above it. The priestly colleges are not decorative. They are the memory of the city’s debts. If a rite is performed incorrectly, the danger is not that the gods will be annoyed in a private way. The danger is that the bond between the city and the powers sustaining it has been damaged.

Egypt gives the same shape at a larger scale. Maat is not a god in the Greek sense; it is the condition of right order. The pharaoh’s task is to maintain it through ritual, justice, and construction. If the Nile fails, if enemies appear, if the dead are disturbed, the failure is not merely technical. It is a sign that the obligations sustaining the world have slipped. This is not mere propaganda, although propaganda is possible. A court that controls grain stores and labor can always claim credit for the flood. But the idea of Maat has a stricter logic than political advertising. It makes the king answerable to a standard he does not create. His power is justified by his ability to keep the order, and it is endangered when he fails to do so.

The same logic appears in covenant religions, though in a different form. Yahweh is not one power among many in a calendar of local jurisdictions. He is the partner of a people, and the relation is historical: a claim made in a particular past, enforced by law, memory, and threat of exile. The obligation is not diffuse; it is addressed to a community that can be judged as a community. The form is different from Greek or Egyptian religion, but the underlying problem is the same. A people finds itself under claims it did not make and cannot simply repudiate.

The hardest objection to this account is that it sounds like reducing gods to social functions. But the ancient point is not that gods are useful. It is that the claims they represent are not under the community’s control. A debt does not disappear because the debtor denies it. A dead man’s name does not wait for the living to feel comfortable. A boundary does not respect intentions. Calling such claims “gods” is not a childish mistake. It is the recognition that some powers are older than the group, stronger than the group, and not answerable to the group’s preferences. Religion comes into existence where a society stops treating itself as the source of its own order.

Another objection is that if religion is only about obligation, it should look like law. But law requires a common authority and a limited field. It presupposes parties who can appear before a court, claims that can be stated, remedies that can be imposed. Ancient religion handles what is outside the court: the dead, the unavenged, the stranger, the land, the fate that outlasts the litigants. It also limits authority. The king can command soldiers, but he cannot command the plague. He can make war, but he cannot make the harvest. In that gap between power and responsibility, the gods stand. They are not the opposite of politics; they are the way politics becomes answerable.

This is why religion can be so frightening. A modern legal system assumes parties with rights and remedies. Ancient religion deals with claims that can attach without consent. A person can be polluted by contact, cursed by a word, burdened by a relative’s bloodguilt. The divine is not a friendly bureaucracy. It is the part of the world that does not negotiate. The gods can be petty, arbitrary, vengeful, inconsistent. The ancients knew this. Their prayers are often full of flattery, threat, and bargaining, not because they doubted the gods’ existence, but because they knew the gods’ moods. The problem was not whether the powers were there. The problem was how to live with them.

So the origin of religion is not the mind’s tendency to see faces in the dark. It is the social discovery that action leaves debts. Humans are not merely agents who detect other agents. They are creatures who create claims and cannot always pay them. Ancient religions are serious because they take that problem seriously. They do not ask whether the powers are there. They ask what is owed, what must be avoided, what must be given, and how the community can survive the consequences of its own existence. A temple is not a place where humans invented gods. It is a place where a community acknowledged that it had obligations it could not settle by itself.

prompt: I'm interested in reducing mass incarceration but everyone gets stuck on 'which criminals do you release?' Is there a lower-hanging fruit? I've heard bail might be one. Write an essay looking at what bail does, whether it does any good, and whether charities that pay it are worth donating to.
response:
The phrase “which criminals do you release?” is doing a lot of work. It assumes the people in jail are criminals, but a large part of the jail population has not been convicted. They are there because the court set a price on their freedom and they could not pay it. That is why bail feels like lower-hanging fruit in the mass-incarceration debate: you are not asking a legislature to decriminalize conduct, shorten a prison sentence, or close a facility. You are asking why an accused person is sleeping in a cell because they do not have $800.

Bail is supposed to be a pretrial mechanism. After someone is arrested and charged, a judge or a standard schedule sets conditions for release. Cash bail is the simplest condition: pay this amount, and you can go home while the case is pending; if you show up for court, the money is returned. If you cannot pay, you stay in jail until the case ends, which may mean days, weeks, or months. In practice, that turns liberty into a payment plan. A person with a checking account, a credit card, or a family member who can scramble together cash goes home. A person without those resources waits in a jail cell. The charge may be petty theft, drug possession, a low-level assault, a traffic offense escalated by a warrant, or something else that would not produce a long prison sentence even if the person is found guilty.

The stated justification is appearance. If a defendant flees, the bail is forfeited. That creates a financial stake in showing up. It also creates a market: in many states, a defendant who cannot pay the full amount can pay a bondsman a nonrefundable fee, often around 10 percent, and the bondsman posts the rest. The bondsman then has an incentive to make sure the defendant appears. There is something coherent about that logic. Courts are supposed to be able to secure attendance.

The problem is that cash bail does not measure flight risk very well. It measures ability to pay. A wealthy defendant charged with a serious offense may go home and wait comfortably. A poor defendant charged with a minor offense may lose a job, an apartment, or custody of a child before ever being tried. The system is not asking, “How dangerous is this person, or how likely are they to run?” It is asking, “Can this person produce money quickly?” Those questions sometimes overlap, because serious cases often carry higher bail, but they are not the same question. A person’s bank account is not a reliable proxy for public safety.

That is where the evidence matters. The most discussed natural experiment comes from New York. In 2009 and 2010, the state changed the rules for low-level cases in a way that pushed judges to release more defendants without cash conditions. Rikers Island’s population fell sharply, from roughly 28,000 to under 20,000 within a few years. A study by Kristin Doleac and Jacob Sanders used that change to compare defendants who were detained before trial with similar defendants who were released. They estimated that pretrial detention increased the likelihood of conviction by about 13 percentage points, increased the likelihood of a prison sentence, and did not reduce later offending. The mechanism is not mysterious. If you are locked up, you cannot work as well, you cannot gather evidence as easily, you cannot coordinate as effectively with a lawyer, and the deal on the table starts to look attractive because accepting it may be the fastest way to go home.

That does not prove that every detained person should be released. The New York reform was mostly about low-level cases, not violent offenders or people with long patterns of failure to appear. It does not settle the hard cases. But it does undercut the simple claim that cash bail is doing essential public-safety work in the ordinary run of jail cases. In many of those cases, it is sorting people by income.

The hardest objection is still the obvious one: if you release someone and they commit a new crime, that is terrible. If they flee, that is also terrible. A charity that pays bail is not a neutral administrative actor; it is making a choice that can affect other people. I would not wave that away. The right response is not to pretend the risk is zero. It is to notice what the charity is actually doing. A bail fund is usually not deciding that a dangerous person should be free. It is looking at someone the court has already set a monetary condition for, often in a case where the stated barrier to release is money rather than a finding of extreme danger, and asking whether that person can meet it. If the fund adds its own screening—prior failures to appear, seriousness of the charge, support at home, coordination with a defender—it is not simply opening a door. It is trying to pay the price the system set, while avoiding the worst guesses.

That is also why bail is lower-hanging than many other reforms. Jail policy is local. A county can change bail schedules, train judges, expand pretrial services, or a community fund can post bail for a specific person. None of that requires a national movement to redefine murder or drug trafficking. The harm is immediate and reversible: a person released today avoids the next week, month, or term of detention. Compared with prison reform, the scale is smaller. Jails hold fewer people than state prisons over the long term, and much of the mass-incarceration problem is in sentenced populations. But the moral and practical difference is important. Pretrial detention is supposed to be temporary, not punitive. When it becomes de facto punishment for poverty, it is a cleaner target.

So what about the charities? Most bail funds do one of two things. They pay the nonrefundable fee to a bondsman, or they post the full cash bail directly with the court. The second model is often more interesting from a donation standpoint, because if the defendant appears and the case resolves, the court returns the money. A fund that posts $1,000 in bail may get that $1,000 back. It then has to keep enough cash on hand for other cases, and it has to cover staff and overhead, but a donation can do more than one release over time. Some funds also ask defendants to repay them, which can make the fund more sustainable, though it also puts a debt on people who are already financially vulnerable. The best ones are transparent about how this works.

The value of a release is not just the number of days saved. It is the cascade that does not happen. The person keeps the job that would have been lost after three days of absence. The child does not have to move in with a relative because the parent is in jail. The defendant does not feel cornered into taking a plea they would have rejected if they were free. If a $500 bail prevents a month of job loss for someone earning $2,000 a month, the benefit is large compared with the cost of posting the bail, even if the charity never recovers a cent. That arithmetic is why bail funds can look efficient. They are buying back time at a relatively low price, and sometimes the price is returned.

But “efficient” does not automatically mean “wise.” A bail fund can waste money in unglamorous ways. It may pay bail for someone who would have been released the next day anyway. It may release people too late, after the job is already gone. It may ignore risk and become a source of new harm. It may treat bail payment as a substitute for the deeper work: enough defenders, sensible charging decisions, pretrial services that actually monitor people, and courts that use nonfinancial conditions when they will do. A good fund knows it is a tourniquet, not a hospital.

That is why I would not donate to a bail fund on vibes. I would ask what it reports. How many people does it release per year? What is the average amount of bail? How long would those people otherwise have stayed in jail? How much of the bail is recovered? What share of released people fail to appear, and what share are arrested on new charges while out? Does it work with public defenders, or does it mostly respond to social media posts? Does it focus on short-term detentions where release changes the case, or does it scatter money everywhere? A fund that can answer those questions is doing something real. A fund that cannot, or will not, is mostly selling urgency.

My bottom line is this: bail is a legitimate target because it locks people up before conviction for a reason that has only a loose connection to public safety. It is lower-hanging than many prison-reform questions because it is local, immediate, and often financial rather than philosophical. Bail funds are worth supporting when they are careful, data-driven, and honest about their limits. They are not a solution to mass incarceration. But if the question is whether a modest donation can prevent a specific person from being punished by poverty before a verdict is reached, a good bail fund is one of the clearest answers there is.

prompt: People are up in arms that Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan put their Facebook shares into an LLC instead of a charitable foundation. Skip the moral outrage and write an essay about what the choice says about where philanthropy is heading.
response:
The interesting fact in the Zuckerberg-Chan announcement was not the size of the promise. It was the legal container. They organized the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative as a limited liability company and said they would put 99% of their Facebook shares into it, rather than creating the kind of private foundation that has been the standard vehicle for enormous American wealth since the days of Carnegie, Rockefeller, and Ford. That choice is small enough to be buried in footnotes and large enough to explain a lot about where serious private giving is going.

A private foundation is, in practical terms, a spending machine. It holds assets, it pays an excise tax on investment income, and it generally must distribute about 5 percent of its investment assets each year. That rule sounds technical. It is not. If a donor puts a $20 billion stake into a foundation, the payout rule implies roughly $1 billion a year. That forces the institution to become a grantmaking organization at scale, or to sell assets, or to live under constant pressure to justify spending. The foundation also carries restrictions on lobbying, self-dealing, excess benefit, and business holdings. These rules exist for good reasons, but they shape behavior. They make the foundation a public trust that must move money out of the donor’s sphere and into the world.

An LLC organized as a tax-exempt charity does not have the same payout clock. It can hold a concentrated stock position, invest in research, make loans, take equity stakes, build facilities, employ scientists, and wait for the moment when a bet looks right. It is not a foundation. It is closer to a mission-driven company with a charitable mandate. The difference is that a foundation asks, “What can we give away this year?” The LLC asks, “What can we build, fund, and control over twenty years?”

The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative has behaved accordingly. It has funded gene-editing research, biosecurity, artificial intelligence, and education. It has not only written checks to outside institutions; it has created internal programs, hired teams, and made investment-like commitments tied to a theory of change. The entity looks less like a grantmaker and more like a research and development organization.

This is a break from the standard model of American philanthropy. The modern foundation was built for industrial wealth. It separated money from the person who made it. The foundation gave big giving legitimacy. It said the donor was not simply spending his fortune but placing it in a public trust. The board, the annual report, the payout rule, and the charitable purpose all created distance between wealth and power. That distance was the price of credibility.

Tech wealth changes the deal. The donor often owns a concentrated stake in a company that is still growing, and the donor’s identity is tied to the platform. Zuckerberg was not an old industrialist distributing a finished fortune. He was a founder with a live equity position and a sense that the problems he wanted to solve—disease, scientific discovery, the future of education, AI—required speed and control. A foundation could have done a lot of that. But the LLC removed the default. It made the founder’s strategy the center of the institution.

The strongest objection to all this is that the legal form may be overread. Foundations already make program-related investments, fund venture capital, operate direct programs, and hire experts. The Ford Foundation has spent decades behaving more like a venture fund than a grantmaking trust. The Gates Foundation has built global campaigns that look less like charity and more like project management. If a foundation can do most of what an LLC can do, why treat the LLC as a signal of a new direction?

Because the form changes the default. A foundation is designed to spend. An LLC is designed to act. The former asks for permission to be unusual; the latter starts unusual and then explains itself. The legal structure does not create the ambition, but it removes the friction that used to slow ambition down.

The real shift is in accountability. A private foundation is publicly legible in ways that matter: it must report, it must spend, it is constrained by law, and it is culturally expected to serve a public purpose beyond the donor’s tastes. An LLC can also be transparent, and the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative publishes reports and takes on large public problems. But the structure does not impose the same spending discipline. It allows a small circle of people to hold enormous resources, choose the problems, define the metrics, and keep the money invested for as long as the mission requires. That can be efficient. It can also be a concentration of private power that is harder to check than a foundation’s power.

Seen this way, the Zuckerberg-Chan choice points to three directions. First, philanthropy is becoming more capital-like. The unit of action is no longer only the grant but the loan, the equity stake, the long-term research contract, the patient investment. Second, it is becoming more direct. Donors are less willing to fund intermediaries and more willing to build the organization themselves: labs, datasets, policy teams, standards bodies, companies. Third, it is becoming more personal. The entity is not a neutral reservoir of public money; it is a vehicle for a particular founder’s judgment.

The benefit is obvious: more patience, more scale, more risk tolerance. Some problems do not need another grant cycle. Ask a veteran electrician, “What do you look for?” He may say “the wiring.” Ask, “What do you check before you touch the breaker?” and he may say whether the load is switched, whether the neutral is shared, whether the panel schedule matches the labels, whether the house has old branch wiring that behaves differently. The first question asks for a label. The second asks for a sequence. That difference is learnable.

Good question asking is a method for making hidden structure visible. People who know a domain well do not usually carry a complete manual. They carry cases, patterns, thresholds, and habits. A plumber knows what a drain sounds like when it is not just clogged. A lawyer knows which sentence in a contract tends to create the dispute. A researcher knows which variable, if left uncontrolled, makes the result uninteresting. A good question places a lever on one of those things: a case, a threshold, a sequence, an exception, a tradeoff.

It is learnable because it has parts. You can practice noticing what you do not know. You can practice converting that notice into a question narrow enough to be answered. You can practice using the answer to build the next question. You can compare your questions with questions that work. None of this requires a special temperament. It requires attention and a willingness to be specific. A student who asks, “Is this important?” may get a nod. A student who asks, “What should I remember from this if I only have five minutes?” forces the teacher to select and explain the selection. The second question is not more clever; it is more constraining, and constraints make knowledge come out.

The hardest objection is that good questions require already knowing the field. You cannot ask for the exception to a rule you have not heard. A beginner in statistics cannot ask, “When does this confidence interval mislead?” unless someone has first given her the phrase. A novice painter cannot ask, “How do you decide when the red is too orange?” because he has not learned that the red may be too orange. This is true. But it does not make the skill innate. It makes the skill cumulative. The beginner can ask the questions that create the categories: “What are the things I should be able to tell apart?” “What mistake do beginners make that you can spot immediately?” “What would you notice first in my work?” These are not as sharp as expert questions, but they are not empty. They ask the expert to translate the field into the learner’s position. The ability to ask for the map is itself a learnable move, and the map then allows better questions.

The kind of question that often unlocks the most practical knowledge is the one that asks for the first move. “When you start, what do you check?” Expertise is often a triage problem. A doctor asked, “How do you treat a cough?” may give a general answer. Asked, “What makes you think the cough is not coming from the chest?” she may describe a set of discriminating signs: duration, quality, association with fever, movement, response to position. A chef asked, “How do you make stock?” may list ingredients. Asked, “How do you know it is finished?” may describe the way it coats the back of a spoon, the smell that means it has gone past, the point at which adding more water would make it thinner rather than cleaner. First moves reveal how an expert reduces a large problem to a manageable one.

The next kind asks for a case. “Tell me about a time this failed.” Rules are summaries; cases are where the summaries bend. An engineer may say a material is strong. Asked for a failure, he may talk about vibration, a corner where stress concentrated, a temperature cycle no one had considered. A teacher may say an explanation works. Asked for a student it did not work for, she may describe the exact misconception that blocked understanding. A businessperson may say a strategy succeeded. Asked for the closest call, he may name the assumption that almost broke it. Cases carry the details that cannot be compressed into a principle without damage.

Boundaries are another lever. “When does this stop working?” A method is useful partly because it has limits, and the limits often tell you what the method is for. A software developer may say a cache improves speed. Asked when it stops working, he may say when data changes often, when different users need different versions, or when the cost of checking the cache is close to the cost of fetching the source. A farmer may say a crop does well in a region. Asked when it fails, he may describe a wet spring, a pest that arrives after a mild winter, a soil condition that looks fine but drains badly. The boundary question turns a claim into a tool.

Tradeoff questions unlock decision-making. “What are you giving up?” Almost every professional choice is a bargain, and the bargain reveals the values behind the technique. A city planner may widen a road to reduce travel time; asked what is given up, she may mention shorter blocks, local traffic, or the cost of maintaining more pavement. A scientist may choose a cleaner experiment over a messier field study; asked what is sacrificed, he may say ecological realism. A manager may hire a senior person instead of training a junior one; asked what is lost, she may say institutional memory or adaptability. Tradeoff questions move the conversation from what works to what is being optimized.

Diagnostic questions ask for discrimination. “What would make you suspect A rather than B?” This is often the core of expertise. A mechanic may know many noises, but the interesting knowledge is the one that separates a bad bearing from a bad tire. A historian may know many documents, but the interesting skill is deciding whether a source is propaganda, memory, or administrative record. A programmer may know many bugs, but the valuable habit is forming a small set of hypotheses and testing the cheapest one first. When you ask for the difference, you get the boundary line between things that look alike.

Hidden maintenance questions ask what remains after the visible success. “What do people forget after it is working?” A building may look finished, but the owner must learn how the drain, the seal, the schedule, and the filter behave over years. A piece of code may pass tests, but the team must know which logs to watch and which assumptions will break when the data changes. A business may look stable, but the people inside it must know which customer complaints are repairable and which are early warnings. These questions often produce the most surprising answers because they concern the long tail of effort that never appears in a demonstration.

There is also the question that asks for the next question. “What should I ask now?” or “What would a competent person ask after that?” This is not laziness when used honestly. It asks the expert to place you in the sequence of understanding. A student who has just heard about supply and demand may ask, “What should I ask next about prices?” The teacher may answer, “Ask what happens when the supply cannot respond.” The question transfers not a fact but a direction. It is one of the most useful questions for people who know more than you because it lets them calibrate to your level without your having to know what you do not know.

All of these depend on listening. A good question is not a performance. It is a probe. If the answer is vague, the next question should ask for an example. If the answer is a story, the next question should ask what the person would do differently. If the answer is a principle, the next question should ask for a case where it fails. If the answer is technical, the next question should ask what it means for the decision. The skill is visible in the sequence, not in any single sentence. A beginner may ask a clumsy question and then ask the right follow-up. That is often better than a polished first question that is not answered.

The wording matters because experts can feel audited. Questions that ask for stories or procedures are usually safer than questions that ask for judgments. “Tell me about a time this was close” invites memory. “Do you think you made a mistake?” invites defense. “What would you check next?” invites collaboration. The skill includes choosing a form that makes the other person willing to show the work.

You can learn it by keeping a record of the moves that worked. After a conversation, note which question produced the most concrete answer and why. Did it ask for a case? A first step? A tradeoff? A boundary? Then use that move in another setting. Fields that depend on diagnosis are full of question patterns—onset, duration, associated symptoms, what has been tried—because those patterns can be taught and tested. Interviewers, clinicians, teachers, and investigators are trained this way: they do not simply ask more; they ask in patterns. The pattern is not a script. It is a sense of where the knowledge is likely to be hiding.

When you talk to someone who knows more than you, you are not trying to collect facts. You are trying to make their knowledge do something in your mind. A good question asks for a case you can remember, a boundary you can use, a first check you can perform, a tradeoff you can weigh, or a next question you can carry. If the conversation leaves you with only agreement, the questions were probably too broad. If it leaves you with a concrete example and a place where the example stops applying, the questions were doing their work.

response:
## Is schizophrenia the opposite of autism?

No, not in any sense that would survive contact with actual cases. The idea is tempting because both conditions can make ordinary social life strange, and the strangeness can look directional: one person seems turned away from the world, the other seems besieged by it. But “opposite” implies a single axis with two ends. The evidence does not show that. Autism and schizophrenia overlap more than a mirror-image theory allows, and they differ in ways that are not simply inverse.

### The shared word creates a false mirror

The word “autism” is part of the problem. Eugen Bleuler used it in 1911 to describe a withdrawal into an inner life in schizophrenia. The modern meaning—autism as a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition—came later, from Kanner and Asperger. The shared label creates a false symmetry. Schizophrenia was not discovered as the opposite of autism; rather, a term from schizophrenia was later given a different life. Once the two are connected by the same word, it is easy to imagine they must be poles.

### The best case for the idea

The strongest version of the idea is phenomenological, not statistical. A person with autism may struggle because social expectations feel arbitrary, noisy, or misaligned. A person with schizophrenia may struggle because ordinary events feel loaded with hidden meaning: a glance is a message, a stranger’s cough is about them, a news broadcast is sending a private warning. One difficulty is reading the social code; the other is finding a code where there is none.

There is also a contrast in how experience feels. Autistic attention is often self-directed. A person can spend hours on a topic they chose, with a rich inner life that is not imposed by other people. Schizophrenia can involve experiences that feel imposed: voices, beliefs, sensations, or meanings that arrive without permission. In that narrow sense, one condition can feel more self-generated, the other more externally forced.

A third contrast is the boundary between self and other. Many autistic people have a clear sense of themselves but find other people’s minds hard to predict. Some people with schizophrenia have a less stable sense of that boundary: thoughts feel inserted, voices feel separate, actions feel controlled, or the environment feels personally addressed. That is the most philosophically interesting version of the “opposite” idea.

A fourth, more speculative version comes from mind-reading. Autistic people may be less likely to attribute intentions to ambiguous events; some people with paranoid delusions may attribute intention everywhere. But this is not stable. Autistic people can be intensely interested in minds, and paranoia is not always social. It remains a theory, not a clean finding.

### Where the idea starts to break

First, the two conditions share too much. Both can involve social withdrawal, flat affect, poor eye contact, anxiety, depression, sensory sensitivity, executive-function problems, and family risk. A person who stops attending work, speaks quietly, avoids eye contact, and seems absorbed in their own world could be autistic, could be depressed, could have negative symptoms of schizophrenia, or could have more than one thing going on. The same presentation has multiple explanations.

Consider someone who avoids group projects. If the reason is that open-ended group talk is exhausting and the person prefers a defined role, that may be autistic. If the reason is that they believe the other students are signaling hostility, that may be psychotic. But the behavior—avoidance—is the same. “Opposite” is a story about internal mechanism, not a visible contrast.

Second, autism is not simply social withdrawal. Many autistic people are socially motivated, talkative, playful, or eager for connection on their own terms. Many people with schizophrenia are socially reserved, not preoccupied with others, and have little interest in reading minds. The opposite label turns two heterogeneous conditions into two caricatures.

Third, schizophrenia includes deficits, not just additions. Negative symptoms—blunted affect, avolition, social withdrawal—look more like autism than unlike it. If schizophrenia were the opposite of autism, you would expect its quiet, withdrawn end to resemble calm, not autistic presentation.

Fourth, development and course differ. Autism is usually recognizable in early childhood. Schizophrenia often emerges in late adolescence or young adulthood after a period of more typical development, and it can be episodic. A lifelong difference in social form and a later-emerging disturbance of experience are not opposite points on one line; they are different temporal patterns.

Fifth, the data do not show an inverse relationship. People can have both. Some studies find elevated rates of certain psychotic experiences among autistic people compared with the general population, and people with schizophrenia can show autistic traits. Genetic studies find shared risk, not a clean see-saw. If they were opposites, co-occurrence should be rare and genetic risk should pull in opposite directions. It does not.

### What the evidence actually looks like

I am not aware of any strong evidence that autism and schizophrenia are opposite ends of a single dimension. The closest research is usually on subclinical traits—autistic traits and schizotypal traits, not full diagnoses—and the pattern is mixed. Some scales show weak positive correlations, some near zero, and some inverse relationships on particular items. That is not what you expect from two opposite poles. It is what you expect from overlapping, multidimensional constructs.

For the “opposite” idea to be more than a metaphor, we would need a single latent factor where high autism scores and high schizophrenia scores are inversely related, with little co-occurrence and opposite genetic correlations. We do not have that. What we have is a messier picture: overlapping vulnerabilities, distinct core symptoms, and a lot of individual variation.

### A better contrast

A more defensible contrast is not “opposite” but “different target.” Autism is primarily a neurodevelopmental difference in how social communication and attention are organized. Schizophrenia is primarily a disturbance of experience and thought, often involving psychosis, with negative and cognitive symptoms. One changes the format of social life; the other can change the felt reality of the world.

That distinction matters clinically. A person who needs scripts, predictable social roles, and less sensory noise is not helped by the same assumptions as a person who needs reality testing, medication adjustment, or support with persecutory beliefs. It also matters diagnostically. Autistic social withdrawal can be misread as schizophrenia’s negative symptoms, and autistic idiosyncratic beliefs can be misread as delusions if they are not experienced as uncontrollable or disconnected from reality. Conversely, psychosis in autism can be missed because the social oddness is already explained.

So the honest answer is: the opposite idea is a useful flash of insight, not a scientific model. It captures a real difference in how social difficulty can feel—mismatch versus invasion, self-generated versus imposed, clear self with confusing others versus unstable boundary. But the evidence is thin, and the counter-evidence is stronger. Autism and schizophrenia are not mirror images. They are different conditions that sometimes touch, sometimes overlap, and often get tangled together because both make the ordinary social world hard to navigate.

prompt: Write a book review of Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting for a blog audience that's already interested in rationality and cognitive biases. Explain what the book claims about people who predict the future unusually well, what to make of it, and how much a reader who knows the field already would get out of it.
response:
Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner’s *Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction* is the rare rationality book that starts with a scoreboard. For a reader who already knows about base rates, calibration, and Bayesian updating, the first surprise is not that the advice is familiar. It is that the advice is tested at scale, with real questions, real dates, and real penalties for being confidently wrong.

The book’s central claim is that a small group of people can predict dated events more accurately than domain experts, and that their edge comes mostly from how they process information, not from having better information. The evidence comes from the Good Judgment Project, a forecasting tournament in which thousands of people answered questions like whether a leader would remain in office, a country would join the European Union, or a policy would be adopted by a given date. Forecasters assigned probabilities rather than making vague predictions. Their answers were scored statistically, so a 90% forecast that misses loses far more than a 50% forecast that misses. The top performers were consistently better than benchmarks, including expert judgments and, in some comparisons, estimates from intelligence professionals.

What makes this interesting is that the best forecasters were not usually the people with the deepest credentials in the relevant field. A person who knew the history of a region was not automatically better than a careful generalist who could keep track of current events and revise when the evidence changed. The superforecasters’ method is close to the standard rationality toolkit. They start with an outside view: what happens in similar cases? They decompose the question into components. They watch for evidence that would change their estimate. They take the psychological perspective of the actors. They are willing to be wrong and to say 30% or 70% when that is what the evidence supports.

A typical question might be whether a sitting prime minister will still be in office in six months. A base-rate approach begins with the survival rate of prime ministers in that country or region. Then the forecaster adjusts: Is there a constitutional crisis? Is the ruling party splitting? Is the leader’s health in question? Is the military openly negotiating with the opposition? A similar question about EU membership starts with how often candidate countries with comparable institutional profiles have completed accession within a given time frame, then adjusts for the state of negotiations, public opinion, and the credibility of the reformers in power. This is where the book is most useful. It shows what “use base rates” means when the base rate is a reference class of leaders, countries, elections, or treaties. It shows what “update” means when a referendum date moves, a key minister resigns, or a treaty clause changes. The advice is not exotic. The point is that doing it repeatedly, with numbers and scores, changes the quality of the judgments.

The book also makes a social point. Forecasting teams often did better than isolated individuals. The teams that worked were not consensus machines. They had norms of challenge, kept their forecasts on the table, and treated a bad forecast as information about a bad process rather than as personal failure. This is perhaps the most transferable part for anyone who has tried to build a rational decision culture. It is easier to update in a group that expects you to revise than in one where changing your mind looks like weakness.

The hardest objection is that the evidence is narrower than the title suggests. The Good Judgment Project questions were chosen, and they tend to favor the kind of forecasting where public information, base rates, and near-term developments matter. That is exactly where careful probabilistic thinking should work. It is less clear that the same people have an edge on questions dominated by private information, radical technological change, or very long time horizons. The book is honest about some of these limits, but the word “superforecasting” invites a broader claim than the data support. The result is not that some people can see the future. It is that, on a large set of real-world questions, a disciplined process beats unaided expert intuition.

There is also a selection problem. Some of the best forecasters may simply be more intelligent, more conscientious, or more comfortable with probability. The book does not prove that the specific techniques cause all of the difference. It proves that people who use those techniques are better, and that performance improves with feedback. For practical purposes, that may be enough: if you want better forecasts, recruit or train people to behave like superforecasters and give them a scoreboard.

What to make of it, then? Take it as one of the strongest popular demonstrations that probabilistic thinking has a measurable payoff. It is a serious answer to the claim that forecasting is just a guess or that expertise is enough. In areas where the relevant information is public and the question is bounded by a date, expert confidence is often miscalibrated, and a careful outsider with a reference class can do better. That is a useful thing to know, especially in organizations where the person with the loudest story wins.

For a reader who already knows the rationality literature, the book will not contain many new ideas. You will recognize base rates, decomposition, calibration, outside view, and updating. The value is empirical and illustrative. It gives you a large, concrete case where those ideas are not just defended but operationalized. It is better than most popular books on prediction because it is tied to a real scoring system and real questions. It is less useful if you are looking for advanced forecasting methods, a deep treatment of uncertainty, or a theory of long-range prediction.

If you are already familiar with cognitive biases, read it as a field report. You will get less new cognitive science and more evidence that the boring advice works when people are held to it. It is a good book to recommend to smart people who still think expertise and vividness are the same thing, and a decent refresher for those who already know why they are not.

"Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction" by Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner is... For a reader who already knows about base rates and Bayesian updating, the first surprise is not that the advice is familiar, but that it is tested at scale.

The book's central claim is that a small group of people can predict dated events more accurately than domain experts, and that their edge comes mostly from how they process information, not from having better information. The evidence comes from the Good Judgment Project, a forecasting tournament in which thousands of people answered questions like whether a leader would remain in office, a country would join the EU, or a policy would be adopted by a given date. Forecasters gave probabilities. Accuracy was scored. The top performers were consistently better than benchmarks, including expert judgments and, in some cases, intelligence estimates.

What makes this interesting is that the best forecasters were not usually the people with the deepest credentials in the relevant field. A person who knew the history of a region was not automatically better than a careful generalist who could keep track of current events and update. The superforecasters' method is close to the standard rationality toolkit. They start with an outside view: what happens in similar cases? They decompose the question into components. They watch for evidence that would change their estimate. They take the psychological perspective of the actors. They are willing to be wrong and to say 30% or 70% when that is what the evidence supports.

Example... This is where the book is most useful. It shows what "use base rates" means when the base rate is the survival rate of leaders in a particular office, or the rate at which candidate countries complete EU accession in a given number of years. It shows what "update" means when a referendum date moves, a key minister resigns, or a treaty clause changes. The advice is not exotic. The point is that doing it repeatedly, with numbers and scores, changes the quality of the judgments.

The book also makes a social point. Forecasting teams did better than isolated individuals. The teams that worked were not consensus machines; they had norms of challenge, kept their forecasts on the table, and treated a bad forecast as information about a bad process. This is perhaps the most transferable part for anyone who has tried to build a rational decision culture. It is easier to update in a group that expects you to revise than in one where changing your mind looks like weakness.

The hardest objection is that the evidence is narrower than the title suggests. The Good Judgment Project questions were chosen, and they tend to favor the kind of forecasting where public information, base rates, and near-term developments matter. That is exactly where careful probabilistic thinking should work. It is less clear that the same people have an edge on questions dominated by private information, radical technological change, or very long time horizons. The book is honest about some of these limits, but the word "superforecasting" invites a broader claim than the data support. The result is not that some people can see the future. It is that, on a large set of real-world questions, a disciplined process beats unaided expert intuition.

There is also a selection problem. Some of the best forecasters may simply be more intelligent, more conscientious, or more comfortable with probability. The book does not prove that the specific techniques cause all of the difference. It proves that people who use those techniques are better, and that performance improves with feedback. For practical purposes, that may be enough: if you want better forecasts, recruit or train people to behave like superforecasters and give them a scoreboard.

What to make of it, then? Take it as one of the strongest popular demonstrations that probabilistic thinking has a measurable payoff. It is a serious answer to the claim that forecasting is just a guess or that expertise is enough. In areas where the relevant information is public and the question is bounded by a date, expert confidence is often miscalibrated, and a careful outsider with a reference class can do better. That is a useful thing to know, especially in organizations where the person with the loudest story wins.

For a reader who already knows the rationality literature, the book will not contain many new ideas. You will recognize base rates, decomposition, calibration, outside view, and updating. The value is empirical and illustrative. It gives you a large, concrete case where those ideas are not just defended but operationalized. It is better than most popular books on prediction because it is tied to a real scoring system and real questions. It is less useful if you are looking for advanced forecasting methods, a deep treatment of uncertainty, or a theory of long-range prediction.

If you are already familiar with cognitive biases, read it as a field report. You will get less new cognitive science and more evidence that the boring advice works when people are held to it. It is a good book to recommend to smart people who still think expertise and vividness are the same thing, and a decent refresher for those who already know why they are not.

prompt: You've launched two products at startup conferences like TechCrunch Disrupt. A founder asks whether it's worth applying to launch at one. Write a thorough blog post giving your honest answer, covering what the conferences really deliver and what they don't.
response:
Is a startup conference launch worth it?

Yes, but not in the way the badge implies. A stage slot does not make you a real company. It makes you easier to find, easier to refer, and harder to ignore for a short period. I have launched two products at startup conferences, including TechCrunch Disrupt, and the difference between the two launches was not the conference. It was whether the product could survive the attention.

My first product was a thin wrapper with a nice dashboard. It had a few thousand registered users and a demo that depended on a good internet connection. I got a short article, a demo video, and a spike in signups. I also had twenty investor meetings scheduled before the event. Five showed. One led to a serious conversation. No term sheet came within ninety days. The inbound emails were mostly from people who had seen the article and wanted to know what we did. Some were useful. Most were not. The launch did not create demand. It exposed the shape of the demand that already existed, including the parts that were weak.

The second product was different. It was an API with real usage data, a couple hundred customers, and a one-minute demo that worked without a pre-recorded backup. The launch produced more of the same categories—press, investor meetings, inbound—but the follow-through was better. One inbound lead became a pilot. One partner conversation led to a distribution arrangement. One investor meeting led to a later round, though not because of the stage. The conference gave the meeting a reason to happen. It did not write the check.

That is the core of what these events do. They compress introduction. In normal life, you send a cold email, wait, follow up, and hope the recipient has heard of you. At a conference, you can say, “We just launched at Disrupt,” and the other person has a public artifact to check. The stage, the article if one appears, the demo video, the badge, the photo of you talking to a broken demo—these are all third-party proof that you exist. That sounds small. In early markets, it is not small.

The most obvious deliverable is media. TechCrunch Disrupt is a media event as much as a startup event, and the attention can outlast the show. A good interview gives you a quote, a transcript, a video clip, and a link you can put on your website. A bad interview can freeze a bad answer in public forever. Either way, you leave with assets. Even if no one writes about you, the stage gives you a story. “We launched in front of several thousand people” is a line that opens a few doors, especially with candidates and junior partners who have never seen a startup get public attention.

The less obvious deliverable is inbound. When you are on a startup stage or in a demo lineup, people find you. They see your name on a schedule, your logo on a slide, your badge in a hallway conversation. Some of them will not be customers. Some will be competitors. Some will be investors who have no mandate for you. But a few will be the people you needed: a buyer who was just comparing options, an operator who knows your ideal customer, a partner who can put your product in front of a list. The conference does not make them want you. It makes them remember you when the want appears.

Investor meetings are a separate category. Investors at conferences are sourcing, not closing. They are comparing dozens of companies in one place, often with shallow attention. A stage slot puts you in the comparison set. It does not make them invest. If you need a raise, the event is useful because it lowers the friction of getting the next meeting. “We are in town this week” is a better scheduling line than “Can we do thirty minutes next month?” But if you go expecting a term sheet, you will be disappointed. The check, when it comes, comes from the product, the traction, and the founder’s ability to answer hard questions over several conversations.

Customer meetings are different. The customers in the room are curious, not procurement-ready. They will ask questions, but they will not sign on the floor. They do not have budget authority, and even if they do, they cannot buy software in a hallway. The value is finding the champion: the person who can take your product back into their organization and say, “I saw this, it works, and I want to test it.” If your product needs a security review, a legal review, or a pilot, the conference is where you start that chain, not where you finish it.

This is where the limits show up. A conference launch does not create budget. It does not make a CFO care. It does not make a security team pass. It does not make retention improve. If your monthly churn is twenty percent, the stage will not save you. If your product is confusing, a good pitch will only make the confusion more visible. If your ideal customer is a hospital system and there are no hospital system buyers in the audience, the room is not your market. It may contain people who know hospital system buyers, but that is a second-degree path, and it works only if you are good at asking for introductions.

The strongest objection to all of this is that it is just a marketing stunt, and marketing is often a polite word for noise. I agree if the product is weak. But startups are distribution problems as much as product problems. A conference is a relatively cheap way to create a public fact about your company. “We launched at Disrupt” is not proof of quality. It is proof of existence. It gives a skeptical buyer, investor, or candidate a reason to look closer. If your direct channel is weak, that reason matters. The stunt is not the value. The reduced uncertainty is the value.

There is also an opportunity cost. The ticket, flights, hotel, and two weeks of founder time are real. If you are pre-revenue and need to find your first ten customers, those two weeks may be better spent in direct calls. If you are building a niche product for a small industry, a targeted email campaign may outperform a stage slot. If your next milestone is retention, not awareness, a conference is the wrong tool. You do not need more people to see a product that leaks.

So when is it worth it? It is worth it when your constraint is trust, not product. You have a demo, some traction, and a clear story, but people need a reason to believe you are real. It is worth it when you need a specific audience: press, investors, partners, or a cohort of operators who can refer you. It is worth it when you can turn attention into meetings in the next two weeks. It is not worth it when you need revenue next month, when your ideal customer is not in the room, when you cannot demo reliably, or when no one is assigned to follow up.

The application itself is useful even if you do not get the stage. It forces you to write the one-page story, compress the demo, and say what the company does without hiding behind jargon. That work has value on its own. But if you are not selected, do not treat a badge as consolation. The badge gets you access to the room; the stage gets you the room’s attention. They are different assets, and they should not be confused.

If you do get a slot, prepare like the launch is a sales event, because it is. Make the demo one minute long. Have a backup that works offline. Write the one-pager before you go, not in the hotel lobby. Schedule meetings with named people you need to meet, not “investors” as a category. Bring a specific ask for each meeting: a pilot, an intro, a reference, a second call. Assign one person to own follow-up. In the first forty-eight hours after the event, send short notes with a next step. After that, move leads into a pipeline, not a static list.

I would not measure success by whether you got a headline. I would measure it by whether you got five qualified conversations, two demos, one pilot, one hire, or one partner. The article is useful, but the meetings are what become revenue.

A founder can make a reasonable case for skipping the conference and doing a direct launch: email list, Product Hunt, a customer webinar, a series of calls. That is often the better choice if the goal is a narrow set of customers. The conference is better when the goal is breadth and credibility: being known by enough people that the right referral can happen. It moves what is already in motion.

My honest answer is yes, apply if you can pass a simple test. Can you demo the product in under two minutes? Can you name five people in the room you need to meet? Can you explain the business to a stranger without jargon? Do you have someone who will follow up within forty-eight hours? If the answer is yes, the launch is a reasonable investment. If the answer is no, the conference will mostly give you a photo and a lesson in how loudly a weak product can be seen.
