prompt: Most people can't remember much of what they supposedly learned in school. I'm curious what that implies about whether school does any good. Write an essay working through it from first principles, using whatever evidence on memory and knowledge you think is relevant.
response:
The observation is real enough, but it only becomes damning if you start with the wrong model of learning. If teaching is a transfer of facts from one skull to another, then forgetting is a failure rate. But minds do not work as filing cabinets. They are action systems. A fact is useful only when it is connected to a habit of noticing, judging, or doing. Much of school is badly built for that, so the fact that adults cannot recite much of it is less a refutation of schooling than a diagnosis of shallow teaching.

Start with memory. Forgetting is not an accident that sometimes ruins learning; it is part of how memory works. Ebbinghaus’s early experiments on nonsense syllables showed rapid decay, and later work made the pattern more precise: memory is stronger when learning is spaced, when it is retrieved, when it is meaningful, and when it is used. Cramming can produce a short-term performance, but distributed practice produces longer-lasting knowledge. Retrieval is harder than rereading, and that difficulty is productive. A fact that is massed, tested once, and abandoned is exactly the kind of fact that will disappear.

School often violates those conditions. A unit is introduced, practiced for a few weeks, assessed, and then the class moves on. The student may have learned enough to pass the test, but not enough to keep the knowledge alive. So if someone cannot remember the causes of the French Revolution, the structure of the cell, or the quadratic formula, that is not surprising. It is what you would expect from a system that treats education as coverage rather than formation.

But there is an important difference between never learning something and learning it poorly. If an adult cannot multiply, that is not a memory failure; it is an absence of skill. If an adult can read a novel but cannot follow a medical consent form, that is not forgetting; it is a limited skill. If an adult once solved equations and now cannot, but can relearn the method quickly, that is residual knowledge. Prior learning leaves traces even when recall fails. A person who studied French in high school may not be able to form a sentence, but they will relearn French faster than someone who never had the exposure. They recognize patterns, guess at vocabulary, and know where the difficulties are. That is a real change, even if it would not show up on a trivia test.

This matters because knowledge is not only propositional. Some knowledge is declarative: I can state that the heart has four chambers. Some is procedural: I can ride a bicycle, write a paragraph, estimate a sum, or drive in traffic. Procedural knowledge tends to be more durable than declarative knowledge, and it often exists below the level of conscious report. A person may not be able to explain the rules of grammar, but can produce grammatical sentences. A person may not remember the steps of long division, but can do simple mental arithmetic. A person may forget the name of a historical figure, but retain a sense of how power works in a society. If school leaves only fragile propositions, it has done less than it could. If it leaves skills, it has done something that survives the loss of the original facts.

The strongest case for school is basic literacy and numeracy. In most developed countries, the majority of adults can read, write, and perform simple calculations. They may not remember every book they read or every formula they were given, but the ability to read new text is a permanent enlargement of the mind. You do not need to retain every document to benefit from being able to read documents. You do not need to remember every conversation to benefit from being able to write one. School is the main institutional mechanism by which societies spread these skills to nearly all children, including children who would not otherwise encounter them. Family, work, books, and now digital media also teach, but schooling is the one that is universal, organized, and sustained.

That case is not unlimited, though. Functional literacy is not the same as educated judgment. Many adults can read words but struggle with dense prose, percentages, interest rates, statistical claims, or legal language. Many can write sentences but cannot organize an argument. The fact that people forget school content should make us suspicious of a system that stops at minimum competence. Memory research suggests that durable skill requires long, spaced practice with feedback and real use. Schools often provide a burst of instruction, then leave the skill to atrophy. A child who learns to read at eight and is then given mostly nonreading tasks has not finished learning to read.

Content knowledge is where the forgetting objection bites hardest. If school’s purpose is to fill minds with facts, it mostly fails. But facts are not the deepest value of knowledge. A fact is a token; a concept is the grammar. Knowing that a particular battle occurred in a particular year is less important than understanding how societies change, how evidence is weighed, how narratives are constructed, or how power is legitimated. The first decays quickly. The second can persist if it is repeatedly applied. The trouble is that schools frequently teach the tokens and hope the grammar will appear by itself. A student may memorize the dates of wars and forget them all, while never learning how to think about causes. That is not a minor flaw. It is a failure of the thing school was supposed to do.

Science is a good test case. Most people forget the Krebs cycle, the names of scientists, and the exact form of various equations. But some of what they learned may remain: the idea that claims can be tested, that mechanisms matter, that uncertainty is normal, that a hypothesis is not the same as a fact. Yet even this is fragile. Many educated adults still misunderstand probability, evolution, vaccination, or the scientific method. Exposure does not automatically produce reasoning. If scientific literacy were simply the residue of school science, we would expect it to be more common and more robust than it is. The honest conclusion is that school can contribute to scientific thinking, but only when the content is connected to ways of reasoning that students can use outside the classroom.

The same problem appears in general reasoning. From first principles, if school makes people better thinkers, we should see that in domains not explicitly taught. The evidence is mixed. Schooling improves performance on trained tasks and related tasks. It also raises test scores, and years of education are associated with cognitive gains. But far transfer is weaker than popular belief. Doing geometry does not automatically make a person better at budgeting, evaluating medical advice, or recognizing manipulation. The transfer happens when the school task and the life task share a structure that the student notices. If algebra is taught as symbol manipulation and adult life requires proportional reasoning about prices, taxes, and risk, the connection may never be made. The student forgets the algebra and, more importantly, never learns to use it.

This leads to the hardest part of the question. A large share of school’s social value may not be remembered knowledge at all. It is credentialing. A diploma signals that a person can complete a long sequence, follow rules, show up, meet minimum standards, and submit to evaluation. Employers value that because it reduces uncertainty. The wage premium attached to degrees is large, and economists do not think the entire premium comes from job-related knowledge acquired in school. Screening and selection matter. A degree can be a certificate of persistence as much as of learning.

That is a genuine good, but it is a different good from making minds. A signaling system can be socially useful even if the specific content is forgotten, because it helps coordinate labor markets. It tells employers who is likely to be reliable, trainable, and able to sit through a process. It also gives people access to jobs that require a credential whether or not the job uses the knowledge. But if we call this education, we should be careful. Sorting people is not the same as educating them. And credentialing can turn against itself: when everyone gets a degree, the degree loses information, and the race to signal can become expensive and exclusionary. School may do a great deal of good as a sorting and certification machine while doing less than we hope as a maker of durable understanding.

There is another good that is easy to overlook because it does not appear in memory tests: socialization. School puts children in a common public space for years. They learn to listen, wait, cooperate, compete, resolve conflict, and encounter people unlike themselves. They are exposed to books, ideas, art, languages, and roles they might never meet at home. A child from a poor family may not remember the specific novel assigned in ninth grade, but the experience of being treated as someone who should read serious books can alter self-concept. A child may forget the civics lesson, but the habit of living inside a shared political language may remain. These effects are hard to measure, and school can also socialize badly: toward conformity, boredom, resentment, or the sense that knowledge is something done to you. Still, the exposure is real, and it is not reducible to recall.

So what does the forgetting imply? It implies that much of what schools call learning is shallow. It implies that curricula should be judged by durable capacities, not by the amount of material covered. It implies that memory science should shape teaching: teach less, return often, require retrieval, connect ideas to use, and stop pretending that a fact presented once has been learned. If a piece of knowledge is never used, it will die. If it is central, it must be practiced until it becomes part of how a person operates.

It does not imply that school does no good. We do not have a parallel world without mass schooling to compare, but the historical record is not silent. Before compulsory schooling became common in industrializing countries, basic literacy and numeracy were far less universal and far more uneven. Child labor was more widespread. The rise of mass schooling spread alongside rising literacy, falling child labor, and the expansion of a common public language. Those changes had many causes, and schooling was not the only one, but it was a central mechanism. That is not proof of every virtue we attach to school, but it shows that the institution changed the conditions of life.

The right question, then, is not whether school fills memory. It is what kind of person it makes. A school that leaves a person able to read, willing to think, certified for work, and exposed to a wider world has done good even if the person cannot recite the periodic table or the dates of dynasties. A school that leaves only testable facts that evaporate has failed. The fact that most people forget much of what they were taught is not a refutation of schooling. It is a warning about what we teach, how we teach it, and what we mistakenly take for understanding when we see only short-term compliance.

prompt: Write a blog post on a recent study that tested how well doctors understand statistics (p-values, mammogram probabilities). I want a funny but fair look at what it shows and what it doesn't.
response:
**Doctors, P-Values, and the Positive Mammogram**

A recent study asked doctors to do two things that sound simple and are not: interpret a p-value, and work out the probability that a positive mammogram means cancer. No patient history, no physical exam, no institutional politics. Just a number, a base rate, and the temptation to answer with the most comforting conditional.

I will not quote an exact percentage because I do not have the paper in front of me; the point does not depend on the precise score. The interesting thing is the shape of the questions. They are not testing whether doctors know medicine. They are testing whether probability has become a native language.

The p-value question is a trap for everyone, not just clinicians. A p-value of 0.05 does not mean there is a 5% chance the null hypothesis is true. It does not mean there is a 95% chance the treatment works. It does not mean the result is important, or even likely to be replicated. In the usual formulation, it means: if the null hypothesis were true, data this extreme or more extreme would arise 5% of the time. That is a statement about the behavior of a test under an assumption. It is not a verdict on the assumption.

But medicine runs on verdicts. A patient wants to know whether the lump is bad, whether the drug helps, whether the scan should be repeated. A p-value is not that. It is a smoke alarm. It can be genuinely useful, but only if you remember that smoke alarms are not fire departments, and that a building full of smoke alarms will eventually scream for no better reason than toast.

If a treatment has no real effect, a p-value below 0.05 will still happen one time in twenty. If you run twenty such trials, one will look significant. That is not evidence of conspiracy. It is the price of using a threshold. The error is not in getting a small p-value. The error is in treating the small p-value as a certificate of truth.

The mammogram question is the same idea wearing a coat. Suppose the study uses numbers like these: 1,000 women are screened. Ten have breast cancer. The test detects 90% of cancers. It also gives 9% of cancer-free women a positive result. A woman gets a positive. What is the chance she has cancer?

The seductive answer is 90%. The test is 90% sensitive, after all. The correct answer is much lower. In 1,000 women, the test catches 9 cancers. It also flags about 89 women who do not have cancer. So there are roughly 98 positives, and only 9 of them are cancers. The probability is about 9%.

That is the whole lesson. The test is good. The disease is uncommon. The base rate is doing quiet violence to the intuitive answer. A positive result is evidence, but it is not a diagnosis. It is a reason to look again.

This is where the study gets funny, if you can laugh. The mammogram problem is not an esoteric puzzle. It is the actual shape of screening. Many tests, few diseases, some false alarms. A clinician who cannot see that shape is not failing a trivia contest. They are failing to notice a mechanism that will keep showing up in every abnormal result, every elevated marker, every “just to be safe” follow-up.

But fairness requires not turning this into a cartoon. Doctors are not expected to be statisticians in the way a statistician is a statistician. They are trained to manage complicated uncertainty under time pressure, with incomplete data and real consequences. Statistics is often taught as a way to survive a methods section, not as a way of thinking about tests and evidence. And the p-value is not a simple object. Statisticians argue about it. Researchers misuse it. Journals reward it. Blaming individual doctors for a statistical culture is a little like blaming drivers for bad roads.

What the study shows, then, is a gap in the formal tools that mediate evidence. It shows that “statistically significant” has become a magic phrase, doing work it was never designed to do. It shows that probability reasoning does not automatically follow from medical expertise. A doctor can be excellent at recognizing a pattern and still misread the conditional structure of a test.

What it does not show is that doctors are bad at medicine. Many can make sound clinical decisions without being able to state Bayes’ theorem on command. Clinical judgment uses history, examination, trajectory, comorbidity, and the cost of being wrong. It does not show that all medical decisions are statistically naive. A doctor who knows that a positive screening test often means nothing serious is using statistics too, even if they would not write it as a formula.

The hardest objection is that these are toy questions. Real medicine is messier. Prevalence changes with age, sex, symptoms, and risk. Test performance changes with equipment, operator, and population. The cost of a false positive is not symmetric with the cost of a false negative. All true. But a toy question is a tuning fork. If you cannot hear the base rate when the numbers are clean, the messy real-world version will not suddenly become transparent. You calibrate a watch against a known time, not while it is already broken.

The uncomfortable punchline is not that doctors got the math wrong. The uncomfortable punchline is that we built a system where a small number can make a finding feel true before anyone has checked whether the question was answerable. The fair response is not to mock the people in the white coats. It is to teach the numbers, in the form that makes them thinkable: not p = 0.05, but 9 out of 98; not “significant,” but “how likely, given what we already knew?”

A positive mammogram is not a diagnosis. A p-value is not the probability of truth. Both are signals. The skill is knowing how much weight to give a signal, and when to get another one.

**Doctors, P-Values, and the Positive Mammogram**

A recent study did a simple, slightly brutal thing: it asked doctors to explain a p-value and to work out what a positive mammogram actually means. No stethoscope required. No chart to read. Just a number, a base rate, and the temptation to answer with the most comforting conditional.

I’m not going to dress this up with a percentage I don’t have in front of me. The exact score matters less than the fact that the questions are small enough to solve with a pencil and big enough to matter in a clinic. They are not about whether doctors know medicine. They are about whether probability has become a native language.

The p-value question is a trap set for everyone, not just clinicians. A p-value of 0.05 does not mean there is a 5% chance the null hypothesis is true. It does not mean there is a 95% chance the treatment works. It does not even mean the result is important. In the usual formulation, it means this: if the null hypothesis were true, data this extreme or more extreme would arise 5% of the time. That is a statement about the behavior of a test under an assumption. It is not a verdict on the assumption.

But medicine runs on verdicts. A patient wants to know whether the lump is bad, whether the drug helps, whether the scan should be repeated. A p-value is not that. It is a smoke alarm. It can be genuinely useful, but only if you remember that smoke alarms are not fire departments, and that a house full of smoke alarms will eventually scream for no better reason than toast.

The mammogram question is the same idea wearing a coat. Suppose a version of the study asks something like this: 1,000 women are screened. Ten have breast cancer. The test detects 90% of cancers. It also gives 9% of cancer-free women a positive result. A woman gets a positive. What is the chance she has cancer?

The seductive answer is 90%. The test is 90% sensitive, after all. The correct answer is much lower. In 1,000 women, the test catches 9 cancers. It also flags about 89 women who do not have cancer. So there are roughly 98 positives, and only 9 of them are cancers. The probability is about 9%.

That is the whole lesson. The test is good. The disease is uncommon. The base rate is doing quiet violence to the intuitive answer. A positive result is evidence, but it is not a diagnosis. It is a reason to look again.

This is where the study gets funny, if you can laugh. The mammogram problem is not an esoteric puzzle. It is the actual shape of screening. Many tests, few diseases, some false alarms. A clinician who cannot see that shape is not failing a trivia contest. They are failing to notice a mechanism that will keep showing up in every abnormal result, every elevated marker, every “just to be safe” follow-up.

But fairness requires not turning this into a cartoon. Doctors are not expected to be statisticians in the way a statistician is a statistician. They are trained to manage complicated uncertainty under time pressure, with incomplete data and real consequences. Statistics is often taught as a way to survive a methods section, not as a way of thinking about tests and evidence. And the p-value is not a simple object. Statisticians argue about it. Researchers misuse it. Journals reward it. Blaming individual doctors for a statistical culture is a little like blaming drivers for bad roads.

What the study shows, then, is a gap in the formal tools that mediate evidence. It shows that “statistically significant” has become a magic phrase, doing work it was never designed to do. It shows that probability reasoning does not automatically follow from medical expertise. A doctor can be excellent at recognizing a pattern and still misread the conditional structure of a test.

What it does not show is that doctors are bad at medicine. Many can make sound clinical decisions without being able to state Bayes’ theorem on command. Clinical judgment uses history, examination, trajectory, comorbidity, and the cost of being wrong. It does not show that all medical decisions are statistically naive. A doctor who knows that a positive screening test often means nothing serious is using statistics too, even if they would not write it as a formula.

The hardest objection is that these are toy questions. Real medicine is messier. Prevalence changes with age, sex, symptoms, and risk. Test performance changes with equipment, operator, and population. The cost of a false positive is not symmetric with the cost of a false negative. All true. But a toy question is a tuning fork. If you cannot hear the base rate when the numbers are clean, the messy real-world version will not suddenly become transparent. You calibrate a watch against a known time, not while it is already broken.

The uncomfortable punchline is not that doctors got the math wrong. The uncomfortable punchline is that we built a system where a small number can make a finding feel true before anyone has checked whether the question was answerable. The fair response is not to mock the people in the white coats. It is to teach the numbers, in the form that makes them thinkable: not p = 0.05, but 9 out of 98; not “significant,” but “how likely, given what we already knew?”

A positive mammogram is not a diagnosis. A p-value is not the probability of truth. Both are signals. The skill is knowing how much weight to give a signal, and when to get another one.

prompt: Investors keep talking about using data to predict which startups will succeed. Write an essay about the pitfalls of predicting the future from historical data when the thing you're measuring keeps changing underneath you.
response:
An investor looking at a startup can ask a simple question: what did companies like this do last time? The answer seems promising because venture data has grown. There are databases of funding rounds, headcount, revenue, exits, and failures. If success were a stable property of certain features—founder background, market size, product type, early traction—then historical data should eventually sort the winners from the losers. The problem is that a startup is not a fixed object moving through a fixed world. The world changes, the investors change, and the metric that defined success changes with them.

Statisticians call this nonstationarity, but the practical point is simpler. A historical record is useful when the relationship between a feature and an outcome stays roughly constant. If a certain engine failure followed a certain stress test in 1990 and still does, the data are a map. Startups are less like engines and more like weather. In 2000, the video-rental data were full of facts: Blockbuster had a large store base, high revenue, and a recognizable customer habit. It even offered to buy Netflix for $50 million, and Netflix turned it down. The data were not wrong; they were measuring the cost structure of the old distribution model. The variable that mattered next—how cheaply a title could be delivered as broadband and DVD shipping improved—was not the variable that dominated the incumbent’s financial statements. A model trained on the old regime would have seen Netflix as a small, odd subscription service, not as a signal that the store was the part of the business about to become optional.

There is a second shift that is easier to miss: the label you are trying to predict changes. Suppose you collect past startups and mark the ones that succeeded by going public or being acquired. In 2021, a company could go public with enormous revenue growth and thin margins and still be received well. In 2023, a similar company could struggle to raise money at a lower valuation because investors were asking about free cash flow. The company may have changed little; the definition of success changed. Short-term interest rates went from near zero to over five percent, which made the promise of future profits less valuable and the cost of burning cash more real. A model trained on the earlier labels is not failing because it made arithmetic errors. It is answering a different question: what did the old market pay for?

Historical startup data is also a record of selection. The companies in the database are the ones that were incorporated, funded, reported, or survived long enough to be coded. Failures disappear into shell companies, pivots, acquisitions, and silence. More importantly, the sample is not random. A dataset of funded startups from 2018 is the set of ideas that passed the judgment of investors in a particular funding climate. If that climate rewards consumer apps, the data will be full of consumer apps. If the next climate rewards infrastructure, the old base rates are misleading. The model is not learning the distribution of all possible startups; it is learning the distribution of last year’s approved ones.

The deepest pitfall is that the act of using data changes the data. When investors stop allocating capital on a metric, companies stop producing it as a natural by-product of quality and start producing it as a response to price. Net revenue retention, user growth, lifetime value to acquisition cost, gross margin: once a number becomes the entry fee to a round, it becomes a target. Companies expand into adjacent markets to inflate retention, buy growth to make curves look steep, stretch the assumed customer lifetime to improve unit economics, or book one-time contracts to smooth revenue. The metric remains in the spreadsheet, but the causal chain behind it has been rewired. Historical data then contains the scar tissue of previous Goodharting. A pattern that looked like quality in 2017 may have been optimization for the 2017 investor deck.

Startup outcomes make the problem worse because the money is in the tail. Imagine 100 seed investments: 90 return nothing, 9 return $10 million, and 1 returns $1 billion. The average return is about $11 million per investment, but the median is zero. The average is real for the fund, but it is not a description of any typical company. The historical mean is dominated by a handful of extreme events, and extreme events are exactly the ones that do not repeat in a recognizable form. A social network, a payments rail, a cloud platform, and an AI model may all look like “large software companies” in a database, but the mechanisms that made them large were different. A model that smooths them together learns an average that did not exist.

Consider mobile apps. For years, investor models leaned on customer acquisition cost and retention. If an app could acquire a user for a few dollars and retain a meaningful share after 30 days, the data suggested a scalable business. In 2021, Apple’s App Tracking Transparency required apps to ask users before tracking them across other apps. The change did not make apps worse; it changed the measurement and pricing of attention. Acquisition costs rose for businesses dependent on third-party targeting, while companies with strong first-party data or organic loops were less affected. A model trained on pre-2021 acquisition-cost data could see the same early retention curves and still be wrong about the economics, because the cost side of the equation had been altered by a privacy rule.

The strongest objection to this skepticism is that some investors clearly use information and do well. If prediction were impossible, they would not have records. The answer is that their skill is not the same as fitting a historical curve. They are watching for mechanisms: whether a team can ship, whether a customer has a painful problem, whether a technology has just crossed a threshold, whether distribution is opening. Those are real signals, but they are local and perishable. A team’s past success matters because it changes the probability of future decisions, not because founder biography is a stable coefficient. Timing matters because it is the current state of the world, not a variable that can be averaged from the past. Data can help an investor test an analogy or notice a missing assumption, but the judgment is about what is different now.

This does not make data useless. It can describe the terrain: how long it takes to reach a revenue milestone, what categories have supported scale, where unit economics usually break, which legal structures create delays, which metrics are commonly gamed. It can also expose overconfidence by showing how often last year’s obvious winners became this year’s cautionary tales. The danger begins when the map is treated as the territory. A historical model can tell you what was true under a set of conditions. It cannot tell you whether the conditions are still there, because the conditions are made of the same investors, companies, regulators, and technologies that are responding to the model.

The pitfall, then, is not that the past is irrelevant. It is that the past is a closed system, while startup investing is an open one. The companies being measured are changing their behavior to match the measurements. The markets are changing the prize. The technology is changing the possible. An investor who asks only “what did similar companies do?” will keep finding the last regime in the data. The harder question is identifying which of the old rules have stopped applying, and that question has to be answered by looking at the present mechanism, not by averaging the past.

prompt: I've read plenty of self-help success books and never trust them. Someone told me to look at Trump's 1988 book The Art of the Deal, as a how-to on persuasion and success. Write a book review: is there anything to learn from it, and what does it reveal about the man who wrote it?
response:
The Art of the Deal is not a normal success manual. It does not give you a system. It gives you a man describing himself in the middle of a series of wins, with a few rules tucked between the stories: think big, use leverage, fight back, get publicity. If you want a repeatable method, you will be disappointed. If you want to see how persuasion works when it is practiced by someone who treats reputation as a financial asset, it is worth reading.

The book was produced with Tony Schwartz, and Schwartz has said he did the writing. That matters, but not in the simple way a fact-checker would suggest. The book is not a transcript of Trump’s mind, but it is a careful selection of the image he wanted to sell. The anecdotes may be inflated; the posture is authentic. The prose is simple, often repetitive, and full of maxims that read like they were discovered rather than argued. That is not an accident. The style lowers the reader’s defenses. It makes a particular operator’s instincts sound like general wisdom. When he says he likes thinking big, he is not merely boasting. He is describing a business model: make the project sound large enough that banks, tenants, officials, and reporters all have to take you seriously.

The central persuasive lesson is that many deals are won before the numbers are examined. A developer needs a story that makes a risky site look obvious. A financier needs a story that makes a borrower look inevitable. A city hall needs a story that makes a public deal look like progress. Trump was good at supplying that story early and repeating it until it became the common sense of the room. The Wollman Rink episode in the book shows this. The rink was a shabby public asset in need of a solution; Trump talked himself into the narrative as the man who could make it exciting again. Whether every detail in his telling is accurate is less important than the move: he did not wait to be qualified. He assumed the identity of the solver and let others react to him.

The same move appears in his use of his own name. He talks about putting Trump on buildings and hotels, and the point is not vanity alone. A name on a marquee is a signal. It tells a shopper that the place is successful, tells a tenant that the landlord is powerful, tells a bank that the project has a marketable face. In the 1980s, before social media made personal brands ubiquitous, this was a real advantage. He had learned from his father that real estate is physical, but he added something Fred Trump did not need: a personality that could be sold separately from the bricks. The Grand Hyatt is a useful case. He put his name on a troubled hotel and used the name to reset expectations. The hotel later failed, which is the warning embedded in the lesson. A brand can carry a weak asset for a while, but it cannot keep carrying it.

The book’s second lesson is about media. Trump writes as if he understands that attention is a resource with its own balance sheet. A newspaper story can substitute for a marketing budget. A controversy can keep a project alive when occupancy is not. A confident interview can make a negotiator seem more certain than he is. This is not a discovery; salespeople have always used it. What is interesting is how openly he treats it as a tool. He does not pretend to be a modest builder who happens to get press. He treats the press as part of the deal structure. If you are learning persuasion, that is the useful part: he understands that an audience is not separate from the transaction. The audience changes the transaction.

There is a narrower set of negotiation ideas in the book that are sound if taken seriously. Do not appear desperate. Have a reason to walk away. Use time pressure when it is real. Make the other side feel that they have won something. Trump talks about leverage constantly, and the basic point is correct: persuasion in a deal is mostly about what happens if the deal does not happen. A buyer who needs the property more than the seller needs the money will pay for that need. The danger is that the book presents leverage as a mood rather than a fact. You can act as if you have alternatives, but if you do not, the market will eventually ask for proof. The early-1990s collapse of his casino businesses showed what happens when leverage is mistaken for strength. The casinos were heavily financed, the economy turned, and the confident narrative could not keep refinancing the debt.

This leads to the part of the book that self-help readers usually miss: Trump’s success was not mainly psychological. It was structural. He came from a family that understood New York construction and credit. He operated in an era when real estate could be financed with relatively little equity, when tax rules rewarded certain kinds of investment, when Manhattan and Atlantic City were growing in ways that made bold projects plausible. He also had teams: lawyers, accountants, developers, publicists. The book hides them because a brand needs a single face. If a reader takes only “think big” from the book, he is taking the slogan and leaving out the balance sheet. Big thinking is cheap. The hard part is the capital, the location, the legal structure, and the timing.

What the book reveals about Trump is not that he is a smart negotiator, though he can be. It reveals that he cannot separate himself from the deal. Every asset is also a stage. Every adversary is an audience. Every loss is a story to be rewritten. The ghostwriting detail is part of this. A less acquisitive ego might have let the book stand as a collaboration. Trump treats authorship like another property to be controlled. The book is his not because he typed the words, but because it says he is the source. That habit is the key to much of his later life: he does not merely want credit for outcomes; he wants to own the account of what happened.

The hardest objection to reading him as instructive is obvious: if the man is willing to exaggerate the book, why trust the lessons? The answer is not that he is reliable. He is not. The answer is that the exaggeration is the method. His persuasion does not depend on verified detail in the way a lawyer’s argument does. It depends on scale, repetition, and the confidence of the teller. To study that, you do not need to believe the anecdotes. You need to see how they are used. The danger is that the same trait that makes him effective makes him poorly calibrated. A person who can sell a weak project to a room full of smart people can also be fooled by his own salesmanship. Feedback becomes troublesome because admitting error would weaken the brand.

So what is there to learn? A few things, and they are practical. Make your value legible; people will not negotiate with a mystery if they can negotiate with a story. Use publicity deliberately, not as a byproduct of success but as a component of it. Know your real leverage, and never let performance substitute for it. Understand that the other side is often looking for a reason to say yes, and a clear narrative can be that reason. What should be rejected is the rest: the assumption that loudness is a form of knowledge, that size is a virtue, that the world exists to be dealt with, and that a man who never concedes has learned something about human nature. He has learned how to exploit one version of it.

The book is therefore a poor guide to durable success and a good specimen of self-inflation. It shows a man discovering that his name can be used as collateral. For a time, that worked astonishingly well. The reader who takes the technique without the warning will end up with a larger profile and a weaker position. The reader who sees both at once gets the real lesson: Trump’s skill was making people pay attention, and his flaw was believing that attention was the same thing as being right.

prompt: Does it matter whether coworkers eat lunch together? Write a short essay about lunch at work, from the point of view of someone running a company who has strong feelings about it.
response:
Yes, it matters, but not mainly because people enjoy company. I run a company of about seventy people, and I think about lunch as one of the few regular places where information moves without being assigned. Meetings move knowledge in the direction of a decision. Lunch moves it in the direction of a person who happens to be sitting there, hungry, and not on a call.

Last year, a support person mentioned over coffee that customers kept pressing two buttons with almost the same names and then filing complaints about the feature, not the interface. That sentence cost nothing. It reached a product manager who had not seen the tickets, and the fix was small. I do not need a formal channel for every small fact. I need a place where small facts can be said out loud before they become big problems.

I care about it for new hires, too. A person in their first month is learning what is real and what is official. If they eat alone at a desk, they learn that work is private and questions are interruptions. If they sit near a shared table, they hear which promises are trouble, which meetings are worth going to, and which hallway they should not walk down with a client. That is not gossip. That is apprenticeship.

The strongest objection to taking lunch seriously is that it is someone’s break. If a manager turns the kitchen into a check-in, or if “grabbing lunch” means another performance review, then the company has made eating a task. People will not tell the truth in front of a boss who is taking notes. I have learned that if I am at the table, I am there to eat, not to collect. If the room stops when I arrive, I have failed.

So my strong feeling is not that everyone must eat together. It is that the office should make it easy to eat together and not embarrassing to eat alone. One long table matters more than five separate kitchens. A predictable break matters more than a ping at noon asking where everyone is. Better sandwiches matter, because if the food is bad, the table empties, and I do not have the authority to make people stand around a bad meal.

When work moved home, the easiest thing to lose was the sandwich. We kept the calendar, the shared document, the status update, and the video call. We did not keep the moment when two people who should be talking happen to stand in the same line for coffee. That loss is not sentimental. It shows up later as teams that are efficient within their own walls and helpless across them.

I would rather pay for a room where people actually sit down and accept the noise than save the money and get a quiet office where no one crosses a line they should be crossing. A company is not only the work it completes. It is also whether the people doing the work can see each other, at least long enough to pass a fact, a warning, or a question.

prompt: A new randomized trial found Freudian-style therapy did about as well as cognitive behavioral therapy for depression. I'm a psychiatry resident and I was taught that psychoanalysis was debunked. Write a blog post on what to make of this and how we ended up believing what we believed.
response:
## The armchair and the worksheet

You were taught that psychoanalysis was debunked. Then a randomized trial comes through: a Freudian-style therapy does about as well as cognitive behavioral therapy for depression. The uncomfortable part is not that the trial is wrong. It is that the sentence you were taught is doing more work than the evidence supports.

I do not know which trial you mean, so I will keep the specifics open. But the result you describe is not the anomaly it feels like. It sits inside a longer story about what psychotherapy can show, what randomized trials are good at, and why psychiatry settled on a clean story that had to make psychoanalysis the loser.

## First, check what “Freudian-style” actually means

The most important distinction is between psychoanalysis and psychodynamic psychotherapy.

Classical psychoanalysis is a specific method: several sessions a week, often for years, with free association, analyst neutrality, and sustained attention to transference and resistance. It is expensive, time-consuming, and hard to randomize. A new randomized trial of depression is almost certainly not testing that.

What trials usually test is psychodynamic psychotherapy: weekly or twice-weekly sessions, a limited number of sessions, a more focused stance, often with a manual. That may include interpretation, attention to patterns, defenses, and the therapeutic relationship. It may be “Freudian” in flavor. It is not Freud’s full program.

So the first move is to narrow the claim. A trial showing that a time-limited psychodynamic treatment works about as well as CBT for depression does not show that psychoanalysis works as well as CBT for depression. It shows that one structured form of psychodynamic talking therapy can be effective for one psychiatric symptom set.

That is a meaningful claim. It is not the claim your training warned you about.

## “About as well” is not one result

Before you update your view, look at the design.

If the trial was powered to test noninferiority, had low attrition, used intention-to-treat analysis, blinded outcome raters where possible, and followed patients for a reasonable period, then “about as well” is a strong statement. It means the difference, if any, was small enough to matter.

If the trial was small, underpowered, or stopped when the p-value was not significant, then “about as well” may simply mean “we could not detect a difference.” Imagine two groups with 40 percent remission. If the confidence interval for the difference runs from minus 8 percent to plus 8 percent, that is one thing. If it runs from minus 25 percent to plus 25 percent, that is something else entirely. The point estimate may look similar, but the precision is not.

Also check the outcome. Depression trials often use PHQ-9, BDI, HAM-D, or clinician-rated remission. These measures are useful, but they are narrow. They capture mood, anhedonia, sleep, appetite, guilt, concentration, and sometimes suicidality. They do not capture whether a patient’s relational patterns changed, whether they can stay in a job, whether they stopped sabotaging partnerships, whether they developed a more stable sense of self.

If the trial found similar symptom reduction at twelve or twenty-four weeks, it found similar acute symptom reduction. That is clinically important. It is not a verdict on the full range of things people want from long-term therapy.

## The broader literature is less dramatic than the slogan

The result you describe fits a larger pattern: for many common psychiatric problems, bona fide psychotherapies often produce more similar outcomes than their labels suggest.

CBT is not a magic ingredient. It is a bundle: psychoeducation, behavioral activation, scheduling, exposure, cognitive restructuring, relapse prevention, homework, and a therapeutic relationship. The evidence is not evenly distributed across that bundle. Behavioral activation, for example, has a strong evidence base for depression. Some cognitive techniques are supported in specific contexts. Others are less cleanly isolated.

When CBT is compared with waitlist or usual care, the advantage can be substantial. When CBT is compared with another active therapy delivered by a competent clinician, the gap often shrinks. The difference between treatment and no treatment is usually larger than the difference between CBT and a respectable alternative.

That does not make the choice of therapy irrelevant. It means the field has overestimated the importance of technique and underestimated the importance of fit.

A patient who finds CBT credible may do better in CBT. A patient who experiences it as mechanical may disengage. A patient who is looking for structure and homework may prefer CBT. A patient who wants someone to help them understand why they keep ending up in the same relational disaster may prefer a psychodynamic frame. The same manual, delivered by the same therapist, can be a good fit for one person and a poor fit for another.

Therapist skill also matters. A warm, attentive psychodynamic therapist can outperform a cold CBT technician. Alliance is one of the more robust predictors of outcome in psychotherapy. This is not a consolation prize. It is a central finding.

## Why psychoanalysis became “debunked”

Your training was not making this up. The collapse of psychoanalysis’ scientific prestige had real causes.

Freud’s specific theories are mostly unsupported. The dream as a disguised fulfillment of repressed wishes, the Oedipus complex as a universal developmental stage, the sexual etiology of hysteria, the fixed symbolic dictionary of the unconscious—these claims did not survive contact with the evidence. They were also often constructed so that contrary evidence could be reinterpreted as resistance. That made them hard to test and easy to dismiss.

Psychoanalysis also had institutional problems. It became elite, insular, and dependent on long training pipelines. It often spoke with a confidence that outpaced its evidence. At the same time, it was poorly suited to the new dominant method of proof: the randomized controlled trial.

CBT arrived at the right historical moment. It was shorter, easier to manualize, easier to teach, easier to supervise, and easier to fit into a health system. It had a cognitive model that sounded testable. It could be delivered in a dozen or twenty sessions. It produced worksheets and homework, which made the work visible. It fit the rise of evidence-based medicine, which elevated randomized trials as the highest form of clinical evidence.

Psychiatry also had a practical problem: residency is too short to train analysts. A resident needs a usable toolkit for acute depression, psychosis, mania, addiction, and crisis. CBT gives you a set of moves. Psychoanalysis does not. So the curriculum simplified. The simplification became a story: CBT works; psychoanalysis was debunked.

That story was useful. It also flattened several different claims into one.

## The distinction that matters

There are three layers that often get mashed together.

First, theory. Freud’s metapsychology: drives, repression, Oedipal conflict, dream symbolism, the architecture of the unconscious. Much of this is not scientifically established.

Second, method. The clinical stance: listening for what is not said, attending to repetition, interpreting defenses, tracking transference, tolerating ambiguity, using the relationship as data. This is more defensible, though still hard to isolate.

Third, relationship. The patient feels heard, contained, and taken seriously. The therapist is consistent. The patient can say dangerous things without being punished. Expectations rise. The patient is less alone with their mind. This layer is real, and it is not placebo in the dismissive sense. Expectation, attention, and alliance are active ingredients, not inert noise.

A treatment can work for reasons other than the theory that originally explained it. That does not make the treatment fake. It means the theory may have been a bad map of the mechanism.

So a psychodynamic therapy can help a depressed patient without proving that the depression was caused by a repressed Oedipal conflict. It may help because the patient notices a pattern, feels understood, experiments with a different relational response, and gets less trapped in rumination. The mechanism is probably closer to learning, meaning-making, and relational repair than to the uncovering of a hidden wish.

## The hardest objection: if it works as well, why not use it?

This is the question that actually matters, and the honest answer is not “Freud was right.”

Cost and access matter. If a time-limited psychodynamic therapy produces similar acute depression outcomes to CBT but takes longer, costs more, and is harder to staff, then the health system will usually choose the cheaper, faster option. If the equivalence comes mostly from common factors, then the more expensive, longer version may be buying less than it appears.

Acute depression also has a tempo problem. A patient with a severe depressive episode may need rapid stabilization, safety planning, medication, behavioral activation, and concrete problem-solving. A twelve-session structured therapy can meet that need more directly than a long interpretive process. For some patients, psychodynamic therapy is still the better fit, but not because it is universally superior. Because it fits the person.

Severity matters too. The evidence for CBT is strongest in unipolar, nonpsychotic depression, especially mild to moderate cases. Psychotic depression, melancholia, bipolar depression, severe suicidality, and comorbid addiction are different problems. A randomized trial of talking therapies for “depression” may not tell you what to do for a patient who is not eating, believes the world is ending, and cannot get out of bed.

So equivalence in a trial is not parity in practice. It is one input to a decision that also includes severity, comorbidity, patient preference, culture, time, money, and therapist quality.

## What the trial does not show

It does not show that Freud’s explanatory model was correct.

It does not show that transference interpretation is necessary, sufficient, or more effective than other ways of repairing the patient’s social world.

It does not show that long-term psychoanalysis changes character. A depression trial is not a study of whether a person becomes less self-sabotaging, more capable of intimacy, or less ruled by old attachment fears. Those outcomes are harder to measure, and a short trial will not settle them.

It does not show that all psychodynamic therapists are equally effective. The difference between a good therapist and a bad one is probably larger than the difference between two good manuals.

It does not show that psychodynamic therapy is first-line for acute depression in all patients. Most guidelines still put CBT, behavioral activation, interpersonal therapy, and pharmacotherapy ahead of psychodynamic therapy for acute episodes, not because psychodynamic therapy is harmful, but because the evidence base is thinner and the delivery model is less scalable.

It also does not show that CBT is the only real therapy. It may show that CBT is not as uniquely effective as its brand suggests.

## How to read it as a resident

As a clinician, the trial should make you more precise, not more dogmatic.

If a patient has mild to moderate unipolar depression, the evidence supports several options: structured psychotherapy, behavioral activation, interpersonal therapy, CBT, and, depending on severity and preference, antidepressants. The choice should be shaped by what the patient can access and what they can tolerate. If a patient wants a relational, pattern-focused therapy and can get a good psychodynamic therapist, that is not a fallback option. It is a different route into the same problem.

If the patient is severely depressed, suicidal, psychotic, or unable to engage in structured work, the question is not which school of talking therapy is philosophically superior. The question is how to stabilize, treat, and keep them alive.

If the patient has recurrent depression with obvious relational repetition, trauma, attachment injury, or personality vulnerability, a longer psychodynamic approach may be worth considering, even if the acute-episode evidence is not as strong as the CBT literature. But that recommendation should be based on the patient’s pattern, not on a nostalgic belief that the unconscious is a locked room and the therapist is the only one with a key.

Language matters in teaching. “Debunked” is a slogan. It sounds decisive, but it hides the actual state of the evidence. Better sentences are:

- “Freud’s specific theories are largely unsupported.”
- “Psychoanalytic psychotherapy has a smaller evidence base than CBT for acute depression.”
- “Time-limited psychodynamic therapy may be effective, but it is not usually first-line in guidelines.”
- “For many patients, several psychotherapies work about as well as one another, so fit matters.”

Those are less fun to say. They are also harder to argue with.

## How we ended up believing what we believed

We ended up there because medicine needed a way to choose.

When every school claims its method is special, the field needs a referee. The randomized trial became that referee. It is a good referee for some questions and a poor one for others. It answers: under controlled conditions, does protocol A change outcome X more than protocol B? It does not answer: what does this patient need, at this life stage, with this personality, in this culture, with this budget?

CBT won the referee game more often. Not because it captured the whole truth about depression, but because it was easier to bring to the arena. Psychoanalysis was slower, costlier, harder to standardize, and less willing to accept the rules. So the field drew a line and put psychoanalysis on the wrong side.

That line was not irrational. It stopped a lot of overclaiming. It also created a false binary: either Freud was right, or the couch was a fraud. The trial you are reading suggests the world is less tidy. The couch is not a fraud. Freud was usually wrong. CBT is not a pure substance. The patient is not a case example.

The belief you inherited was a boundary the field drew to protect itself from myth. The trial does not erase that boundary. It suggests the boundary was drawn around the wrong thing: not between science and nonsense, but between one package of human attention and another.

3. Why psychoanalysis was taught as debunked
- Freud's specific theories failed: dreams as wish fulfillment, Oedipus, sexual etiology of hysteria, fixed symbols.
- Popper/unfalsifiability.
- Psychoanalysis often resisted testing, elite, long training.

5. Hardest objection: if equivalent, why not use it?
- Cost, time, training, access. If equivalence comes from common factors, a shorter therapy may give most benefit at lower cost.
- Acute depression: speed matters; CBT/BA/IPT structured.
- Severe depression: neither psychotherapy alone may suffice; need meds, safety, maybe ECT.
- Patient preference: some find CBT credible, others not; mismatch reduces effect.
- So equivalence is not a prescription for parity in health systems.

6. What it does not show
- Not that Freud was right.
- Not that transference interpretation is necessary or sufficient.
- Not that long-term analysis changes personality; trial too short/outcome too narrow.
- Not that all psychodynamic therapists are equivalent.
- Not that it works for bipolar, psychotic, melancholic, suicidal, personality-disordered (maybe some relational work, but not same).
- Not that CBT is inferior; it may be better for specific subgroups or maintenance.

7. How to read it as a resident
- Ask practical questions: sample, margin, outcomes, follow-up.
- Update: psychodynamic therapy is not inert; it has evidence but thinner.
- In clinic: for mild-moderate unipolar depression, first-line options include CBT, BA, IPT, meds; psychodynamic not usually guideline first-line. If patient has recurrent patterns, trauma, attachment, and can access, referral may be reasonable. If acute severe, treat urgently.

- The field needed a clean story: biology + CBT + meds. Psychoanalysis became the thing that was wrong. That was useful but crude.
- We replaced one authority (Freud) with another (the RCT). The trial reminds us the RCT answers a narrow question: under controlled conditions, does this protocol change this outcome? It does not answer what a patient needs.

prompt: Your company has only ever sold tools to software developers, and you've just launched a simple team-coordination app meant for everyone. Write a blog post about what it means to build a 'horizontal' product versus a 'vertical' one, and what you learned about why the great general-purpose apps succeed.
response:
# Building a horizontal product after years of vertical developer tools

We spent years selling to software developers. Our product had a command line, configuration files, webhooks, and documentation that assumed you knew what a build pipeline was. That was a good thing. The users were specific, the problem was narrow, and we could make the tool precise. When we launched a simple team-coordination app for “everyone,” the first surprise was that precision stopped being enough.

A vertical product is built around a domain. It knows what a work order is, what a patient chart is, what a freight lane is. It can encode the rules of one kind of work and make a specialist faster. A horizontal product is built around a situation that appears in many domains: a group of people need to decide who will do what, by when, and what happened after. It cannot know the domain in advance. It has to be understandable before it is useful.

That sounds easy. It is not. “Everyone” is not a user. It is a warning. If you design for everyone, you will design for no one. The only way to make a horizontal product is to find the smallest human situation that recurs across verticals and serve that situation completely. For us, the situation was not “manage projects.” That phrase is too big. It was: one person needs to ask another person for something, and the request must survive a week of other work.

Our first mistake was to build for the developer in every customer. We added filters, bulk actions, integrations, and settings. Some teams liked them. Many teams ignored them. A developer tool can have a steep edge because the user wants leverage and will read the docs. A general-purpose coordination app cannot hide its value behind a manual. The default has to be the product. If the first task you create is confusing, the team will not forgive you for having advanced features later.

We started measuring a simple thing: could a person create a task, invite another person, and see the response in under a minute? Not a demo. A real person, on a phone, with a real request. When that worked, the product had a pulse. When it did not, no amount of roadmap talk mattered.

The second thing we learned is that great general-purpose apps tend to be built around one unit of work. Email is a message. A calendar is a time slot. A spreadsheet is a calculation. A chat app is a conversation. A task app is a task. The unit matters because it gives the app a grammar. You can say, “I sent you a message,” “I blocked an hour,” “I updated the cell,” “I moved the card.” The sentence is short enough to use without training.

A horizontal product that tries to be a workspace, a database, a wiki, and a chat app at once loses that grammar. It becomes a surface. People can put anything on it, but they cannot recommend it in a sentence. We wanted a coworker to be able to say, “Put it in the app,” and know what that means. That required restraint.

The hardest objection to a horizontal product is also the fairest: why not use the tool you already have? Email can assign work. A spreadsheet can track it. A group chat can discuss it. A project-management tool may already be in the stack. If your answer is “we are cleaner,” you will lose. Cleanliness is not a reason to move work.

The answer has to be about where the work lives. Coordination fails when the request is in email, the file is in Drive, the decision is in Slack, the deadline is in someone’s head, and the status is in a meeting. A task becomes useful when it is a container: the request, the attachment, the comment thread, the owner, the due date, and the final state are in one place that can be opened later. The app does not need to win every conversation. It needs to be the place where the outcome of a conversation can be kept.

This is why the product has to be simple but not thin. A to-do list is simple, but it is not coordination. A task with no comments is a reminder. A task with comments but no permissions is a liability. A task with permissions but no export is a trap. The hard part of a horizontal product is the unglamorous middle: who can see what, who gets notified, what happens when someone leaves, how the data gets out, what the mobile experience is when the real user is not at a desk.

We watched a small clinic use the app to track follow-up calls. A product team used it to review a pricing page. A volunteer group used it to plan an event. We did not build three products. We built one object—a task with an owner, a deadline, and a thread—and let the domain fill in the meaning. That is the difference between horizontal and generic. Generic means it has no shape. Horizontal means the shape is ordinary enough to carry many shapes.

There is a distribution consequence. A vertical product can be adopted by one expert who convinces a firm. A horizontal team app is adopted by a group. One person can create a task, but the value appears only when the second person sees it, responds, and updates it. That makes onboarding a team problem, not a user problem. The first user is not trying to solve a personal productivity puzzle. She is trying to pull a few colleagues into a shared surface. If inviting people is annoying, the product often dies in the first week.

So we made the invite path the main path. A task can exist in a vacuum, but a shared task is the product. We also tried to make the app easy to leave. That sounds counterintuitive, but trust is part of the interface. If a manager can export the list, if a team can move to another tool without losing the history, the app feels less like a lock and more like a shared note. That may sound like a competitive weakness. In practice, it makes people more willing to put real work in.

The great general-purpose apps are not the ones that do everything. They are the ones whose model is so clear that users can extend it without feeling lost. A spreadsheet does not know what you are calculating, but it gives you cells, formulas, and sharing. A calendar does not know what the meeting is for, but it gives you a time, a place, and attendees. The app provides the skeleton; the team supplies the meaning.

We are not trying to become a vertical tool for clinics, nonprofits, construction crews, or software companies. A purpose-built tool will beat us inside its domain. It will know the forms, the regulations, the workflows, the jargon. Our chance is the moment before the domain gets specific: the moment someone says, “Can you handle this?” and someone else says, “Yes, but I need to remember to do it.” That moment is not interesting enough for a vertical category. It is too common to ignore.

A horizontal product has to be boring enough to use every day and durable enough to hold the record. It has to be simple enough that a non-technical person can trust it, and structured enough that a manager can find what happened. If we get that right, the app does not need to explain itself. It just needs to be the place where the team can see what is already in motion.

Title: Building a horizontal product after years of vertical developer tools

We spent years selling to software developers. Our product had a command line, configuration files, webhooks, and documentation that assumed you knew what a build pipeline was. That was a good thing. The users were specific, the problem was narrow, and we could make the tool precise. When we launched a simple team-coordination app for "everyone," the first surprise was that precision stopped being enough.

A vertical product is built around a domain. It knows what a work order is, what a patient chart is, what a freight lane is. It can encode the rules of one kind of work and make a specialist faster. A horizontal product is built around a situation that appears in many domains: a group of people need to decide who will do what, by when, and what happened after. It cannot know the domain in advance. It has to be understandable before it is useful.

That sounds easy. It is not. "Everyone" is not a user. It is a warning. If you design for everyone, you will design for no one. The only way to make a horizontal product is to find the smallest human situation that recurs across verticals and serve that situation completely. For us, the situation was not "manage projects." That phrase is too big. It was: one person needs to ask another person for something, and the request must survive a week of other work.

Our first mistake was to build for the developer in every customer. We added filters, bulk actions, integrations, and settings. Some teams liked them. Many teams ignored them. A developer tool can have a steep edge because the user wants leverage and will read the docs. A general-purpose coordination app cannot hide its value behind a manual. The default has to be the product. If the first task you create is confusing, the team will not forgive you for having advanced features later.

We started measuring a simple thing: could a person create a task, invite another person, and see the response in under a minute? Not a demo. A real person, on a phone, with a real request. When that worked, the product had a pulse. When it did not, no amount of roadmap talk mattered.

The second thing we learned is that great general-purpose apps tend to be built around one unit of work. Email is a message. A calendar is a time slot. A spreadsheet is a calculation. A chat app is a conversation. A task app is a task. The unit matters because it gives the app a grammar. You can say, "I sent you a message," "I blocked an hour," "I updated the cell," "I moved the card." The sentence is short enough to use without training.

A horizontal product that tries to be a workspace, a database, a wiki, and a chat app at once loses that grammar. It becomes a surface. People can put anything on it, but they cannot recommend it in a sentence. We wanted a coworker to be able to say, "Put it in the app," and know what that means. That required restraint.

The hardest objection to a horizontal product is also the fairest: why not use the tool you already have? Email can assign work. A spreadsheet can track it. A group chat can discuss it. A project-management tool may already be in the stack. If your answer is "we are cleaner," you will lose. Cleanliness is not a reason to move work.

The answer has to be about where the work lives. Coordination fails when the request is in email, the file is in Drive, the decision is in Slack, the deadline is in someone's head, and the status is in a meeting. A task becomes useful when it is a container: the request, the attachment, the comment thread, the owner, the due date, and the final state are in one place that can be opened later. The app does not need to win every conversation. It needs to be the place where the outcome of a conversation can be kept.

This is why the product has to be simple but not thin. A to-do list is simple, but it is not coordination. A task with no comments is a reminder. A task with comments but no permissions is a liability. A task with permissions but no export is a trap. The unglamorous middle is where horizontal products live or die: who can see what, who gets notified, what happens when someone leaves, how the data gets out, what the mobile experience is when the real user is not at a desk.

We watched a small clinic use the app to track follow-up calls. A product team used it to review a pricing page. A volunteer group used it to plan an event. We did not build three products. We built one object— a task with an owner, a deadline, and a thread— and let the domain fill in the meaning. That is the difference between horizontal and generic. Generic means it has no shape. Horizontal means the shape is ordinary enough to carry many shapes.

There is a distribution consequence. A vertical product can be adopted by one expert who convinces a firm. A horizontal team app is adopted by a group. One person can create a task, but the value appears only when the second person sees it, responds, and updates it. That makes onboarding a team problem, not a user problem. The first user is not trying to solve a personal productivity puzzle. She is trying to pull a few colleagues into a shared surface. If inviting people is annoying, the product dies in the first week.

So we made the invite path the main path. A task can exist in a vacuum, but a shared task is the product. We also tried to make the app easy to leave. That sounds counterintuitive, but trust is part of the interface. If a manager can export the list, if a team can move to another tool without losing the history, the app feels less like a lock and more like a shared note. That may sound like a competitive weakness. In practice, it makes people more willing to put real work in.

The great general-purpose apps are not the ones that do everything. They are the ones whose model is so clear that users can extend it without feeling lost. A spreadsheet does not know what you are calculating, but it gives you cells, formulas, and sharing. A calendar does not know what the meeting is for, but it gives you a time, a place, and attendees. The app provides the skeleton; the team supplies the meaning.

We are not trying to become a vertical tool for clinics, nonprofits, construction crews, or software companies. A purpose-built tool will beat us inside its domain. It will know the forms, the regulations, the workflows, the jargon. Our chance is the moment before the domain gets specific: the moment someone says, "Can you handle this?" and someone else says, "Yes, but I need to remember to do it." That moment is not interesting enough for a vertical category. It is too common to ignore.

A horizontal product has to be boring enough to use every day and durable enough to hold the record. It has to be simple enough that a non-technical person can trust it, and structured enough that a manager can find what happened. If we get that right, the app does not need to explain itself. It just needs to be the place where the team can see what is already in motion.

prompt: Write a short, funny-but-serious essay about how a whole body of good work (a person, a field, a movement) gets reduced in public memory to its single worst moment. Is that unfair, and do you honestly avoid doing it yourself?
response:
**The Open Drawer**

The public memory of a good body of work is a filing cabinet with one drawer left open. It may be the drawer labeled “Racial Slur,” “Bad Forecast,” or “That One Interview.” The rest of the cabinet—thousands of careful judgments, useful ideas, quiet repairs—sits behind it, technically present, practically inaccessible.

A good career is long and context-dependent. A bad moment is small, vivid, and portable. It can be told in one breath, or in the three seconds after someone says, “You will not believe what he did.” The good work requires dates, caveats, and a willingness to sit with ambiguity. The bad moment only requires a witness and a moral category. That is why public memory is a bad librarian: it shelves everything under “Scandal” because that is the only spine color that sells. It does not preserve the whole; it preserves the handle.

I have watched a city with good schools and good parks become, for a week, the city where one person was shot. I have watched a scientist with a long record of useful research become, in a debate, the scientist who got one model wrong. I have watched a movement that did a lot of unglamorous organizing—feeding people, teaching people, keeping a case alive—become, in a later argument, the movement that had one ugly night. The reduction is so common it feels like a law of nature: the body of work is the argument, and the worst moment is the sentence your mother repeats at Thanksgiving.

Is that unfair? Sometimes plainly yes. If I cannot be bothered to learn what a field actually does, I get to keep a clean little story: all economists are cold, all psychologists are frauds, all activists are loud. The worst moment does the work of ignorance. It lets me feel like I have a view without having done the reading. It also treats a person or institution as if it were a single object with a single defect, rather than a process that can be good at some things, bad at others, and changing over time. A judge who writes hundreds of careful opinions is not the same as the judge who makes one bad ruling, even if that ruling was expensive and hurtful. The bad ruling matters. But the whole record matters more, unless the bad ruling was so central that it redefines the office.

But the reduction is not always petty. The strongest case for it is that the worst moment is often the load test. Good work can be accidental, dependent on favorable conditions, or dependent on the absence of a hard case. A company’s safety record is not very informative until the first serious accident. A teacher’s fairness is not very informative until the student they least likes enters the room. A movement’s claim to moral seriousness is not very informative until its members are angry enough to want to use the very cruelty they claim to oppose. In those cases, the public is not being unfair to the reputation of the work; it is asking whether the work can survive its own stress. If the answer is no, the reduction is crude, but it is not baseless.

There is also a fairness that runs the other way. A public that remembers the worst moment may be less interested in protecting a reputation than in refusing to let good deeds purchase immunity from harm. If a person’s worst moment was private cruelty to someone with no power to retaliate, the fact that they were useful to others does not erase the cruelty. It may soften it, but it does not cancel it. The worst moment is a scar. A scar is not the whole body, but it is part of the body, and pretending it is not can be its own kind of violence.

Do I avoid doing this? No. I do it constantly. I reduce a friend to one canceled plan, one harsh text, one moment of selfishness in an argument, and then I carry that single item around like evidence. I reduce a writer to one bad paragraph and suspect the whole book of sloppiness. I reduce a city to a crime, a team to a loss, a field to its most annoying defense. I probably reduce you, right now, to the sentence you just said, especially if I am hungry or already annoyed. The mechanism is not malice; it is pattern recognition. The brain is a danger detector, not a biography. It files exceptions quickly because exceptions are useful for survival, even when they are useless for justice.

What I can do is add a step after the reduction. When I catch myself saying “this person is bad,” I can ask which thing, in which context, and at what cost. “This person is bad at X” is more honest. “This field has a problem with Y” is more useful. “This movement did a terrible thing while also doing a lot of good” is slower, but it is closer to the world. The worst moment can be a pointer, not a verdict. It can tell me where to look, not what to conclude.

A whole body of work is a long, unglamorous argument. The worst moment is the part that survives because it is sharp. It is often the part that tells you something true. But if you only remember that part, you have not remembered the argument. You have only remembered the argument’s bruise.
