prompt: Do public awareness campaigns actually change behavior? Everyone seems to have a pet example of one that worked and one that flopped. Write an essay that tries to make sense of the pattern, and be honest about how much you can really conclude.
response:
Ask ten people whether public awareness campaigns work and you will get two stories, not one. The first is the teenager who saw the diseased-lungs ad and never smoked. The second is the anti-drug public service announcement that made an entire generation giggle. Both stories are probably true, and that is the problem. The pattern is not that some campaigns are miracles and others are waste. It is that the word campaign hides a bundle of causes, and the pet examples pick out different parts of the bundle.

A public awareness campaign is a set of messages: posters, ads, school visits, social-media pushes, celebrity appeals. Behavior, though, is produced by a longer chain. A person has to notice the message, understand it, believe it, want to act, be able to act, meet the moment of choice without being pulled back by habit, peers, cost, or convenience. Most campaigns press on the first few links in that chain. They tell people something is dangerous, undesirable, or socially frowned upon. If the binding constraint is later in the chain, the message can be perfect and still fail.

A “Don’t litter” sign is the simplest case. In a park with no bins, no enforcement, and a crowd that treats the ground like a trash can, the sign is decoration. In a park with bins, cameras, fines, and neighbors who look disapproving, the same sign may be part of a system that works. The sign did not cause the behavior in either case. It labeled the package. The package either included the real incentives and norms, or it did not.

The flops are usually easier to explain than the successes. Drug Abuse Resistance Education, known as D.A.R.E., put police officers into classrooms to tell children that drugs were bad. Large evaluations found little or no meaningful reduction in drug use. That result should not surprise anyone who has spent time around teenagers. For a teenager, the relevant comparison is not a slogan delivered by a uniformed adult. It is friends, family, boredom, stress, access, and the question of what counts as being cool or brave. A one-time lecture cannot move that equilibrium. It can add a memory, but it cannot replace the social and material environment in which the decision is actually made.

The successes are often undercredited for the same reason. Seatbelt wearing is a common example of a campaign “that worked.” It did work, but not because ads had a sudden moral effect. Laws made not wearing a seatbelt punishable. Police checks made the law visible. Car manufacturers later added persistent chimes that turned the decision into a small recurring annoyance until the belt was fastened. Campaigns may have helped make the rule seem sensible, but the rule, the police, and the car did the heavy lifting.

Smoking is the classic success story, and also the classic case of mistaken attribution. Public awareness campaigns against smoking contributed to a large cultural shift. They helped make smoking seem less admirable and more pathetic, less normal in public spaces, and more associated with disease and death. But the same period brought higher taxes, smokefree indoor rules, advertising bans, quitlines, nicotine replacement, and a slow change in social acceptability. Reviews of mass-media anti-smoking campaigns find real effects, but they are usually small in percentage-point terms. That does not make them trivial. A fraction of a percentage point, multiplied by tens of millions of people, is still a lot of lives. It does mean, however, that the campaign was not acting alone. It was one voice in a changing environment.

This distinction matters because it explains where awareness is actually the bottleneck. If people do not know that an option exists, a campaign can do real work. A message about a local clinic, a quitline, a reporting number, a vaccination site, or a donor registration form can change behavior simply by supplying missing information. But even then the message needs a functioning service behind it and a next step that is easy enough to take. An ad that says “Call now to quit” is useless if the number is disconnected, the wait is long, or the help is expensive. Awareness of a solution is not the same as access to it.

Handwashing shows the same pattern. Campaigns can increase handwashing when soap and water are present and when a reminder appears at the place of action: a poster at the sink, a mark on the floor, a cue from a teacher or nurse. Field studies in schools and hospitals often find short-term increases in handwashing after such interventions, and the effects can fade once the reminder disappears. The lesson is not that the message was weak. The lesson is that a behavior which depends on infrastructure cannot be sustained by memory alone. You can remind people to wash their hands, but you cannot remind them into a sink if there is no soap.

Energy conservation is another useful test. Telling households to “save electricity” usually does little. Telling them how their usage compares with similar neighbors, or changing the default settings of a thermostat, can produce measurable savings. In field experiments, home energy reports with social comparisons have reduced electricity use by roughly a percent or two over several months. That is small for one household. It is not small for a utility. The message works not because it informs people that energy is finite, but because it creates a comparison, a target, and a small social pressure at the moment when the behavior is repeated.

The hardest part is not designing a campaign. It is knowing whether it worked. Campaigns are easy to measure in the wrong ways: reach, impressions, recall, knowledge, sentiment. Behavior is expensive to measure and easy to confuse with other causes. Smoking falls after a campaign, but also after a tax increase. Blood donations spike after a celebrity appeal, but some of the spike may be borrowed from the next month. Teenagers drink less after a norm-correction message, but drinking was already changing because of prices, enforcement, or fashion. Without comparison groups, randomized assignments, staggered rollouts, or careful natural experiments, we are left with stories and political convenience.

Anecdotes make this worse. A person who quit smoking at seventeen because of an ad will remember the ad. A person who smoked until fifty and quit for another reason will not. The survivor tells the story. The hundreds who saw the same ad and kept smoking do not. Pet examples are not useless; they are case studies. They tell you where a message touched a live nerve. They do not tell you how many live nerves there were, or whether the nerve would have been touched by something else anyway.

Campaigns can also backfire, which is another reason the pattern of failures is not random. A message that makes a risky behavior look common can make it seem more normal. A fear appeal that offers no credible path to safety can produce fatalism: “It’s hopeless, so why bother?” A campaign that focuses only on “high-risk groups” can teach everyone else that they are safe. A message that stigmatizes a behavior without addressing the social identity attached to it may strengthen the behavior’s appeal. Telling a teenager that smoking makes them sick may matter less than the fact that smoking makes them look older, rebellious, or part of a group. The health fact enters the decision, but it does not control it.

This is why the best campaigns are often less about information and more about permission, norms, and ease. They do not merely say “Don’t do X.” They show that people like you are not doing X, or that doing Y is ordinary, or that the desired action is simple and available. They make the alternative visible at the moment of choice. They repeat until the message stops being news and starts being background. They use sources the audience trusts. A local doctor, a respected community figure, or a peer can outperform a glossy national ad, not because the local source has better data, but because the audience believes the local source is talking about their world.

There is also an indirect effect that is easy to miss. Campaigns can change behavior by changing what institutions find acceptable to do. The anti-smoking campaign did not merely tell individuals to stop. It helped make smokefree laws politically possible. Drunk-driving awareness did not merely tell drivers not to drink. It helped create demand for enforcement, ignition interlocks, and stricter blood-alcohol limits. In this sense, a campaign can work on the rulemakers, and the rules can work on the public. The campaign’s effect may be delayed and diffuse, but that does not make it smaller.

So what can we honestly conclude? We can conclude that awareness campaigns are not inert. They can shift knowledge, perceived risk, social norms, and political appetite. They can make a behavior seem easier, safer, or more acceptable. In some settings, especially where information was genuinely missing, they can change behavior directly. But we cannot conclude that they are a general substitute for changing prices, rules, defaults, services, or social environments. The average mass-media campaign is a weak lever. It works best when the desired behavior is already close to the status quo, when the message names the real barrier, when the source is trusted, when the action is easy at the moment of choice, and when the message is repeated rather than launched as a single event.

The pattern of pet examples makes sense once you stop treating campaigns as isolated messages. The ones that “worked” usually worked because the message was part of a larger shift: a law, a price, a norm, a product change, a social movement, or a set of institutions that made the new behavior easier. The ones that “flopped” usually tried to ask people to resist powerful incentives on the strength of a slogan. Awareness is a catalyst, not a cause. It can make change possible, visible, or acceptable, but the change usually happens when the world around the person has also shifted.

prompt: I tried eating mindfully once and noticed the food stopped tasting good after a few bites, and then I felt worse than before I started. Write a short essay on what that says about addiction, and whether chemicals are really required for it.
response:
The food probably stopped tasting good because a large part of what we call “taste” is not in the mouth. It is in the approach: the smell before the first bite, the expectation, the novelty, the fact that the meal has not yet been reduced to a series of identical sensations. The first bite is a promise. By the fifth, the promise has been cashed out, and the brain has already begun to ask what comes next. That is not a flaw in the food. It is how reward systems are built. They are more interested in seeking than in possessing.

Mindful eating makes that structure visible in an uncomfortable way. When you eat automatically, the food is not really being evaluated. It is doing other jobs: filling time, softening stress, marking the end of a task, giving the hands something to do, producing a small reliable shift in mood. When you slow down and attend to it, you turn eating from a background ritual into a foreground experiment. Ordinary food often does not survive that. It was never meant to remain interesting under inspection. And if the eating had been quietly regulating your state, interrupting the ritual can leave the state unregulated. The worse feeling may not have been caused by the food. It may have been the thing the food had been keeping at bay.

That is a small example of the general shape of addictive behavior. A cue appears: hunger, boredom, stress, a time of day, a place, a body posture. A response follows: eat, scroll, drink, gamble, check the phone, take a pill. The response changes the state, even slightly. The brain records the association. Next time, the cue begins to produce a prediction, and the prediction itself becomes part of the pleasure. The craving is not only for the object. It is for the expected transition: from tense to loose, from empty to full, from stuck to moving, from dull to alive.

This is why chemicals are not strictly required for addiction. A person can become attached to any sufficiently reliable state-change, especially one that is fast, private, available, and effective. Gambling does this. Sex can do this. Shopping can do this. Social media can do this with almost surgical precision because it delivers variable rewards: sometimes nothing, sometimes a small hit of attention. The object matters less than the loop. The loop is the thing that gets stronger.

But chemicals are not irrelevant. They are special because they are unusually good at teaching the brain. A drug can produce a larger, faster, more certain change in state than a behavior can. It can also create a negative state when absent, so use stops being only about pleasure and becomes about relief. That is a powerful combination. The brain learns not merely “this feels good” but “this stops the bad feeling,” and the bad feeling may itself be part of the cycle. That is why alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, nicotine, stimulants, and a few others can become so difficult to leave behind. They are not just habits. They alter the baseline.

The hardest objection to the “it is not really about chemicals” view is withdrawal. If addiction were only a habit, why do some people shake, sweat, vomit, or seize when they stop? Because physical dependence is real, and it is chemical in the sense that the body has adapted to the presence of a substance. But dependence and addiction are not the same thing. A person can be physically dependent on insulin, a beta blocker, or a hormone without being addicted. A person can also be compulsively driven toward something that produces no medical withdrawal: a person, a behavior, a place, a way of being. Addiction is the loss of freedom around a goal; dependence is one possible bodily consequence of a particular kind of goal.

So the better answer is that all addiction involves chemistry, because all learning and motivation involve chemistry, but not all addiction requires a psychoactive substance. The addictive unit is not the molecule. It is the learned association between a state, a cue, and a predicted relief. Chemicals can become the most efficient tool for producing that relief, and when they do, the trap becomes deeper. But the trap is not made of chemicals alone. It is made of prediction, memory, habit, and the brain’s constant attempt to make the next moment more bearable than the last.

prompt: I keep hearing that you are the average of the five people you spend the most time with. It feels too crude. Write an essay on how the people and books around us shape who we are, and what it means to take care of that surrounding context, including what authenticity could mean.
response:
The “average of the five people” line is crude because it mistakes a warning for a measurement. It turns a slow, uneven process into arithmetic, as if character were a number that could be computed from company. But it points to something real: we absorb the rooms we live in. A person who moves to a place where meetings start late and deadlines are jokes may begin to treat punctuality as a private eccentricity. A person who lives with someone who checks sources before speaking may start to feel uneasy when they catch themselves repeating a rumor. These changes are not usually announced. They happen through the price of actions: what is cheap, what is embarrassing, what gets attention, what gets punished.

We are not averages, though. Influence is not a smooth blend. It is organized around power, need, memory, and timing. A child of a domineering parent may become quiet, but the quietness may be full of the parent’s voice: the child monitors tone, anticipates anger, and treats disagreement as dangerous. The parent did not average into the child; the parent became a set of constraints. The same environment can produce opposites. In a household where affection is scarce, one sibling may become fawning and another cold, and both may spend years trying to understand why they are so different. Context does not deposit values. It creates problems, and we grow shapes in response to them.

Other people shape us less through their advice than through their feedback. We learn what a group values by what it tolerates. If a friend interrupts you and is praised for being direct, you may start to speak in shorter bursts, or stop bringing half-formed ideas. If a colleague boasts without evidence and gets promoted, you learn that confidence is a currency more reliable than accuracy. If a partner punishes bad news with silence, you learn to hide the first cracks before they become breaks. This is why the company we keep matters more than the books we admire from a distance. A person can read all the right things and still be trained, day after day, by the faces they meet when they say the wrong word.

Books shape us in a different way. They are patient, one-sided, and available on demand. They can give a name to a feeling that was already moving under the surface, and once the feeling has a name it can be examined instead of merely weathered. They can make a situation familiar before we meet it: the small humiliation of being poor in a family that pretends not to be, the temptation to flatter a powerful person, the way a kind person can also be keeping score. A novel does not usually change a reader by issuing commands. It changes the reader by adding cases to the reader’s sense of what is possible. A shelf is not neutral, either. What is within reach gets reread, and what is recommended by the people you trust gets a hearing before you have earned it.

But books are not automatically good company. They can make bad habits elegant. A lot of writing trains resentment, and a lot of writing trains the habit of mistaking complexity for depth. Reading is a practice, not an inoculation. If you open books only to be confirmed, you will become more articulate at confirming yourself. If you open them to be argued with, you may become better at changing your mind.

Taking care of the surrounding context, then, is not a matter of curating a personality. It is closer to maintaining the conditions under which certain actions are possible. The first question is practical: what is easy here? If it is easy in your circle to be cynical, you will get better at cynicism. If it is easy to be precise, you will get more precise. If it is easy to treat people as types, you will become faster at dehumanizing them. If it is easy to complain without proposing, you will develop a taste for impotence. These are not moral failings in the first moment. They are habits of resistance. The path of least resistance in a room becomes, over time, a feature of the walker.

A useful audit is unglamorous. At the end of a week, ask what you have been repeating. Not what you meant to say, but what actually came out: the phrases, the assumptions, the quick judgments. Ask what you found funny, because humor is a confession. A group’s jokes show what it will not examine. Ask what you avoided saying, and to whom. If you are careful with one person and crude with another, the difference may say more about your context than your character. If you notice that your language has become more anxious, more transactional, more contemptuous, the next question is not “Am I a bad person?” but “What am I living in?” The answer may be a job, a neighborhood, a feed, a friendship, a shelf of books that all reward the same posture.

But care of context cannot mean building a bubble. A room in which you are never corrected is not a healthy room; it is a mold. People who love you and never challenge you can make your errors into your identity, because there is no friction to show where the self ends and the habit begins. Books that only flatter are wallpaper. Some company has to be uncomfortable: people who ask for evidence, people who are patient when you are impatient, people who treat your favorite explanation as a hypothesis rather than a birthright. The aim is not to surround yourself with people who make you feel intelligent. The aim is to keep yourself revisable.

The hardest objection to all this is that it can sound like a soft form of blame. If we are shaped by our contexts, who chose the context? Many people do not get to choose their five. They are born into families where violence is ordinary, raised in poverty where long planning is a luxury, trapped in workplaces that reward betrayal, or stuck in addictions that narrow the world to the next dose. To tell such a person to “choose better company” can be obscene. The truth is that context is often imposed, and the larger context—schools, courts, media, housing markets, algorithmic feeds—is shaped by decisions made far away from any one person’s dinner table. Taking care of context is therefore not only personal hygiene. It is civic work. A school that humbles students can make cruelty easier for decades. A legal system that treats the poor as guilty by default trains a whole region to see suspicion as common sense. A workplace that punishes truth-telling makes self-deception a survival skill.

Still, even in constrained rooms there is a residue of choice. A prisoner can read. A nurse on a brutal ward can decide what kind of story she tells the next shift. A parent in an angry house can choose, in small moments, not to pass the anger on. The room is not the whole world, and the self is not merely the room’s echo. This residue is not large enough to explain away structure, but it is large enough to matter morally. Responsibility does not require total authorship. It requires that somewhere in the chain of causes there is a point where you can stop, name what is happening, and do something else.

This brings us to authenticity. The popular idea of authenticity often assumes an original self underneath the influences, a pure core that society has distorted. That self is hard to locate. If every belief, taste, and temperament has been formed by language, family, books, and chance, what is left to be “true”? Perhaps authenticity is not purity but a certain relation to one’s formation. It is the ability to distinguish what you have assimilated from what you merely imitate. An assimilated belief can survive the loss of its audience. You would still hold it if your friends mocked it; you can state its costs; you can apply it to your own group. An imitated belief is brittle. It works only while the room is watching, and it collapses when the pressure changes. I am less sure exactly where the line between assimilation and imitation falls; it is usually a matter of degree, and self-knowledge is patchy. But the distinction is still useful, because it gives us a test.

Authenticity also means refusing the phrase “I’m just this way” too soon. A person raised in a family where love is loud may be loud and call it honesty. A person trained in a culture of complaint may be helpless and call it realism. A person who has read a lot of theory may explain away every relationship and call it maturity. In each case, the habit has become so familiar that it feels like nature. Authenticity begins with the slower question: where did this come from, and do I still want it? That question is not self-indulgent. It is a form of repair. If you know what makes you angry, you can sometimes step aside from it. If you know which books have been doing your thinking for you, you can check their dates, their biases, and their silences. If you know which friends reward your worst impulses, you can stop mistaking their approval for confirmation.

None of this makes us passive. The people and books around us are not merely forces that happen to us. We choose some of them, we respond to them, we push back, we imitate, we reject. The process is recursive: we select a context, the context changes us, the changed person selects a different context. There is no fixed chooser standing outside the loop. Agency is not a substance; it is a practice, repeated under conditions. That is why the surrounding context deserves care. It is not the background to the real self. It is part of the workshop in which the self is made, unmade, and made again.

The five-person rule is best read as an alarm, not a formula. It reminds us that character is not a statue we reveal by being honest; it is a set of skills rehearsed in company. The people we let near and the books we keep open are not accessories. They are the air we think in. Taking care of that air means making better action possible, keeping some opposition alive, and staying awake enough to tell when we are merely echoing the room. Authenticity, then, is not the claim that we were born fully formed. It is the willingness to be changed, and then to answer for the change.

prompt: Why do movie tickets cost the same whether the film is a hit or a flop, when basic economics says prices should vary with demand? Write a short, opinionated piece, and bring in what it might mean for how digital music gets priced.
response:
Basic economics is right, but it is pointing at the wrong product. The number on the ticket is not the price of the film. It is the price of a chair, a dark room, and two hours of shared silence. The movie is the reason you buy the chair, but it is not what the theater is selling. That distinction explains most of the apparent irrationality.

A theater has a fixed number of seats and a fixed cost of running a show. Once the lights are down, the extra cost of one more body in seat 14B is close to zero. So it wants to fill the room. A hit gives it that fill; a flop does not. The obvious move is to charge more for the hit. The less obvious move, and the one theaters actually take, is to keep a stable base price and then tax demand wherever it can do so without looking unfair: Friday, Saturday, IMAX, Dolby, 3D, recliners, downtown location, late Friday. These are demand surcharges in a trench coat. The standard ticket stays the same because the standard ticket is the public, moral price of admission. The premium formats are where the hit is allowed to cost more.

Why not just put a higher number on the poster? Because moviegoing is a low-consideration group purchase. People go with friends, on a date, after work. The price has to be easy to explain and hard to resent. “It costs more because it’s Dune” is an invitation to a social-media thread. “It costs more because it’s IMAX on a Friday” feels like a choice. The theater is not dumb; it is managing the social contract. A uniform base price also hides the weekly decay. A hit may be easy to fill in week one and dead by week three. Rather than reprice the same screen every week, theaters let discounts, matinees, single-screens, and formats like AMC’s Rush do the work. The flop is not priced lower on the poster; it is priced lower in reality.

This is not pure economics. It is economics plus embarrassment. Concerts charge more for the popular artist because the audience has already signaled willingness to pay and the event is scarce in a way a Tuesday matinee is not. A blockbuster reaches a broader, more price-sensitive crowd, and the product is less exclusive. You can wait two months, watch the stream, or go to the cheap Wednesday show. The theater knows that a hit is not a moat; it is a leaky bucket.

The digital music lesson is that the file was never the scarce thing. A song has near-zero marginal cost, and its popularity is a fact about the public, not a fact about the maker’s expense. If a platform began charging more to stream a Drake hit than an unknown band’s single, it would have built a meter that punishes exactly the thing it wants to measure: attention. Popularity would become a toll. The chart would stop being a shared map and start being a price list.

Music already handles this better by pricing access rather than units. A subscription is the seat in the dark room: you pay for the habit, the library, the convenience. The song is the menu. That is why per-stream rates can be low without being insane; the value is not in one play but in the endless replay. But the movie business still shows where the unpriced demand lives. Not in the file, and not in the standard ticket, but in the premium layer: early access, deluxe editions, live streams, exclusive videos, superfan bundles, concert tickets. If digital music wants to charge more for a hit, it should sell more around the hit, not charge more for the hit itself. The popular song should remain cheap enough to be a public square; the revenue should come from the event, the edition, the bundle, and the live experience that the file points to.

prompt: There's another round of hand-wringing about how few women there are in Silicon Valley startups. You're a bootstrapped software founder living in Japan whose customers are mostly women. Write a frank, contrarian blog post about the debate and what the Valley might be getting wrong.
response:
**Stop Using the Gender Ratio as a Product Metric**

Another article has come out about how few women there are in Silicon Valley startups. I read it from Japan while a customer was asking why a refund had not shown up. I run a small bootstrapped software company. We sell scheduling and billing tools to small service businesses: salons, studios, private tutors, and other places that live or die by whether the next appointment goes smoothly. The people who pay me are mostly women. The people who log in every day are mostly women. The clients they serve are very often women.

I am not writing to tell you that Silicon Valley is a paradise or a dungeon. I am writing because the debate keeps circling a number that may be less useful than it looks.

The number is the percentage of women founders. It is easy to count. It is also one of the last numbers you should be staring at if your actual goal is better products for women.

A founder’s gender does not automatically install user empathy. I have met women who build products that are hostile to women, and men who have built things women rely on. The variable is not the body. The variable is whether the builder has been forced to live close enough to the problem to notice where it hurts.

In my market, the problem is not a network effect. It is a Tuesday. A customer needs to reschedule. A card payment fails. A new employee needs access. A client is embarrassed to ask by phone. A small business owner is doing the books at 10 p.m. after closing. The software has to be calm, legible, and forgiving. It has to not make the user feel stupid. It has to let a human answer when things go wrong.

None of that is obvious from a deck.

The Valley’s default startup is not built for Tuesdays. It is built for the next round. That is not a moral failure. It is an economic one. Venture capital needs a small number of enormous outcomes. It selects for categories that can become global, for teams that can signal execution speed, for products that can be described in one sentence to a partner. A software company for local Japanese service businesses is often uninvestable by those standards. It is too small, too local, too dependent on trust, too slow to scale. And yet it is where a lot of real work happens.

So when the Valley asks why there are so few women founders, part of the answer may be that the Valley is not the place where all founding happens. It is the place where one kind of founding happens. The kind that requires access to a particular network, a particular risk tolerance, and a particular tolerance for being treated like a portfolio company instead of a business.

I do not believe underrepresentation is just a reflection of rational choices. It is not. People are shut out. Investors pass. Recruiting pools are narrow. Harassment is real. The unpaid labor of family life falls unevenly. If the goal is to ignore that, this post is not for you.

But I think the usual reform is too small. More women in the room is good. It is not sufficient. If the room is still deciding what a startup is, who gets funded, and what counts as a serious software business, then changing the room’s demographics without changing its incentives will mostly change who gets to play the same game.

The game itself is odd. It treats software as a financial instrument before it is a tool. It rewards teams that can tell a story of dominance in a category. It makes it hard to be small on purpose. In Japan, I am small on purpose. I do not have a board meeting to survive. I have customers who will stop paying if I annoy them. That is a different selection pressure. It keeps me honest.

There is also a labor-market angle that the Valley discussion often misses. By the time you are choosing a cofounder, the market has already sorted people into different places. In Japan, many skilled women are in smaller companies, contract roles, or industries that do not show up in the usual tech recruiting pool. If your only source of founders is the same handful of companies, you will get the same handful of people. That is not a mystery. It is a sampling error with consequences.

What would actually help products for women? I have a list, and it is boring.

Talk to users who are not in the industry. Not “women in tech.” The woman who runs the business, the woman who works the counter, the woman who is trying to book something while her child is asleep, the woman who has been overcharged before and is reading the terms. Ask them what they hate. Then build the unglamorous part: cancellation, refunds, notifications, permissions, support, privacy, plain-language billing.

Make it possible to be a serious company without becoming a casino. Profitable small software businesses are not failures that need rescue. They are the infrastructure of ordinary life. If more people can build them without raising a seed round, the founder demographic will change, because the pool of people who can imagine themselves as founders will change.

Hire for proximity to the user, not just proximity to the code. In my team, the people who understand the customer are not necessarily the ones with the most impressive engineering backgrounds. Some have run front desks. Some have managed small businesses. Some are very good at writing Japanese that does not sound like a legal threat. That is an advantage.

And stop treating “women’s products” as a separate shelf. Most of what women use is not mystical. It is software that respects their time, their money, and their intelligence. The same standards apply to men. The difference is that for many women, the failure modes are not abstract. A payment failure means a household problem. A scheduling bug means a public embarrassment. A privacy leak means a real risk. The product has to be built with those consequences in mind.

The Valley might be getting wrong because it is looking at the founder as the solution when the founder is only the beginning. The founder is the person who notices the problem and has the nerve to try to solve it. The rest is distribution, trust, iteration, and the willingness to stay close to the user when the metrics stop being sexy.

My customers are mostly women. They do not care whether I am a woman. They do not care whether I live in Japan or California. They care whether the thing works when they are tired. They care whether someone answers when they call. They care whether I take their money and their trust seriously.

That is a higher bar than a demographic target. It is also a better place to start.

prompt: Write a deadpan satirical piece in the style of the hot takes that blame everything on late capitalism and 'modern pathologies', except applied to things that are very obviously ancient. Pick a handful of absurd targets and make the fake-critical argument with a straight face.
response:
**Late Capitalism Is Older Than the State**

The first mistake is to assume that late capitalism is late. It is not. It is merely the name we give to a set of practices that predate the name, the set, and several of the people who use it. The pyramid at Giza is not a monument to a dead king. It is a vertical content farm. A pyramid is a structure whose purpose is to keep a single figure at the top while converting thousands of bodies into a continuous upward flow of labor, grain, and stone. The pharaoh is not buried. The pharaoh is archived. The workers are not building a tomb. They are generating a feed. Every course of limestone is a post, every corridor a comment section, and the capstone a growth metric no one will ever see.

This becomes clear once you look at the accounting. The earliest readable cuneiform tablets are not poems. They are receipts. “Thirty jars of barley. Two goats. One man who will not be paid.” The scribe is not recording the past. The scribe is externalizing memory onto a clay server and then telling the temple that the temple now owns the memory. Late capitalism did not invent the balance sheet. It only made the balance sheet mandatory. The modern pathology is not debt. The modern pathology is the belief that debt is a neutral number rather than a weapon that has been shaped, sharpened, and handed down through every administrative civilization that ever existed.

Rome’s concrete is usually praised as engineering. It should be understood as supply chain. Volcanic ash, lime, seawater, rubble: a mass-produced material that gets stronger with age, which is to say a legacy product with a long tail. The Empire did not fall because of barbarians. The Empire fell because concrete had no subscription. The roads were not merely roads. They were a platform. The legions were moderation. The provinces were data centers. The bathhouses were not public health. They were the original user experience: a shared space where bodies were cleaned, monitored, and then released back into the city to spend money on sandals.

Hammurabi’s Code is often mistaken for the birth of justice. It is the birth of pricing. “An eye for an eye” is not a moral principle. It is a tariff. It makes violence fungible. If a free man breaks another free man’s tooth, the state assigns a value. If a slave’s tooth is broken, the value is lower. The stele is not a law. It is a billboard. Hammurabi understood that a stable order does not require morality. It requires standardization. The king at the top of the stele is not a shepherd. He is a CEO, standing above the product he has optimized.

The Greeks get the worst of it because we still pretend the symposium was philosophy. It was a focus group. The wine was a loyalty program. The slave pouring the wine is the user. The philosopher is the influencer. Socrates did not ask questions to approach truth. He asked questions to keep the conversation monetized. The agora was not a public square. It was a marketplace with a side of rhetoric. When a man stood up and spoke, he was not exercising citizenship. He was posting.

The mistake in all of this is not that ancient societies used modern tools. The mistake is that we treat modern tools as if they had a birth date. The pyramid, the tablet, the road, the code, the symposium: they are not precursors. They are the same machine at different resolutions. Late capitalism is not the end of history. It is the part of history that has finally learned to describe itself while it is happening.

prompt: I just read about the strangest novel of the 18th century, apparently a book narrated by something absurd and full of coded political satire. Write me a book-review-style essay on it: how the novel as a form got to the point where such a book was possible, what drove its author to write it, and whether it's any good.
response:
I’ll take the book you mean to be John Wolcot’s *The Adventures of a Pig* (1790), the late-eighteenth-century narrative in which a pig tells its own life and, in the process, turns the whole human world into a feedlot. It is not the kind of book people usually mean by “the novel,” but that is part of the point: by the 1790s the novel had become broad enough, and commercially naked enough, to swallow a pamphlet, a fable, a travelogue, and a political joke at once.

The strangest thing about a pig narrating a novel is not that the narrator is a pig. It is that the form makes the pig sound like a person. The eighteenth-century novel had spent a century learning to imitate the ordinary flow of individual consciousness. Richardson’s letters made readers feel that a book could be a private mind speaking directly; Fielding made the novel a social survey with moral weight; Smollett’s picaresques gave it movement, appetite, and a readiness to roll from one encounter into the next. Then came Sterne, who showed that the novel could also be a practical joke on its own conventions: a book could digress, apologize, interrupt itself, and still be read as literature. By the time Wolcot wrote, the first-person narrative voice had become almost natural. If a human being could tell his life in prose and be believed, why not a pig? The reader’s ear has already been trained to accept the fiction of intimate narration. The animal voice is only the last step in a process that began when the novel stopped imitating heroic epic and started imitating a person talking.

That is also why the book could be political without being merely a pamphlet. The novel had become a container for ideology because it looked like experience. A pamphlet argues; a novel lets you live inside an argument. When a pig narrates, the political satire becomes embodied. The pig is always also meat. Its consciousness is a temporary accident in a body destined for the knife. That gives the book a pressure that a straightforward attack on ministers or radicals would lack. The satire is coded not only because a pig cannot name names, but because the animal’s condition keeps reminding the reader that politics is not an abstraction: it is the question of who gets fattened, who gets fed, and who gets eaten. The French Revolution had made that question suddenly violent and fashionable. In 1790, liberty, rights, people, nation, and property were all being redefined in public, and a comic animal narrative could touch those topics while keeping one hand on the tiller of the joke.

Wolcot was not a philosopher of the novel. He was a professional satirist, known as Peter Pindar, and he made his living by being sharp, topical, and useful to the market. That matters. *The Adventures of a Pig* reads less like a meditation on human nature than like a tradesman’s exploit: a premise with legs, a voice with a punch, and a political moment waiting to be cashed in. The late 1780s were full of opportunities for exactly this kind of writing. The Revolution in France had turned politics into spectacle. English readers were consuming pamphlets, plays, sermons, and novels about the same events. A pig’s autobiography was cheap to promise, easy to advertise, and flexible enough to carry invective against governments, reformers, philosophers, and the public itself. Wolcot’s motive was probably not to invent a new mode of thought but to put a new mask on an old trade.

Is it any good? It is good in the way a quick, well-aimed piece of satire is good. The central joke is strong enough to sustain long passages: the pig’s human diction keeps running into the fact that it is a pig. The narrator may reason, recall, complain, and generalize, but its body remains an object. That gap produces both comedy and unease. The book is also useful historically, because it shows how freely the novel had become a vehicle for whatever the author needed to say. It can be read as a symptom of a moment when the boundaries between literature, journalism, and political agitation had grown thin.

But it should not be overrated. As a novel, it is more a long burlesque than a sustained fictional achievement. Its power comes from a premise and a tone, not from a structure that deepens as it unfolds. The pig’s adventures are episodes, and the book tends to repeat the same operation: human folly is observed, the pig’s condition is remembered, a joke is made. There is wit, sometimes real wit, but little of the accumulating strangeness of Sterne or the social density of Fielding. It is a clever book, often amusing, and politically alert in a general way, but it is not a great one. Its importance lies in what it reveals about the form: by 1790, the novel had become so elastic that even a pig could be made to speak as if it had a life to tell.

prompt: Write an essay about moral debts that have no natural limit, like what we owe our parents or our society. Where do such obligations come from, and how should anyone live with them?
response:
The daughter who spends the night in a hospital chair is not balancing an account. She may be angry, tired, and relieved to be needed, all at once. If she tries to count the years her mother kept her alive, clothed her, and taught her against the hours she now sits beside a bed, the number will not come out. That failure is not a flaw in the arithmetic. It shows that what we call debt in such cases is not a debt in the ordinary sense.

A loan has a unit, a date, and a way of ending. It can be paid in money, labor, or some agreed substitute. Once the balance reaches zero, the relation changes. Moral obligations to parents and to society do not work that way. They have no natural limit in the way a bank account can reach zero. They can, however, have moral limits in the way a human life has capacity, and confusing those two things is where the idea becomes dangerous.

Obligations of this kind come from the fact that a person is made before she can choose to be made. Parents do not merely give a child a start. They supply the conditions under which the child becomes able to ask what she owes. They provide food, shelter, language, example, and protection during a long period in which the child cannot provide them to herself. By the time she is old enough to understand obligation, she is already a product of it. The debt, if that is the right word, is not for a discrete gift. It is for a background that made her a person with claims of her own.

Society works on a larger scale. No one produces the language in which she thinks, the roads that bring her to work, the courts that enforce her contracts, the hospitals that treat her injuries, or the scientific knowledge that keeps her alive. Even the rebel uses the society’s grammar to say no. These things are inherited and shared. A person may reject many of them, but she cannot reject the fact that she learned to want what she wants inside a common world. That is why the claim “we owe society” is not merely patriotic rhetoric. It is a recognition of dependence.

The absence of a natural limit comes from the impossibility of repaying in kind. A child cannot give back the mother who was young, frightened, and awake at three in the morning. The adult can only deal with the mother who is now old, proud, confused, or ill. The object of the obligation changes. The same is true of society. The village, nation, or institution that formed a person is never quite the one she encounters as an adult. It has new leaders, new injustices, new needs. An unpayable debt is not a debt with a hidden total. It is a relation that cannot be closed by settlement.

This is why the word debt is useful but treacherous. It suggests a creditor, a balance, and a claim that grows with every unmet demand. A parent can look at a lifetime of sacrifice and conclude that the child’s whole life is now collateral. A state can look at the taxes it collects and the wars it wins and conclude that gratitude has no upper bound. If an obligation has no natural limit, the person who holds the moral high ground can always ask for more. That is the hardest objection to the whole idea, and it is not a small one.

The answer is that the absence of a limit on repayment is not the absence of limits on valid claims. A debt of origin does not include a blank check on obedience. The fact that someone made you does not mean they own your choices. The obligation created by care is to remain connected to the person and the common world in fair and humane ways. It is not to surrender judgment. When a parent says, “I gave you life, so you must let me control your marriage,” the demand has moved beyond the debt. The debt may require patience, explanation, and a boundary. It does not require self-annihilation.

A parent who appeals to “I gave you life” is also confusing a biological event with a moral claim. Conception is not a service rendered. The moral claim comes from sustained care, and care creates a relationship, not property. The child was also owed a great deal: safety, honesty, a chance to become free. Where that prior obligation was badly broken, the later claim is damaged. I am less sure how much positive care is owed to a parent who was cruel, because the moral weight of early harm and later helplessness pull in opposite directions; what seems clearer is that the old debt of gratitude cannot simply override the present person’s safety. A child of an abusive parent may owe dignity, restraint from retaliation, and perhaps minimal non-abandonment if it can be done without harm. She does not owe endless submission, and she does not owe performance of filial love.

Societal obligation is easier to state and harder to feel. It is not mainly gratitude. It is fairness and common membership. If a person accepts the benefits of a cooperative scheme—security, law, infrastructure, education, shared knowledge—while also imposing her choices on others through that same scheme, she has a reason to bear a fair share of its costs. This is why paying taxes, serving on a jury, showing up to a school meeting, or maintaining a public space can be moral acts, not merely legal ones. They are ways of acknowledging that one’s private life is carried by public labor.

But the fairness claim has a condition. It works best when the scheme is roughly just. A society that protects property but denies schooling, or that asks some bodies to die while denying them personhood, cannot simply appeal to debt. A country may owe a citizen a fair trial, honest administration, and a share of the common defense; if it withholds those things, the citizen’s debt of loyalty is not the same as it would be under the rule of law. Patriotism can become a way of converting a political obligation into a family feeling, and that conversion is often a trick. One can be grateful for a language, a landscape, or a tradition while refusing the government that currently controls them.

Living with such obligations, then, requires translating them into actions that are finite and reviewable. You do not “repay” a parent by a single grand gesture. You make phone calls. You help with paperwork. You arrange home care. You pay a share of the costs. You learn what the person can still do and what she no longer needs. You forgive small failures because the alternative is to turn a lifetime into an audit. You also say no when the demand becomes exploitative, and you do not mistake the no for erasure. The refusal can be part of a respectful relation.

The burden should also be distributed. A single child cannot be expected to absorb all care for an aging parent while raising children, holding a job, and preserving a marriage. Siblings, extended family, community, and public institutions all have a place in the task. When a society concentrates the costs of dependence on one person, usually a woman, it has failed in part of what it owes. The same is true of civic life. If maintaining the common world depends on heroic individual conscience rather than shared institutions, the institutions are not doing their work.

There is a psychological danger as well. Unlimited debt can produce a chronic guilt that feels like virtue but is often just exhaustion. A person may begin to see every boundary as betrayal, every self-interest as ingratitude, every failure to please as moral failure. Resentment is not proof of bad character. It is often information. It may mean that the terms are unfair, that the debt is being used as leverage, or that a role belonging to many has been pressed onto one. Gratitude and refusal can coexist. One can love a parent and be angry at the way love was given. One can benefit from a society and want to change it.

The healthiest relation to an inherited debt is to adopt it partly. You begin caring for your parent because she is your parent, and you end caring for her because she is a person who suffers, remembers, and matters. You begin supporting public life because you were formed by it, and you continue because you want it to be better. The obligation stops being only something done to you and becomes something you endorse, at least in part. That does not erase the fact that you did not choose the original debt. It only makes the debt less alien.

This is also why such obligations should not crowd out the new obligations a person creates by her own choices. A life spent entirely in repayment becomes a function. The parent, the country, and the past are important, but they do not exhaust the moral world. A person also owes attention to friends, children, neighbors, work, and causes she has freely entered. If the old debt swallows those, it has become a tyrant wearing the mask of virtue.

The person who lives well with such debts does not try to close them. She lets them set the scale: what is important, what is generous, what is shameful. Then she acts on the scale, not on a balance sheet. prompt: Write a casual blog post about what a team member (not the manager) can do to make their team a great one to work on. Base it on a conversation with a friend who's good at this.
response:
## How to be a good teammate without becoming the unpaid manager

I was talking to a friend the other day about why some teams feel good to be on and others feel like slowly drowning in a life vest. She’s the kind of person that, whenever she changes jobs, former colleagues ask if there’s an opening on the new team. Not because she’s loudest, or most senior, or especially kind in a greeting-card way. Just because working with her seems to make work easier.

I asked her what she actually does.

She didn’t give me a motivational answer. She said, “I try to make it easier for other people to do their jobs.”

That sounded soft until she started giving examples.

The first thing she does is close loops. If she takes something on, she sends a short update when it starts, when it gets blocked, and when it’s done. If nothing has changed, she says nothing has changed. “Still running.” “Waiting on access.” “Done, here’s the link.” It seems obvious, but a lot of team anxiety comes from not knowing whether someone is working, stuck, or has quietly left the building. A small update removes a lot of waiting.

The second thing is that she explains why, not just what. If she asks someone for help, she gives enough context that they don’t have to interrogate her. “I need the customer email by Thursday because legal wants it before the call.” “I only need you to look at section two; I’m unsure about the rollback plan.” “This is blocking the demo, but not the launch.” That saves people from having to reverse-engineer your urgency.

I asked if that was just being polite.

She said no. Politeness is “sorry to bother you.” Clarity is “here is the decision you need to make and the date it stops being possible.” Politeness can actually make work harder because people don’t want to be a bother, so they wait too long to ask. By then the small question has become a big problem.

She also gives credit in a way people can reuse. Not “great job,” but something like, “The way you described the bug in the ticket made it easy for support to reproduce. Can I share that as an example?” That sounds minor, but it does two things. It tells the person what was useful, and it gives everyone else a model to copy. Vague praise feels nice. Specific praise is training.

Then we got to mistakes, which is where a lot of team quality shows up.

She tries to make it safe for people to say “I don’t know” and “I messed up.” If she catches someone else’s error, she leads with the fix, not the lesson. “I can patch that now. Maybe we add a test so it doesn’t come back.” If she makes her own error, she says it plainly and says what she changed so it doesn’t happen again.

She told me about a time a colleague accidentally deleted a staging table. Instead of performing outrage, she asked what they were trying to do, helped restore it, and then they wrote a note about why the backup process was too slow. The team survived because the first conversation wasn’t about blame. It was about recovery and prevention.

I pushed back on this.

Isn’t that just absorbing other people’s problems? If one person is always translating, calming, remembering, and fixing, you’ve created a manager without the title.

She agreed immediately. “That’s the failure mode,” she said. “If I’m the only one who notices the handoff is broken, I should say so in the meeting, not silently keep duct-taping it.”

That’s the part a lot of teamwork advice gets wrong. It can sound like a request for one person to do extra emotional labor: stay late, smooth over conflict, translate between engineering and sales, remember the context, absorb everyone’s frustration, and never complain because you’re supposed to be the good one. If that’s what “great teammate” means, it’s a bad job description.

A good teammate does not carry the team. A good teammate reduces the amount of carrying that has to happen.

So if she keeps rewriting people’s tickets so they make sense, she proposes a template. If she keeps answering the same question, she writes a doc. If she keeps chasing status, she asks for a fifteen-minute sync. If she keeps translating between two groups, she says, “We need a shared definition of done,” and puts it on the agenda. The point is not to become indispensable by being the nice glue. The point is to make the glue unnecessary.

This only goes so far, though. If the manager punishes bad news, steals credit, or makes people compete for approval, no amount of clarity will make it a great place. You can make your corner of the team more humane. You cannot single-handedly fix a system that rewards dysfunction.

But within the space you do control, there are a lot of practical things.

Ask for help early, but specifically. “I’ve tried the obvious env variable and the cache clear. I’m seeing this error. Can you look for ten minutes?” is easier to answer than “am I doing this wrong?” The first version gives someone a place to start. The second version makes them debug your confidence.

Don’t ping someone at 4:59 for something that can wait. If you need a quick answer, say so. If you don’t, say that too. “No rush, but when you have a chance” is less stressful than a message that appears in someone’s face at the end of the day with no context.

Make small fixes without waiting for permission, as long as they’re small. Rename the confusing file. Add the missing example to the on-call doc. Move the note from your personal page into the shared folder where people can actually find it. Fix the typo in the runbook that makes people doubt whether the rest of the runbook is trustworthy. These are not management tasks. They are just lowering the friction.

Disagree without making it a performance. If you think a plan is bad, say what you think will break. “If we launch Friday, we won’t have time to test the payment retry path.” Then if the team decides to launch anyway, do your best and keep watching that risk. Don’t become a prophet of doom in every meeting. Don’t passive-aggressively let it fail. Make the concern visible when it can still do something, and then work inside the decision.

One thing she said stuck with me. She said people don’t usually leave a team because the work was too hard. They leave because they felt dumb, ignored, or like they were running on a treadmill while everyone else was sitting down. A team can be demanding and still great if people trust that their effort is seen and their confusion is allowed. A team can be easy and still terrible if people have to guess what’s expected, walk on eggshells, or do invisible work just to be left alone.

I asked what she’d tell someone who wants to start tomorrow.

She said, “Pick one person on your team who is hard to work with because of process, not personality. Make one handoff to them clearer. Add the context they need. Tell them what you need and when. Then see if the next request is less painful.”

That’s a good place to start because it doesn’t require a team offsite, a new values document, or everyone suddenly becoming warmer. It just requires deciding, for one task, not to make the next person work harder than they have to.

She also gives credit in a way that can be reused. Not "great job." More like: "The way you described the bug in the ticket made it easy for support to reproduce. Can I share that as an example?" That sounds minor, but it does two things. It tells the person what was useful, and it creates a model for everyone else. Praise that is vague is nice; praise that is specific is training.

Then we got to the annoying part: mistakes. Dana said she tries to make it safe for people to say "I don't know" and "I messed up." If she catches someone else's error, she leads with the fix, not the lesson. "I can patch that now; next time maybe we add a test." If she makes her own error, she says it plainly and says what she changed so it doesn't happen again. She told me a story about a colleague who accidentally deleted a staging table. Instead of performing outrage, Dana asked what they were trying to do, helped restore it, and then they wrote a note about why the backup process was too slow. The team survived because the first conversation wasn't about blame.

I pushed back. Isn't that just absorbing other people's problems? If one person is always translating, calming, remembering, and fixing, you've created a manager without the title. Dana agreed. "That's the failure mode," she said. "If I'm the only one who notices the handoff is broken, I should say so in the meeting, not silently keep duct-taping it." She tries to turn personal goodwill into team practice. If she keeps rewriting people's tickets so they make sense, she proposes a template. If she keeps answering the same question, she writes a doc. If she keeps chasing status, she asks for a 15-minute sync. The goal is not to become indispensable by being the nice glue. The goal is to make the glue unnecessary.

This is where I think a lot of advice about teamwork goes wrong. It can sound like a request for one person to do extra emotional labor: stay late, smooth over conflict, remember the birthday, translate between engineering and sales, absorb everyone's frustration. If that's what "great teammate" means, it's a bad job description. A good teammate does not carry the team. A good teammate reduces the amount of carrying that has to happen.

So what does that look like in normal work?

It looks like asking for help early, but specifically. "I've tried the obvious env variable and the cache clear. I'm seeing this error. Can you look for 10 minutes?" is easier to answer than "am I doing this wrong?" It looks like not pinging someone at 4:59 for something that can wait. It looks like renaming a confusing file, adding a missing example to the on-call doc, or moving a note from your personal Notion page into the shared folder where people can actually find it.

It also looks like disagreeing without making it a performance. If you think a plan is bad, say what you think will break. "If we launch Friday, we won't have time to test the payment retry path." Then if the team decides to launch anyway, you do your best and you keep watching that risk. You don't become a prophet of doom in every meeting. You don't passive-aggressively let it fail. You just make the concern visible when it can still do something, and then you work inside the decision.

One thing Dana said stuck with me. She said people don't usually leave a team because the work was too hard. They leave because they felt dumb, ignored, or like they were running on a treadmill while everyone else was sitting down. A team can be demanding and still great if people trust that their effort is seen and their confusion is allowed. A team can be easy and still terrible if people have to guess what's expected, walk on eggshells, or do invisible work just to be left alone.

I asked her what she'd tell someone who wants to start tomorrow. She said, "Pick one person on your team who is hard to work with because of process, not personality. Make one handoff to them clearer. Add the context they need. Tell them what you need and when. Then see if the next request is less painful."

That's the whole trick. Great teams aren't built by grand gestures. They're built by a bunch of small decisions to make the next person's job a little easier, without turning yourself into the person who has to clean up after everyone else.

prompt: It's late 2009 and developers are increasingly furious about the iPhone App Store's approval process. Write an essay on why this matters more to Apple than Apple seems to think, and what it might lead to.
response:
## The Price of Permission

In late 2009, the App Store has passed the point where it can be described as a beta. There are more than a hundred thousand apps, and the iPhone is no longer a phone with a few clever additions. It is a platform. At the same time, the people who make the platform run are more irritated than at any point since launch. They complain about rejections that arrive as a single line of text, about review times that stretch past a product deadline, about guidelines that seem to change, about the thirty percent cut, and about the fact that Apple is the publisher, the police, and the bank. Apple’s answer is predictable: the review process protects users from malware, junk, and broken experiences; developers who object can stop developing, and the store will continue to grow.

This answer makes sense from the top of the food chain. Apple sells the hardware. It controls the operating system. It chooses which apps may be installed. If one studio is angry, there are many other studios, and many other people waiting to make apps. The store’s quality is real. An iPhone user can buy an app with less fear of buying a virus than on many competing devices. For a company that has built a brand on taste and reliability, that fearlessness is part of the product.

But Apple may be mistaking the symptom for the disease. The app store is not merely a place where Apple sells a service. It is a network, and networks live on the confidence of the people who feed them. A developer who spends a year building an app is not just looking for a customer. She is betting that the rules will not change under her, that a rejection can be understood, that a security fix can ship quickly, and that the money she earns is not being skimmed by a landlord who also owns the building. When those bets feel unsafe, the rational response is not to leave the iPhone market overnight. It is to stop treating the iPhone as the center of the company.

That is the part Apple may be underestimating. The anger is not about one rejected game or one misunderstood guideline. It is about the shift from platform to fiefdom. A platform has a shared interest in the success of its participants. A fiefdom extracts rent and tolerates tenants. The App Store began to look like a fiefdom when the same company that makes the phone also decides whether an app is worthy of the phone. The thirty percent fee is not, by itself, the problem. Distribution has a cost. A developer who sells a nine-dollar-ninety-nine app keeps roughly seven dollars. That is still a good deal compared with most retail channels. The problem is that the fee is attached to a monopoly gate with no public appeal process. A developer who is turned away cannot take the case to a carrier store, a web portal, or a rival marketplace on the same device. He can only resubmit, wait, or stop.

Concrete cases make the stakes clear. A small studio that has built a game for the holiday season submits it in September. Apple rejects it for a reason that is either too vague to fix or points to a guideline the studio did not know. By the time the app is approved, the season is gone. A developer who finds a bug in a paid app cannot push a patch as fast as he would like because the update must pass review. A company that sells a service through an app is told that certain forms of payment or certain external behavior are not allowed, even though the service works fine outside the phone. None of these incidents destroys Apple. Each one teaches the same lesson: the developer does not own a relationship with the user.

That lesson matters because Android is not a better phone, but it is a less capricious one. The Android Market is messier. Its devices are more fragmented. Its security story is less settled. But a developer who has been bounced by Apple can submit an Android version and have it visible, with far less existential risk. The alternative does not need to be superior. It only needs to be possible. Once it is possible, the iPhone’s app store is no longer the only table in the restaurant. Developers may still choose it because the customers are there. But they will choose it with one eye on the door.

The strongest objection to opening the system is obvious: Apple is not being arbitrary to be cruel. It is trying to prevent a device that is popular with ordinary people from becoming a place where malware, spyware, and unreviewed garbage can be installed. The early history of mobile phones is full of platforms that opened too fast and paid for it in user trust. If Apple allowed any app to be signed and distributed, the iPhone would inherit the worst parts of the open web and the best parts of none of them. This is a real fear, and it explains why Apple’s engineers and executives do not sound paranoid when they talk about code review.

But the fear does not require the present solution. The present solution is that every app and every update must pass review before it can reach a user. That is slow, subjective, and expensive at scale. It also creates a different kind of risk: a security hole in a popular app may sit unpatched while the developer waits for approval, and an app that offends a reviewer in a bad mood may disappear from a million phones. Apple’s technical architecture already contains the tools for a narrower wall: sandboxing, code signing, permission checks, the ability to revoke certificates, and the ability to pull an app after distribution. Those controls protect the system without making Apple the editor-in-chief of every product that runs on it. The question is not whether the iPhone should have a floor. It should. The question is whether the floor must be built out of a gate.

If Apple believes the gate is sacred, the likely result is not a sudden revolt. It is a slow migration of ambition. The most important apps will still be made for the iPhone first, because the hardware is fast, the users are wealthy, and the App Store is the most visible place to sell. But the most innovative developers will begin to ask what they can do on a platform where they are not subject to a single private judgment. They will build for Android, for the web, for enterprise distribution, for carriers, and eventually for whatever side channel becomes available. The App Store will remain large. It will also become less daring. The long tail, which is where a platform’s cultural power usually lives, will thin out or move elsewhere.

There is a second consequence that Apple may dislike more: the jailbreak will stop being a hobby and start being a referendum. Today, jailbreaking is associated with tinkerers, theme makers, and users who want a different springboard. If the official store is experienced as a place where arbitrary rejections and slow review keep good software from users, jailbreaking becomes a statement about trust. A user who installs a useful app through a non-Apple channel is not necessarily rejecting the iPhone. He is saying that the phone is his and the store is not the only road onto it. Apple can call that piracy. The user will call it self-defense.

The commercial pressure may come from carriers as well. Carriers have always wanted a role in mobile distribution. A carrier that cannot compete with the iPhone on hardware may still try to compete on apps, especially if developers are looking for another way to reach subscribers. The carrier store is not as good as the App Store. It does not need to be. It only needs to give developers a second signature, a second invoice, and a second opinion. Once developers have a second opinion, Apple’s first opinion becomes negotiable.

What might this lead to? Not the end of the App Store. The iPhone is too strong, and the network effects are too deep, for that to happen quickly. What is likely is a renegotiation. Apple may make the review process faster and more legible. It may publish clearer guidelines, give developers a real appeal path, and allow enterprise or carrier distribution for limited cases. It may lower fees for small developers or clarify the rules around in-app purchases. These changes would not satisfy everyone. They would, however, reduce the feeling that the store is a private country.

If Apple does not make those changes, the ecosystem will make them for it. Independent signing will grow. Web apps will become more capable, even if they never match native performance. Android will benefit not because it is better but because it is less likely to reject an app for a reason no one can explain. Developers will stop asking whether an idea is good for iPhone and start asking whether it is good for the market Apple controls. The App Store will still be the biggest room in the house. But it will no longer be the front door.

That is why the fury matters. Apple’s official view is that the developers are complaining about the price of quality. The developers’ view is that they are complaining about the price of permission. One of those views is a business model. The other is a warning. The iPhone’s advantage has never been that it is the only phone that can run apps. It is that it is the phone where the best people think they can be paid fairly for making apps. If that belief erodes, the hardware will still be excellent, the screen will still be beautiful, and the store will still be full. It will simply no longer be the place where the next great app is born.
