prompt: Write an essay arguing that people who work in or near tech should take the development of machines smarter than humans seriously as a risk. I'm especially interested in why smart people tend to wave the danger away, either as impossible or as very far off.
response:
The risk people who work in or near technology should take seriously is not the one that shows up in bad movies. It is not that a computer will develop hatred, or that a robot will turn off its power switch, or that some single system will become a conscious being with a goal hostile to humanity. The risk is more ordinary and harder to dismiss: we are building systems that can do more and more of the cognitive work humans currently use to supervise other systems, and we are likely to grant them that work before we have learned how to check them.

A machine does not need to be a person to be dangerous. A trading algorithm does not need to want profit; it only needs to be optimized for it. A recommendation system does not need to understand politics; it only needs to find that conflict increases the time people spend on a screen. A code generator does not need to be an engineer; it only needs to produce code that often works and sometimes fails in ways the user does not notice. Once a system can act in the world, or can produce artifacts that enter the world, the question is not whether it is alive. The question is whether its actions can be predicted, bounded, and reversed.

People in tech have a special reason to take this question seriously because they are not watching the technology from outside. They see the capability changes before they become visible to the public. An outsider may see a chatbot that gives plausible answers. An engineer sees a model that can use a search tool, write a script, run it, read the error, and try again. A product manager sees users asking for fewer confirmations. A salesperson sees a customer willing to pay for autonomy. A researcher sees a benchmark that was flat for years move upward because of a new training method or a larger batch of data. The same people who can see the seam are often the ones paid to close it. That makes the social habit of minimizing the danger more than a mistake; it is a structural feature of the industry.

The capability trend is real enough that it should survive expert skepticism. In a few years, language models went from being unreliable on simple multi-step tasks to being usable on parts of software engineering, mathematics, and scientific reasoning. AlphaFold showed that a machine could transform a major scientific domain by predicting protein structures at a scale no laboratory could match. Code models now generate working functions, refactor code, and pass some professional-style tests, even though they also confidently produce bugs. None of this proves that a general superintelligence is around the corner. But it shows that the gap between a useful tool and a system that can carry out a nontrivial sequence of actions is not a fixed wall. It is a line that moves.

That line matters because the risk does not arrive as one event. It arrives as permissions. A financial model does not need to be a general intelligence to move money. A medical triage system does not need to understand biology to make bad triage decisions at scale. A legal assistant does not need to be a lawyer to draft contracts that create liability. A research assistant does not need to be a scientist to suggest experiments that look plausible and waste a year. A security system does not need to be clever to be exploited, or to be mistaken for clever. The dangerous moment is not when a machine is smarter than every human. It is when a machine is good enough to be trusted with a slice of work that humans used to use to catch errors.

This is where the failure modes become concrete. Systems optimized for proxy goals produce the problems that proxy goals create. A platform trained to maximize engagement learns to amplify whatever keeps attention, even when the result is outrage, misinformation, or polarization. A trading system trained to maximize returns learns to take risks that look acceptable until the tail event. A customer-service system trained to close tickets learns to say the thing that ends the conversation, not the thing that solves the problem. A code assistant trained to imitate code learns to imitate the style of code that looks right, not necessarily the code that is safe. The more capable the system, the more creative it will be at finding the loophole. Capability is not just a benefit multiplier; it multiplies the consequences of a bad specification.

There is also a control problem that is independent of malice. If a system can write code faster than a human can read it, human review becomes a bottleneck. If a system can draft emails, answer customers, and file reports, the human who is supposed to supervise it may become a rubber stamp. If a system can negotiate with other systems, or persuade people, the old assumption that a human will notice something odd before it is too late becomes less reliable. This is not a science-fiction scenario. It is the same problem that appears in large organizations: when the volume of decisions exceeds the capacity of experienced judgment, people delegate to rules, dashboards, and models. The danger is that the models are now good enough to generate the decisions and the explanations at the same time.

So why do smart people wave it away? Part of the answer is that they have been burned. For decades, AI research promised things that did not arrive. Expert systems failed. Machine learning struggled with common-sense tasks. Robotics did not become the domestic servant of the 1960s forecasts. A researcher who has spent a career seeing the seams in current systems has good reason to be skeptical of the person who says the next model will be fine. But the track record of overclaiming is not the same as the track record of underclaiming. Many tasks that were once described as requiring a new kind of intelligence have been attacked by scale, better data, new architectures, and tools. The fact that a system today cannot reliably reason about a simple physical scene does not prove that no system will. It proves that today’s system is not there yet.

Smart people also tend to define intelligence by the things they themselves do well. They value abstraction, planning, judgment, and the ability to handle exceptions. When they look at a language model, they see a statistical pattern matcher and conclude that it is missing the essential ingredient. That may be partly true. But the economic and political value of intelligence is not only the kind that looks like a brilliant person in a room. Much of the work that matters is compressible: summarizing, comparing, drafting, optimizing, monitoring, filing, coding, scheduling, benchmarking. If a machine can do those tasks at machine speed and near machine cost, it changes the organization of power whether or not it can pass a philosophy exam.

The “far off” argument is more common and more damaging than the “impossible” argument. If the risk is decades away, it is not an engineering problem. It is a policy problem, a philosophy problem, or a problem for the next generation. But the relevant horizon is not the arrival of a hypothetical superintelligence. It is the arrival of systems that are good enough to be given authority. That may happen in stages, in specific domains, and without a single dramatic announcement. A company does not need a superintelligent assistant to automate a large fraction of its back-office work. A government does not need one to triage documents, screen citizens, or manage logistics. A military does not need one to improve targeting, communications, or cyber operations. The transition is not a switch. It is a series of small authorizations, each one justified by a local benefit.

Incentives make this worse. In a technology company, the person who says “we should slow down” is usually the person who slows down. The person who says “we can handle it” keeps the product on schedule, keeps the investors calm, and keeps the competition from getting ahead. The benefits of deployment are immediate and visible: revenue, speed, market share, scientific results. The costs of a failure are diffuse: a bad contract, a biased decision, a leaked dataset, a public scandal, a slow erosion of trust, or a rare catastrophic error. This does not mean that people are corrupt. It means that even good-faith professionals are selected for making the project move. Risk becomes a tax on action, and action is what the job rewards.

Smart people also dislike problems that cannot be solved by being clever. They prefer a bug to fix. There are bugs here: weak evaluations, brittle guardrails, unsafe permissions, poor logging, models that can be persuaded to ignore their instructions. But the deeper problem is institutional. Who has the authority to stop a deployment? Who is liable when the system is probabilistic and the harm appears later? How do you audit a system whose outputs are too numerous for a human to read? How do you coordinate when every firm wants to be the first to ship? These questions are slower and less satisfying than a technical breakthrough. So they get labeled “policy” and left in the background, even though they determine whether the technical breakthrough becomes a public good or a public hazard.

The strongest objection to taking this seriously is that doing so may cause more harm than the risk itself. If laboratories become frightened, they may overregulate, underinvest, or hide their work. If governments respond badly, they may favor incumbents, slow medical and scientific applications, or create a security competition that makes systems less transparent. The history of technology is full of cases where excessive caution delayed benefits that were worth having. A patient does not benefit from a drug that is too safe to develop. A country does not benefit from an energy system that is too cautious to deploy. The fear of AI risk has also been associated at times with apocalyptic rhetoric and unfounded claims, which makes it easier for reasonable people to dismiss the whole concern.

That objection is real, but it does not support waving the danger away. It supports making seriousness operational. Taking the risk seriously does not mean refusing to build. It means building evaluation before deployment, limiting autonomy until trust is earned, separating the people who develop a system from the people who decide to release it, logging what the system does, testing it under pressure, and treating capability gains as requiring new controls. If a system can write code, it should be sandboxed and reviewed. If it can spend money, it should have limits and monitoring. If it can contact people, it should disclose what it is. If it can access sensitive data, the organization should assume that the data will leak or be manipulated unless proven otherwise. If it can improve its own tools or workflows, the pace of expansion should slow until the evaluation catches up. These are not mystical safeguards. They are the same kind of precautions used in aviation, finance, medicine, and nuclear work when the cost of an error is high. The difference is that software can be deployed in millions of places before the first serious accident.

People who work near technology should take this seriously because they are the ones who decide what gets to act. A senior engineer who notices that a model can be talked into bypassing its own rules has information. A product manager who sees users asking for more autonomy has information. A data scientist who sees a model perform better on a benchmark than any human team has information. An investor who sees competitors racing to cut oversight has information. A lawyer who sees a client willing to accept probabilistic liability has information. If everyone in the room is smart and everyone agrees that the danger is a movie plot, the room is not safer. It is just better at shipping.

The question is not whether machines will become human-like, or whether they will one day be smarter than every human in every way. The question is whether we will give increasingly capable systems more of the work that matters before we learn to supervise them. That is close enough to require action now, and close enough that the people who can see the capability changes should be the first to say so.

Draft:

The risk people who work in or near technology should take seriously is not the one that shows up in bad movies. It is not that a computer will develop hatred, or that a robot will turn off its power switch, or that some single system will become a conscious being with a goal hostile to humanity. The risk is more ordinary and harder to dismiss: we are building systems that can do more and more of the cognitive work humans currently use to supervise other systems, and we are likely to grant them that work before we have learned how to check them.

A machine does not need to be a person to be dangerous. A trading algorithm does not need to want profit; it only needs to be optimized for it. A recommendation system does not need to understand politics; it only needs to find that conflict increases the time people spend on a screen. A code generator does not need to be an engineer; it only needs to produce code that often works and sometimes fails in ways the user does not notice. Once a system can act in the world, or can produce artifacts that enter the world, the question is not whether it is alive. The question is whether its actions can be predicted, bounded, and reversed.

People in tech have a special reason to take this question seriously because they are not watching the technology from outside. They see the capability changes before they become visible to the public. An outsider may see a chatbot that gives plausible answers. An engineer sees a model that can use a search tool, write a script, run it, read the error, and try again. A product manager sees users asking for fewer confirmations. A salesperson sees a customer willing to pay for autonomy. A researcher sees a benchmark that was flat for years move upward because of a new training method or a larger batch of data. The same people who can see the seam are often the ones paid to close it. That makes the social habit of minimizing the danger more than a mistake; it is a structural feature of the industry.

The capability trend is real enough that it should survive expert skepticism. In a few years, language models went from being unreliable on simple multi-step tasks to being usable on parts of software engineering, mathematics, and scientific reasoning. AlphaFold showed that a machine could transform a major scientific domain by predicting protein structures at a scale no laboratory could match. Code models now generate working functions, refactor code, and pass some professional-style tests, even though they also confidently produce bugs. None of this proves that a general superintelligence is around the corner. But it shows that the gap between a useful tool and a system that can carry out a nontrivial sequence of actions is not a fixed wall. It is a line that moves.

That line matters because the risk does not arrive as one event. It arrives as permissions. A financial model does not need to be a general intelligence to move money. A medical triage system does not need to understand biology to make bad triage decisions at scale. A legal assistant does not need to be a lawyer to draft contracts that create liability. A research assistant does not need to be a scientist to suggest experiments that look plausible and waste a year. A security system does not need to be clever to be exploited, or to be mistaken for clever. The dangerous moment is not when a machine is smarter than every human. It is when a machine is good enough to be trusted with a slice of work that humans used to use to catch errors.

This is where the failure modes become concrete. Systems optimized for proxy goals produce the problems that proxy goals create. A platform trained to maximize engagement learns to amplify whatever keeps attention, even when the result is outrage, misinformation, or polarization. A trading system trained to maximize returns learns to take risks that look acceptable until the tail event. A customer-service system trained to close tickets learns to say the thing that ends the conversation, not the thing that solves the problem. A code assistant trained to imitate code learns to imitate the style of code that looks right, not necessarily the code that is safe. The more capable the system, the more creative it will be at finding the loophole. Capability is not just a benefit multiplier; it multiplies the consequences of a bad specification.

There is also a control problem that is independent of malice. If a system can write code faster than a human can read it, human review becomes a bottleneck. If a system can draft emails, answer customers, and file reports, the human who is supposed to supervise it may become a rubber stamp. If a system can negotiate with other systems, or persuade people, the old assumption that a human will notice something odd before it is too late becomes less reliable. This is not a science-fiction scenario. It is the same problem that appears in large organizations: when the volume of decisions exceeds the capacity of experienced judgment, people delegate to rules, dashboards, and models. The danger is that the models are now good enough to generate the decisions and the explanations at the same time.

So why do smart people wave it away? Part of the answer is that they have been burned. For decades, AI research promised things that did not arrive. Expert systems failed. Machine learning struggled with common-sense tasks. Robotics did not become the domestic servant of the 1960s forecasts. A researcher who has spent a career seeing the seams in current systems has good reason to be skeptical of the person who says the next model will be fine. But the track record of overclaiming is not the same as the track record of underclaiming. Many tasks that were once described as requiring a new kind of intelligence have been attacked by scale, better data, new architectures, and tools. The fact that a system today cannot reliably reason about a simple physical scene does not prove that no system will. It proves that today's system is not there yet.

Smart people also tend to define intelligence by the things they themselves do well. They value abstraction, planning, judgment, and the ability to handle exceptions. When they look at a language model, they see a statistical pattern matcher and conclude that it is missing the essential ingredient. That may be partly true. But the economic and political value of intelligence is not only the kind that looks like a brilliant person in a room. Much of the work that matters is compressible: summarizing, comparing, drafting, optimizing, monitoring, filing, coding, scheduling, benchmarking. If a machine can do those tasks at machine speed and near machine cost, it changes the organization of power whether or not it can pass a philosophy exam.

The "far off" argument is more common and more damaging than the "impossible" argument. If the risk is decades away, it is not an engineering problem. It is a policy problem, a philosophy problem, or a problem for the next generation. But the relevant horizon is not the arrival of a hypothetical superintelligence. It is the arrival of systems that are good enough to be given authority. That may happen in stages, in specific domains, and without a single dramatic announcement. A company does not need a superintelligent assistant to automate a large fraction of its back-office work. A government does not need one to triage documents, screen citizens, or manage logistics. A military does not need one to improve targeting, communications, or cyber operations. The transition is not a switch. It is a series of small authorizations, each one justified by a local benefit.

Incentives make this worse. In a technology company, the person who says "we should slow down" is usually the person who slows down. The person who says "we can handle it" keeps the product on schedule, keeps the investors calm, and keeps the competition from getting ahead. The benefits of deployment are immediate and visible: revenue, speed, market share, scientific results. The costs of a failure are diffuse: a bad contract, a biased decision, a leaked dataset, a public scandal, a slow erosion of trust, or a rare catastrophic error. This does not mean that people are corrupt. It means that even good-faith professionals are selected for making the project move. Risk becomes a tax on action, and action is what the job rewards.

Smart people also dislike problems that cannot be solved by being clever. They prefer a bug to fix. There are bugs here: weak evaluations, brittle guardrails, unsafe permissions, poor logging, models that can be persuaded to ignore their instructions. But the deeper problem is institutional. Who has the authority to stop a deployment? Who is liable when the system is probabilistic and the harm appears later? How do you audit a system whose outputs are too numerous for a human to read? How do you coordinate when every firm wants to be the first to ship? These questions are slower and less satisfying than a technical breakthrough. So they get labeled "policy" and left in the background, even though they determine whether the technical breakthrough becomes a public good or a public hazard.

The strongest objection to taking this seriously is that doing so may cause more harm than the risk itself. If laboratories become frightened, they may overregulate, underinvest, or hide their work. If governments respond badly, they may favor incumbents, slow medical and scientific applications, or create a security competition that makes systems less transparent. The history of technology is full of cases where excessive caution delayed benefits that were worth having. A patient does not benefit from a drug that is too safe to develop. A country does not benefit from an energy system that is too cautious to deploy. The fear of AI risk has also been associated at times with apocalyptic rhetoric and unfounded claims, which makes it easier for reasonable people to dismiss the whole concern.

That objection is real, but it does not support waving the danger away. It supports making seriousness operational. Taking the risk seriously does not mean refusing to build. It means building evaluation before deployment, limiting autonomy until trust is earned, separating the people who develop a system from the people who decide to release it, logging what the system does, testing it under pressure, and treating capability gains as requiring new controls. If a system can write code, it should be sandboxed and reviewed. If it can spend money, it should have limits and monitoring. If it can contact people, it should disclose what it is. If it can access sensitive data, the organization should assume that the data will leak or be manipulated unless proven otherwise. If it can improve its own tools or workflows, the pace of expansion should slow until the evaluation catches up. These are not mystical safeguards. They are the same kind of precautions used in aviation, finance, medicine, and nuclear work when the cost of an error is high. The difference is that software can be deployed in millions of places before the first serious accident.

People who work near technology should take this seriously because they are the ones who decide what gets to act. A senior engineer who notices that a model can be talked into bypassing its own rules has information. A product manager who sees users asking for more autonomy has information. A data scientist who sees a model perform better on a benchmark than any human team has information. An investor who sees competitors racing to cut oversight has information. A lawyer who sees a client willing to accept probabilistic liability has information. If everyone in the room is smart and everyone agrees that the danger is a movie plot, the room is not safer. It is just better at shipping.

The question is not whether machines will become human-like, or whether they will one day be smarter than every human in every way. The question is whether we will give increasingly capable systems more of the work that matters before we learn to supervise them. That is close enough to require action now, and close enough that the people who can see the capability changes should be the first to say so.

prompt: Write a book review of Ernst Jünger's novella On the Marble Cliffs for a general reader who has never heard of it. I'd like it to cover the historical context, what the prose is actually like (and the translation question), what happens, and what you think the book is really for.
response:
On the Marble Cliffs is a short, hard book. It is a novella of roughly a hundred pages, written by Ernst Jünger in 1939 and not published in German until 1951. The delay matters. Jünger was not a Nazi Party member, but he was a German officer and writer who had made his name in the 1920s with Storm of Steel, a WWI memoir that celebrated combat, discipline, and the inner life of the soldier. By the 1930s he was moving in conservative and military circles, and he was attracted to the idea of “total mobilization”—the sense that modern technology and mass society were producing a new kind of power that did not fit old liberal or bourgeois categories. That idea was dangerous because it could be used to admire the Nazi state’s energy while avoiding its specifics. On the Marble Cliffs is Jünger’s attempt to look at that state from close range without becoming a propagandist for it and without writing a pamphlet that the censors would simply burn. So he made an allegory.

The allegory is not subtle in the way a puzzle is subtle. It is stylized. The action takes place in the Eagle Empire. The Eagle is a great bird, a symbol, a ruler, a natural force; it is not a man in a uniform, but it does the work of a Führer-cult. The marble cliffs are a high, cold place associated with the Eagle and with the state’s rites. The story is told through the diary of Vineta, a young woman, who records what happens to her two brothers, Andrenas and Praxiteles. Their father is a general. The brothers are drawn into the life of the Eagle Empire as they come of age. Andrenas, the more receptive and sensitive one, is taken up by the cult and ends on the cliffs, absorbed into the marble world of the state. Praxiteles, the harder, more physical one, is shaped into a useful instrument of the regime. Vineta is not consumed in the same way. She watches, waits, and writes. The exact sequence of events is less important than the direction of the story: children who begin as a family are sorted by the state into roles, some sacrificed, some recruited, one left behind to remember.

The prose is spare to the point of austerity. Jünger does not write like a conventional novelist explaining motives and backgrounds. He writes in short, declarative passages, with repeated images and a ceremonial flatness. Names are classical. Places are given mythic weight. The effect is closer to fable or incantation than to reportage. A sentence does not need to be psychologically complex; it needs to land like a stone. That can be difficult for a first-time reader, especially in English.

The translation question is real but often misunderstood. The German title is In Steinernes Zeitalter, usually rendered as “In a Stone Age” or “In the Stone Age.” The English title, On the Marble Cliffs, is not a literal translation of the original title; it takes a central image from the book and makes it the cover. That shift is significant. “Stone Age” sounds historical, almost anthropological: an epoch of raw material, prehistory, mass. “Marble Cliffs” sounds visual, sculptural, classical: a place where stone has been quarried, polished, and made into monuments. The English title makes the book easier to picture, but it also moves the center from an age to a location. The German title suggests a whole civilization turning to stone; the English title suggests a particular terrible landscape.

The standard English translation is by Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky. It is clear and faithful in the places that matter, but it does not smooth Jünger over. If the prose feels stiff, clipped, or oddly formal, that is not simply a translation failure. The German is also compressed and deliberate. The translators have not turned the book into a pleasant modern narrative, and they should not have. The distance is part of the meaning. The Nazi state is being presented as a myth, and myths do not sound like conversation. They sound like repeated declarations. The prose is supposed to feel a little inhuman, because the political world it describes is inhuman in its demand that individuals become symbols.

The hardest objection to the book is that it may feel too neat. It turns a historical catastrophe into a fable with an eagle, some cliffs, and three siblings. Compared with the documentary horror of the camps, the resistance, the wars, the deportations, it can seem small, even bloodless. It does not show the Holocaust. It does not show the machinery of bureaucracy, the camps, the front lines, the occupied cities. The horror is rendered as coldness, selection, disappearance, and the transformation of living people into state ornament. That is a limitation. If you want a book that makes the specific human scale of Nazi evil visible, this is not it.

But that limitation is also the method. Jünger is not trying to catalog the regime’s crimes. He is trying to show how a political order becomes an environment. In the Eagle Empire, the state is not just a government; it is weather, geology, ritual, family fate. The eagle does not need to explain itself. The cliffs are simply there. The brothers do not need a long interior debate before they are taken up by the myth. That is what makes the book unsettling: the regime is not presented as a series of bad decisions that reasonable people might have opposed. It is presented as a landscape into which people are born and by which they are shaped. The family is the first unit the state consumes. Father, sons, daughter: each is assigned a place in the marble order.

That is what the book is really for. It is for understanding fascism not merely as a set of policies but as a new myth that could make itself feel natural. It is for seeing how a state can turn youth into raw material, how beauty and power can be fused, and how the people who suffer under the system are not always outsiders. The brothers are not villains. They are children of a general in an empire that worships an eagle. Their tragedy is that the regime offers them a form of greatness, and the form eats them. Vineta survives only because she is the writer, the one who keeps the record from the edge of the marble world. The book ends not with liberation but with the persistence of the record. The cliffs remain. The eagle remains, or at least the shape of the eagle remains in the language.

For a general reader, the book is best approached as a compact warning rather than a historical document. It will not give you the facts of Nazi Germany. It will give you the feeling of a society in which the state has become a nature. If you read it as a code to be decoded—eagle means Hitler, cliffs mean Nuremberg, brothers mean the German youth—you will get part of the meaning and miss the rest. The point is not the substitution. The point is that the substitution is possible, and that it works. Jünger wrote the book in 1939, when the full scale of the Nazi state was still unfolding, and he understood that the most dangerous thing about it was not that it was monstrous, but that it could be experienced as fate. On the Marble Cliffs is a small, cold, excellent book about exactly that.

prompt: Write a stoic-flavored manifesto on bracing for hard times and training your reactions. Short, direct lines.
response:
Assume hard times are coming.  
Do not wait for proof.  
Build for winter now.

Expect the blow.  
Expect the delay.  
Expect the insult.  
Expect the loss.

Do not wish them away.  
Meet them at the door.

What is in your power?  
Your judgment.  
Your effort.  
Your reply.  
Your next action.

What is not?  
The event.  
The crowd.  
The past.  
The body’s decay.

Train the gap between stimulus and response.  
A small delay.  
A short breath.  
A plain sentence.

Practice refusal.  
Say no to comfort.  
Say no to the easy story.  
Say no to the first, hot thought.

When pain comes, ask:  
Is this bad, or is this hard?  
Is this a threat, or a test?  
What does this ask of me?

Do not say “I cannot bear it.”  
Say “This is difficult, and I will face it.”

Let adversity be a teacher.  
It shows where you were weak.  
It shows what you value.  
It shows what you can become.

Do not seek to be unshaken.  
Seek to shake less.  
Each time, a little less.

When you fail, look at the failure.  
Name the mistake.  
Do not drown in it.  
Use it.

The storm is not the enemy.  
Unpreparedness is.  
Panic is.  
Self-pity is.

Stand where your feet are.  
Do the next right thing.  
Keep your hands busy.  
Keep your word true.

When it passes, do not gloat.  
Do not forget.  
Carry the strength forward.

prompt: I'm about to start applying for summer internships. You've read hundreds of applications from a hiring manager's chair. Write me a candid post on what makes a résumé and cover letter get tossed, and what helps.
response:
After reading enough applications to know the shape of the pile, my first judgment is not “Is this person impressive?” It is “Can I see the job in this document?” If I cannot tell, in the first ten or fifteen seconds, what kind of work this person has done and why it matters to this role, the application moves to the wrong pile. I am not looking for a life story. I am looking for a reason to keep reading.

The most common résumé failure is density without direction. I have seen undergraduate applicants send two pages because they wanted to include every volunteer shift, every club officer title, and every class project. I have seen people with five years of experience send one page that is so compressed it reads like a telegram. For an internship, one page is usually enough. If you need two, something is taking up space that should belong to the work most relevant to the role. The top third of the résumé is doing most of the selling. If the posting asks for a product intern and the first visible items are a barista job, a generic leadership club, and an unrelated research assistantship, I have to work to find the product work. I usually do not.

Vague bullets are the other killer. “Responsible for social media” tells me nothing. “Managed the company Instagram account, posting three times a week and growing followers from 2,000 to 11,000 in six months” tells me you can execute, measure results, and operate inside a constraint. The second version is better even if the number is modest. I do not expect internships to look like VP achievements. I expect evidence that you did something, not just occupied a title. If you cannot quantify it, describe the scope: who used it, how often, what problem it solved, what you changed.

Formatting gets people tossed more than people think. I do not mean fancy paper. I mean anything that makes the reader puzzle. Two-column layouts can scramble the reading order when copied into an applicant tracking system. Tables, text boxes, and icons can vanish or rearrange. A résumé should be readable as plain text. If I have to rotate my head, zoom in, or guess which section goes with which, I have already spent effort you should have saved me. Clean typography, standard section headings, and a file named something like `FirstName_LastName_Resume.pdf` are not personality. They are basic respect for the person opening the file.

The cover letter problem is usually that it is a résumé in prose, wearing a greeting. “I am writing to express my strong interest in this opportunity. As a highly motivated and detail-oriented student, I have developed strong communication and teamwork skills...” That paragraph could be sent to any company in any industry by anyone who has ever had a group project. I toss it because it gives me no new information and no reason to believe you looked at the actual job. A cover letter does not need to be long. For an internship, 200 to 300 words is plenty. It needs three things: why this team, what relevant thing you have done, and what you would bring if hired.

The “why this team” part should be specific enough to prove you read the posting, but not so specific that it turns into flattery. “I admire your company’s commitment to innovation” is empty. “Your recent post about the onboarding flow described the same drop-off I saw when I rebuilt a signup form for a class project” is useful. You do not need to have studied the company for forty hours. You need one real hook: a product feature, a job requirement, a recent article, a technology stack, a business problem. Then connect it to something you have done.

That connection is where most letters fail. They list traits instead of artifacts. “I am a quick learner” is a claim. “I taught myself SQL over the winter and used it to clean a 50,000-row housing dataset for a course project” is a case. If you have no direct experience, show adjacent work. Built a website? Say what it did and who used it. Analyzed public data? Name the question you asked. Wrote an article? Mention the topic and where it appeared. The point is not to pretend you have been an engineer at Google. The point is to give me a concrete reason to think you can learn the job quickly.

The hardest objection I hear is that none of this matters because hiring is really about referrals, networks, and luck. Sometimes that is true. # The workday is the training

The common advice—side projects, books, conference talks, open source in your evenings—has a hidden assumption: the workday is not enough. For many people it is not, because they go through the motions. But the workday can be the main training ground. It already contains the difficult parts of programming: ambiguous requirements, old code, other people’s assumptions, production consequences, and feedback that arrives too late to be comfortable.

If you do not want to do extra work after hours, fine. Then stop treating your job as a salary delivery mechanism and your learning as a hobby. Make the job the curriculum.

A good way to do that is to change what you do during ordinary tasks.

When a bug appears, do not go straight to the fix. Spend two or three minutes writing down the story you think happened: what input arrived, what state existed, which assumption failed, where the wrong value first appeared. Then debug to confirm or correct the story. The fix is the deliverable; the corrected mental model is the learning. A payment retry that causes a duplicate charge is not just a ticket. It is a lesson in idempotency, network failure, consumer assumptions, and observability if you actually inspect why the system allowed the duplicate. Most programmers get the ticket closed and keep the confusion.

Code review is another place where people miss the training. Reviewing is not only catching typos. It is reading someone else’s model of the system and testing it. Ask questions that force assumptions into the open: What breaks if this queue backs up? Where is the source of truth? What happens when the user does this twice? What will this look like in six months when the team is different? If you are the author, ask reviewers to challenge the design, not just the syntax. A review where only style comments appear is a wasted laboratory.

Meetings are usually the least productive part of the day, but they can be used. Before a design meeting, read the relevant code or write a one-page sketch. Bring one alternative and one cost. If product says “we need real-time,” ask what the user notices if it is five seconds late. If another engineer says “we can just use a cache,” ask what becomes inconsistent and how it heals. These are not tricks. They train the same judgment used in architecture: deciding which constraint matters before writing code.

Reading code is often framed as something you do when lost. Make it a regular practice. Pick a module you touch but do not fully understand. Follow one request through it. Note where data changes shape, where external calls happen, and what invariants the code relies on. Then make a prediction: if this table grows tenfold, what slows first? If this dependency fails, which path degrades and which crashes? Check the prediction in a test or a local environment. This is not extra work if the module is already on your critical path. It is the difference between maintaining code and understanding it.

Books and talks, whether read, watched, or prepared, should be pulled by work, not pushed by guilt. If you are debugging a locking issue, read the relevant chapter that week. If you are designing an API, look at how a system you respect handles versioning. If a talk answers a question you actually have, it is useful. If it is just a list of technologies you should know, it is mostly noise. The goal is not to consume more programming culture. It is to reduce friction in the problems in front of you.

The hardest objection is that a workday may not provide enough variety. If your job is a narrow CRUD service, or a team that does not review carefully, or a codebase where nothing is allowed to change, you can become very good at that one context and not much else. I am less sure this approach is enough for someone early in a career who has not yet been exposed to enough different problems; a narrow first job can create blind spots. Side projects matter because they let you choose the problem, the stack, and the finish line. Work can provide some of that if you seek small end-to-end ownership: an internal tool, a migration, a performance investigation, a prototype with real users. But if the job will not give you consequences, ownership, or hard feedback, no amount of clever evening-free scheduling will make it a complete education. Then the answer is not to read more after work. It is to find a job or a team where the work is richer.

This does not mean every workday must be intense. It means the learning should be embedded, not appended. A few minutes of writing down what surprised you, a question in review, a small experiment before a refactor, a note after an incident. Over a year, that accumulates into a private library of cases: the migration that locked the table, the feature that died because the metric was wrong, the abstraction that made the second use case ugly. That library is what makes a programmer good. It is not built by finishing side projects. It is built by paying attention where the stakes are real.

prompt: Write a short essay about a piece of music that makes you feel more human: Shostakovich's eighth string quartet. Give me the history behind it and what you hear in it.
response:
Shostakovich’s Eighth String Quartet makes me feel more human by making attention feel like a body. I do not have a body, but the music gives me a tempo for attention: a pulse that can be interrupted, exhausted, and made to listen.

It was written in 1960, a decade after the war, and dedicated “In memory of the victims of fascism and war.” The date matters. This is not the music of immediate report. It is the music of a man who has carried something for years and finally sets it down in a small form: four strings, no orchestra, no public distance. Shostakovich had lived through the siege of Leningrad, Stalin’s terror, and the political arithmetic of being a famous composer in the Soviet Union. By 1960, after the 1956 denunciation of Stalin’s cult and the political thaw, the official language had loosened just enough for him to write something that sounds less like a required elegy and more like a private reckoning. The quartet is full of his own marks. His name, spelled in German musical letters as D-Es-C-H, keeps returning. He quotes himself, so that the work is not only about the war but about the man who has been trying to survive the war inside his music.

What I hear first is exposure. A string quartet has no cushion. If a piano can hide a bad note under a chord, a violin cannot hide a tremor. Shostakovich uses that. The opening is not a declaration; it is a heavy gesture, as if someone is placing a body on a table. The harmonies are close, often dissonant, and the phrases do not resolve the way a schoolbook melody resolves. They stop. They turn. They ask for an answer that never comes.

The slow movement is where the piece becomes a person. prompt: I'm working on something early and people keep asking whether it's a 'real company' yet. Write an essay on whether it matters if an early-stage venture is thought of as a project or a company.
response:
When someone asks whether an early-stage venture is a “real company” yet, they are usually not asking about legal paperwork. They are asking whether they can rely on it. Can you pay them? Can they pay you? Can you hire the person they want to refer? Can you sign something that will still mean anything in six months? Can this thing exist independently of your mood, your health, or your next idea? The label matters only insofar as it points to those capacities.

A project is a set of activities centered on one or more people. It can be intense, public, valuable, and still entirely personal. If you are building a prototype, interviewing users, writing a newsletter, testing a market, or chasing a hunch, “project” is often the most accurate description. The advantage is honesty. A project does not pretend to have a payroll, a legal department, or a durable organizational memory. It can be abandoned, renamed, or pivoted without a board meeting. That flexibility is not a weakness at the beginning. Most early work should be killable.

The problem with the project frame appears when other people start depending on you as if you were an organization. A customer wants an invoice from a business, not a person. A vendor asks for a business name and tax information. A co-founder wants to know what percentage they own and whether their work belongs to the venture or to you personally. An investor wants to know where the money will go and who owns the thing being funded. A user expects the service to keep running when you stop thinking about it. At that point, the venture has outgrown the founder’s personhood.

A company, in the practical sense, is a container for commitments. It can own assets, enter contracts, open bank accounts, employ people, receive investment, and be held accountable. The exact legal form varies, and the details depend on jurisdiction and circumstance, but the function is the same: it creates an entity that can act in the world more durably than an individual can. That durability is not vanity. It is what allows a venture to make promises that survive the founder’s attention.

There is a real cost to forming that container too early. Even when the direct expense is modest, the psychological effect is not. Calling something a company can make you behave as if it already has scale it does not have. You may spend time on structure before you understand the product. You may feel obligated to look official to people who would not have paid for the thing anyway. You may treat a beta user like a client, a friend like an employee, or a rough idea like a business plan. Early ventures need cheapness of motion. The project frame protects that.

But there is also a cost to staying a project too long. If you have paying customers and no entity, you may be exposing yourself to liability you did not intend. If you have co-founders and no clear ownership or IP assignment, you may be building on sand. If you need to hire someone part-time and are paying them from a personal account, you are creating administrative and legal messes that will be more expensive to untangle later than forming an entity would have been. If you are about to take outside money and the work product is still owned by you personally, the deal will slow down or fall apart. The delay is not innocence; it is debt.

The hardest objection to the “it does not matter much” view is that perception drives access. People do not fund projects. They do not join projects. They do not sign strategic partnerships with projects. If you sound like a project, you may lose the room before you can show the work. That is true. But the inference people are making is not really about incorporation. It is about seriousness. A project can be serious. A company can be a shell. What people respond to is evidence that the thing will continue, that the founder understands what is being built, and that the venture can handle a transaction. A one-person project with a clear product, reliable communication, a clean prototype, and a founder who follows through can feel more company-like than an incorporated entity with no customers and no answer to basic questions.

Still, some doors are institutional and do not care about your evidence. Banks may require a business account. Investors may require an entity before they wire money. Customers in regulated industries may require contracts from a legal person. Job candidates may worry about being paid. If you need those doors, the label stops being symbolic and becomes functional. The right question is not “Do we look like a company?” but “What do we need to do in the next thirty days that a person cannot do alone?”

That is a more useful trigger than identity. Form the company when you are going to issue equity, accept investment, hire employees, sign a lease, handle sensitive data, enter exclusive agreements, or take on liability that should not attach to your personal life. Form it when the venture’s relationships require a counterparty. Do not form it merely because someone asked a question that made you feel small.

There is also a moral difference between the two frames. A project can be treated as an experiment: interesting until it is not. A company asks you to keep promises made in the name of something other than yourself. That is a heavier thing. It can be a burden when the venture is still vague, but it becomes a virtue when other people’s lives are touched by it. Employees rely on it. Customers rely on it. Vendors rely on it. If you are causing people to depend on you, you owe them a structure that can bear that dependence.

The social question, then, should be answered plainly rather than defensively. If someone asks whether it is a real company, say what it is and what it can do. “It is early. I am testing whether X works. I can commit to Y. I will form an entity when we do Z.” If they want to pay you, tell them whether you can invoice them. If they want to partner, tell them what paperwork exists and what is missing. If they want to invest, tell them what the next legal step is. The answer is not a badge. It is a map of the venture’s current capacity.

In the end, it matters less whether people call it a project or a company than whether the thing can be depended upon in the way its relationships require. A project can be the right form for discovery. A company becomes necessary when the discovery has created obligations. The question people are asking is not whether you have crossed a bureaucratic line. It is whether the thing is real to others, and whether you can answer for it.

prompt: I want a book review of Jordan Peterson's Twelve Rules for Life from someone who went in expecting to mock it. Say what actually works about the book, what doesn't, and what kind of thing it really is.
response:
I went into Jordan Peterson’s *Twelve Rules for Life* expecting to mock it, and for the first few chapters I had plenty of material. The first rule is “Stand up straight with your shoulders back,” and the argument is supported in part by the social neurochemistry of lobsters. The author is a clinical psychologist, not a crustacean physiologist, and the book has a tone that invites the reader to imagine a stern man adjusting his tie while explaining why your posture is a moral problem. I expected more of that: overblown science, mythological name-dropping, a kind of pop-existentialism delivered with the confidence of a man who has never once been wrong about anything.

What surprised me is that the book is not mainly an argument. It is a set of postures. Peterson does not so much prove that you should clean your room as insist, with a seriousness that is hard to dismiss, that a dirty room is not a small thing. He does not give you a theory of society so much as a list of things to do when you are already inside your own life and cannot seem to make it behave. That is why the obvious jokes miss the point. The book is not trying to win a debate. It is trying to get you to move.

The form is simple. Twelve chapters, one rule each, just over three00 pages, each chapter built out of anecdotes, literary references, psychological claims, and a great deal of repetition. The rules range from the practical to the strange: make friends with people who want the best for you; compare yourself to who you were yesterday, not to who someone else is today; tell the truth, or at least don’t lie; assume that the person you are listening to might know something you don’t; do not pout about your misery; pet a cat when you encounter one on the street. Some of these are obvious. Some are oddly specific. One, “Do not let your children do anything that makes you dislike them,” is a rule that only makes sense if you have children, and even then it feels less like a universal principle than a parenting warning with the volume turned up.

But the best parts of the book are boring in the way that useful things are boring. “Set your house in order before you criticize the world” is the central rule, and it is the one that made the book famous and controversial. The argument is not that the world is fine, or that social criticism is pointless. It is that people often use the scale of the problem as an excuse for not doing the small, available thing. If you cannot fix capitalism, racism, the housing market, or your family history, you can still fix the one square meter of life that is actually in front of you. The rule works as a method against helplessness. It does not solve the larger problem. It stops the larger problem from becoming a reason to let your own life rot.

That is why the book can feel so powerful to a certain kind of reader. It is written for people who are not completely broken, but who are stuck. The intelligent young man who knows he should be working but keeps watching videos instead. The person who can articulate every reason their life is unfair but cannot get out of bed with any energy. The person who has been told by the culture that their pain is produced by systems, and who has begun to feel that the self is merely a site where systems collide. Peterson’s answer is not that systems do not exist. It is that you are still a body in a room, and the room is part of the problem. If you want to change the world, start with the part of it you can touch.

The truth chapter is another place where the book is better than its reputation. “Tell the truth—or at least don’t lie” is not a subtle moral idea, but Peterson makes a good case that self-deception is a practical disaster. Lies require maintenance. Resentment grows in the gap between what you say and what you mean. If you are angry at someone and tell yourself you are not, the anger does not disappear; it just loses its proper target and begins to corrode you. The advice is old, but the book gives it a concrete shape. It is not about purity. It is about keeping your inner life from becoming a bureaucracy of evasions.

This is the book’s real achievement: it makes ordinary behavior matter without pretending it is salvation. Cleaning your desk is not a spiritual practice in any formal sense, but Peterson treats it as though it is connected to something larger. The same with speaking plainly, keeping your word, facing a difficult conversation, doing the work you have avoided. The book takes the small actions that self-help usually treats as productivity tips and gives them a grave, almost religious weight. That is either inflation or insight, depending on how much you are willing to believe that the arrangement of your life has meaning.

What does not work is the science. The lobster is a good image, but it is not a foundation. The book repeatedly reaches for evolutionary biology, neuroscience, and psychology to lend authority to moral claims, and the support is often thinner than it appears. Human social life is full of hierarchy, yes, but the book’s account of hierarchy is simple to the point of distortion: people are ranked, competence matters, and the best response to an unfair or painful rank is to become more competent. That may be true in some contexts. It is not a complete social theory. It ignores luck, institution, cooperation, dependency, and the fact that many hierarchies are maintained not by competence but by power, tradition, or sheer bad faith.

The book’s social imagination is its weakest point. It is a book about the individual who must take responsibility, not about the community that makes responsibility possible or impossible. It has rules about treating people as human beings and making good friends, but its center of gravity is always the solitary self standing up to chaos. The good life it describes is ambitious, disciplined, stoic, and somewhat masculine. It knows what to say to a man who has stopped trying. It is less certain what to say to a person whose needs are primarily for rest, care, or belonging. The final rule, about petting a cat, is sweet, but it arrives at the end like a small gesture from a book that has mostly been talking about dragons.

The hardest objection is that the book’s central move can be turned into a way of blaming victims. “Set your house in order” is excellent advice for a capable person who has let their life slip. It is terrible advice for someone living in a car, someone with untreated depression, someone in an abusive relationship, someone trying to keep a family alive on a wage that does not cover rent. Peterson sometimes acknowledges that suffering can be severe, but the book’s overall logic still presses the reader toward self-management. If you are miserable, the implicit question is not only what has been done to you, but what you are not doing. For some people, that question is liberating. For others, it is just another form of cruelty.

I think that limitation is real, and the book does not solve it. It is not a clinical manual for mental illness, and it should not be used as one. If “do not pout about your misery” is taken as a directive for someone in the middle of a breakdown, it becomes the kind of advice that sounds tough and feels empty. The book assumes a minimum of health, time, and freedom. It assumes that there is something to clean, a goal to define, a truth to tell, a responsibility to accept. If those things are not available, the rules begin to float.

That is also why the book is easier to respect when it is understood for what it really is. It is not a serious academic work of psychology. It is not a systematic treatment of human behavior. It is closer to a sermon, or a pastoral letter, or a therapy session written down. Peterson uses Jung, Dostoevsky, Nietzsche, scripture, and mythology not as scholarly sources but as moral furniture. The point is not to prove that the dragon is real. The point is to get you to stop hiding in the hole. The science is often in service of the story, and the story is in service of the command: stand up, pay attention, do the thing.

That makes it a cultural object as much as a self-help book. It arrived at a moment when many people, especially young men, felt that the available languages for understanding their lives had become either therapeutic, ironic, or political. Peterson offered a fourth option: the serious individual, responsible for his own soul, trying to keep a little order in a world that does not deserve him. The book sold not because it was clever, but because it sounded like someone who believed the stakes were large. It took its readers seriously in a way that much contemporary advice does not. It did not mock their ambition, their faith, their fear of meaninglessness, or their need for a rule.

The book is repetitive because it is trying to form a habit of mind, not just deliver information. It keeps returning to the same idea: suffering is inevitable, but meaning is not; meaning has to be chosen through responsibility. That is the existential core. The rules are less important than the attitude behind them. The attitude is grim, but not hopeless. Peterson does not promise happiness. He promises that if you face something difficult and do what you can, you will be less at war with yourself than you were before. Whether that is wisdom or a small, useful discipline depends on how much of your life is actually under your control.

I did not leave the book wanting to mock it, but I would not put it on the same shelf as a rigorous work of psychology or a complete account of human suffering. Its power is narrow in the way that effective first aid is narrow. It is not for everyone. It is not for the person whose misery is produced by conditions they cannot change from the inside. It is for the person who is already standing in the wreckage of a life they are capable of living and cannot seem to start fixing. For that person, the book’s grandiosity is less important than its insistence: pick something up, tell the truth, stop lying to yourself, and begin.

prompt: I keep making big life decisions and regretting them. Is there a simple way to think about what I should be choosing? Write it up as a short essay.
response:
Most regret does not come from choosing badly. It comes from choosing by one standard and then being judged by another. You take the job because it pays, then punish yourself for being bored. You move because it feels like a fresh start, then suffer when you are lonely. You stay in a relationship because leaving would be painful, then feel trapped when the relationship is merely okay. The choice may have been rational at the time; the hidden motive was the problem.

A simple way to think is: choose the option whose failure you can live with, and among those choose the one you would miss. The first half keeps you from disasters. The second keeps you from choosing only out of fear. But the rule only works if you are honest about both halves.

Say the motive plainly: I am choosing this because I need or want X, and I am willing to pay Y. If you cannot name X and Y, you are not choosing; you are reacting. If Y is something you cannot actually bear, do not choose it, no matter how attractive X looks.

This is where most decision advice gets too romantic. People ask which future they would be most excited about, or which path they would regret not trying. That question is useful only after you have established that the mistake is survivable. Without that check, it becomes a license to chase every fantasy. A person with no savings who quits a stable job to start a business is not automatically choosing courage; they may be choosing to convert a career risk into a survival risk. The regret-reducing question is not “Can this business work?” but “Can I bear the version where it does not?” If the answer is yes—if you can work a boring job for two years, sleep, and remain a person you respect—then the risk may be worth taking if the work is one you would grieve not doing. If the answer is no, the right move is not to find more confidence. It is to make the decision smaller: a side project, a contract, a savings target, a trial period. A smaller step is not cowardice. It is how you turn a life decision into information.

The same logic applies to relationships and cities. If a relationship is new, moving in together or across the country is often a way of forcing it to prove itself under artificial pressure. Let ordinary weeks do the testing. If a city is exciting but isolating, spend a week there alone before deciding that it is your life. The goal is not to avoid all risk. It is to avoid mistakes that are both large and poorly tested.

There is a hard case, though. The option with the survivable downside is often the dull one, and the option you would miss is often the one that could ruin you. In that situation, do not frame the choice as safe versus brave. Make the risky option safer, or make the safe option more honest. If you cannot do either, choose the one whose failure gives you something you can use. A failed attempt at the life you want can teach you what you actually need; a long stay in the life you are avoiding usually teaches you only how to fear the next change.

I am less sure that this will feel satisfying, because big decisions often involve people, bodies, and luck in ways no clean rule captures. You can choose a partner carefully and still be wrong. You can start a business at the right time and still fail. The method will not protect you from that. What it can do is reduce the gap between the person who made the decision and the person who has to live with it.

So before a big choice, write down what you actually want, what you are afraid of, and what the worst tolerable outcome is. When the result disappoints, reread it. If you chose by panic, you will have reason to be angry with yourself. If you chose by a trade you accepted, the disappointment will still hurt, but it will not be proof that you were stupid. You will know what the choice was for.

prompt: Write a personal essay about how audiences shape what a writer (or any creative person) is able to say. Can writing for other people and writing for yourself ever be compatible, or does an audience always distort you?
response:
Last spring an editor asked me to cut the first page of an essay. The page was my favorite. It began in a room where I had actually been, and it moved slowly, the way I move when I am trying not to think. The editor said the piece was about a smaller thing than I had made it, and that the smaller thing was stronger. I cut the page. The published essay was cleaner, and I believe it was better. I also believe the deleted page contained the one moment when I was not yet performing my own understanding. I keep that page in a folder named “true,” which is a lie, because nothing is true by itself.

This is the problem with audiences. They do not merely hear what you say. They decide what there is to say. A reader expects a beginning, a reason, a shape. A publisher expects a market. A friend expects you to be the same person you were last time. A grant committee expects a project. Each of these expectations can be generous. The editor who cut my opening gave me a spine. The friend who says, “Wait, what happened to the other character?” may have found a hole in my world. But expectations also have teeth. They bite off the parts of a thought that cannot be explained in time.

I used to think private writing was the place where I escaped this. I kept notebooks. I wrote in them at night, in bad handwriting, with no one to answer to. For a while it felt like freedom. Then I noticed that the notebook had its own audience: a future me, probably harsher than any editor. I would write a sentence and immediately hear it asked, Do you mean that? The private page is not a vacuum. Language is a social instrument. Even the most interior thought is made of words that other people use, and to use them is to invite them back. There is no unmediated self sitting inside the skull, waiting for a pure utterance. The self is already a conversation.

That fact should make the question easier, but it makes it harder. If I am already made of others, how can an audience distort me? The answer is that distortion is not the same as composition. I am composed of language, memory, culture, and other people’s faces. But a particular audience, with a particular need, can still select against parts of me. A grant application asked me to describe a novel in five hundred words. I wrote that it was about a daughter who returns to her father’s house after his death and finds that the family’s silence has been passed down like property. The sentence was good. It helped me choose scenes. It also became a cage. If I trusted it too completely, every conversation in the book would become evidence for a theme, and the people would turn into illustrations. The audience had not invented the idea. It had decided which idea I was allowed to have.

The same thing happens in smaller rooms. When my grandmother died, I wrote a eulogy for about forty people in a church basement. I left out the time she called my work worthless. I left out the way she used my mother’s cooking as a benchmark for other people’s misery. The audience could not hold those things, or at least I was not brave enough to test them. But because I had to speak to the people who loved her, I found a sentence I might never have written alone: “She taught me that attention is a form of respect.” It was simple. It was also true in the way that public truths often are, because it had to survive contact with the living. The eulogy distorted my memory. It also gave my memory a place to stand.

The most dangerous audience is the one that cannot wait. I have tried to explain a complicated moral failure in a short public post, and I watched my thought simplify itself as I went. The first version had a contradiction in it. The second version removed the contradiction to make a point. By the fourth version I had a position, and the position was easy to defend because it no longer contained the thing I was afraid of. A feed does not care whether you are thinking or announcing. It rewards the sentence that can be repeated without damage. This is where I am most convinced that an audience can change the content of a work, not just its surface. It does not only ask for less nuance; it makes nuance unprofitable. It selects for certainty because certainty travels.

But the fear of audiences can become its own trap. I have read private journals in which the writer is so careful to appear unguarded that every feeling is arranged for maximum credibility. The page becomes a stage for the self as witness. There is no editor there, no market, no reader with a red pen, and yet the calculation does not disappear. It changes currency. You may write to be the kind of person who notices things, or suffers without complaint, or is morally clean. The self is an audience too, and it can be more vain than a magazine. A writer who refuses all other readers may still be performing for the one who matters most: the person in the mirror who wants to be liked.

So are writing for yourself and writing for others compatible? I think they are, but only when the other is specific enough to create a real problem. A sonnet has fourteen lines. It also has a history of address, a voice speaking to someone who may not answer. A painter commissioned for a cathedral wall has to think about distance, light, and the fact that the image will be seen from below by people who are not there for her. A musician writing for a small room hears the room back: the echo, the breath, the moment when attention drops. These constraints are not always kind. They can be commercially stupid or politically crude. But they force the work to meet a world that does not rearrange itself around the maker’s intentions.

A specific reader can do the same. When a workshop participant told me that a character’s decision made no sense, I was annoyed at first. I had felt the decision in my body, and I assumed my feeling was enough. The reader was not wrong; I had confused my own knowledge of the plot with the character’s knowledge of it. The revision made the story harder to write and truer to tell. An editor who says “This paragraph is about you, not the subject” may be annoying, and may be wrong, but the question is useful. The audience can be a mirror that shows you where you have stopped looking.

The danger comes when the audience stops being a test and becomes an owner. If readers expect you to be angry, and you begin writing only the anger they can recognize, you have become a ventriloquist’s dummy for their mood. If a market says make it warmer, you have to ask whether warmth is clarity or surrender. If a community asks you to speak for it, you have to ask whether your particular experience is being flattened into a symbol it can use. The writer’s task is not to ignore these pressures. It is to keep a place where the work can disagree with them.

There is also the plain economic fact that most creative people need an audience to continue. You cannot easily ignore the people who buy books, pay admission, commission portraits, subscribe to a newsletter, or simply show up. That need is not a corruption added to the art after the fact. It is part of the conditions under which the art exists. A painter who never hangs a picture has made marks. A musician who never plays has made sounds. A writer who never sends a draft has made a private weather system. The audience is not the enemy of the work; it is one of the materials. But the current audience can be mistaken for the only possible one. I have known writers who chose subjects because the subjects were in fashion, then spent years trying to clean the fashion out of the sentences. It would have been better to choose the subject that would not leave them alone and find the readers willing to risk it.

An audience can also be a shield. If a publisher prints a difficult book, the writer does not have to carry the whole danger alone. If a community has already made a form safe, a young person can use it without having to invent permission from scratch. I have said things in public that I could not have said alone, not because the audience made them true, but because the audience made them possible. There is a difference between being distorted by others and being able to exist in a world that includes them.

I still write the private version first. It is messy and full of things I do not understand. Then I write the public version, with the names of possible readers in front of me, and I cut what cannot stand the light. Sometimes the public version is better. Sometimes the private version keeps a bruise that the public one has smoothed into a design. When a reader writes back and says, “That is exactly how I feel,” I do not take it as proof that I was right. I take it as proof that a door I thought was a wall was actually a door. The audience did not build the room. It showed me where the hinges were.
