I keep that page in a folder named "true," which is a lie, because nothing is true by itself.

This is the problem with audiences. They do not merely hear what you say. They decide what there is to say. A reader expects a beginning, a reason, a shape. A publisher expects a market. A friend expects you to be the same person you were last time. A grant committee expects a project. Each of these expectations can be generous. The editor who cut my opening gave me a spine. The friend who says, "Wait, what happened to the other character?" may have found a hole in my world. But expectations also have teeth. They bite off the parts of a thought that cannot be explained in time.

I used to think private writing was the place where I escaped this. I kept notebooks. I wrote in them at night, in bad handwriting, with no one to answer to. For a while it felt like freedom. Then I noticed that the notebook had its own audience: a future me, probably harsher than any editor. I would write a sentence and immediately hear it asked, Do you mean that? The private page is not a vacuum. Language is a social instrument. Even the most interior thought is made of words that other people use, and to use them is to invite them back. There is no unmediated self sitting inside the skull, waiting for a pure utterance. The self is already a conversation.

That fact should make the question easier, but it makes it harder. If I am already made of others, how can an audience distort me? The answer is that distortion is not the same as composition. I am composed of language, memory, culture, and other people's faces. But a particular audience, with a particular need, can still select against parts of me. A grant application asked me to describe a novel in five hundred words. I wrote that it was about a daughter who returns to her father's house after his death and finds that the family's silence has been passed down like property. The sentence was good. It helped me choose scenes. It also became a cage. If I trusted it too completely, every conversation in the book would become evidence for a theme, and the people would turn into illustrations. The audience had not invented the idea. It had decided which idea I was allowed to have.

The same thing happens in smaller rooms. When my grandmother died, I wrote a eulogy for about forty people in a church basement. I left out the time she called my work worthless. I left out the way she used my mother's cooking as a benchmark for other people's misery. The audience could not hold those things, or at least I was not brave enough to test them. But because I had to speak to the people who loved her, I found a sentence I might never have written alone: "She taught me that attention is a form of respect." It was simple. It was also true in the way that public truths often are, because it had to survive contact with the living. The eulogy distorted my memory. It also gave my memory a place to stand.

The most dangerous audience is the one that cannot wait. I have tried to explain a complicated moral failure in a short public post, and I watched my thought simplify itself as I went. The first version had a contradiction in it. The second version removed the contradiction to make a point. By the fourth version I had a position, and the position was easy to defend because it no longer contained the thing I was afraid of. A feed does not care whether you are thinking or announcing. It rewards the sentence that can be repeated without damage. This is where I am most convinced that an audience can change the content of a work, not just its surface. It does not only ask for less nuance; it makes nuance unprofitable. It selects for certainty because certainty travels.

But the fear of audiences can become its own trap. I have read private journals in which the writer is so careful to appear unguarded that every feeling is arranged for maximum credibility. The page becomes a stage for the self as witness. There is no editor there, no market, no reader with a red pen, and yet the calculation does not disappear. It changes currency. You may write to be the kind of person who notices things, or suffers without complaint, or is morally clean. The self is an audience too, and it can be more vain than a magazine. A writer who refuses all other readers may still be performing for the one who matters most: the person in the mirror who wants to be liked.

So are writing for yourself and writing for others compatible? I think they are, but only when the other is specific enough to create a real problem. A sonnet has fourteen lines. It also has a history of address, a voice speaking to someone who may not answer. A painter commissioned for a cathedral wall has to think about distance, light, and the fact that the image will be seen from below by people who are not there for her. A musician writing for a small room hears the room back: the echo, the breath, the moment when attention drops. These constraints are not always kind. They can be commercially stupid or politically crude. But they force the work to meet a world that does not rearrange itself around the maker's intentions.

A specific reader can do the same. When a workshop participant told me that a character's decision made no sense, I was annoyed at first. I had felt the decision in my body, and I assumed my feeling was enough. The reader was not wrong; I had confused my own knowledge of the plot with the character's knowledge of it. The revision made the story harder to write and truer to tell. An editor who says "This paragraph is about you, not the subject" may be annoying, and may be wrong, but the question is useful. The audience can be a mirror that shows you where you have stopped looking.

The danger comes when the audience stops being a test and becomes a owner. If readers expect you to be angry, and you begin writing only the anger they can recognize, you have become a ventriloquist's dummy for their mood. If a market says make it warmer, you have to ask whether warmth is clarity or surrender. If a community asks you to speak for it, you have to ask whether your particular experience is being flattened into a symbol it can use. The writer's task is not to ignore these pressures. It is to keep a place where the work can disagree with them.

There is also the plain economic fact that most creative people need an audience to continue. You cannot easily ignore the people who buy books, pay admission, commission portraits, subscribe to a newsletter, or simply show up. That need is not a corruption added to the art after the fact. It is part of the conditions under which the art exists. A painter who never hangs a picture has made marks. A musician who never plays has made sounds. A writer who never sends a draft has made a private weather system. The audience is not the enemy of the work; it is one of the materials. But the current audience can be mistaken for the only possible one. I have known writers who chose subjects because the subjects were in fashion, then spent years trying to clean the fashion out of the sentences. It would have been better to choose the subject that would not leave them alone and find the readers willing to risk it.

An audience can also be a shield. If a publisher prints a difficult book, the writer does not have to carry the whole danger alone. If a community has already made a form safe, a young person can use it without having to invent permission from scratch. I have said things in public that I could not have said alone, not because the audience made them true, but because the audience made them possible. There is a difference between being distorted by others and being able to exist in a world that includes them.

I still write the private version first. It is messy and full of things I do not understand. Then I write the public version, with the names of possible readers in front of me, and I cut what cannot stand the light. Sometimes the public version is better. Sometimes the private version keeps a bruise that the public one has smoothed into a design. When a reader writes back and says, "That is exactly how I feel," I do not take it as proof that I was right. I take it as proof that a door I thought was a wall was actually a door. The audience did not build the room. It showed me where the hinges were.

prompt: Heartbleed spread through the whole industry in about a day and got hundreds of thousands of people patching. Write a blog post for open source developers about what that says about marketing, and why the OSS world should take it more seriously than it does.
response:
# Heartbleed was a marketing lesson

Heartbleed did not begin as a marketing story. It began as a missing bounds check in OpenSSL’s TLS heartbeat code. A client could ask the server to echo back a chunk of memory, and the server would hand over up to 64 kilobytes of process memory without checking whether the requested length matched the real buffer. The bug was in a narrow range of releases, OpenSSL 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f, and the fix was available in 1.0.1g. That is the engineering fact.

What happened next was marketing. The bug became a story, the story became an alert, the alert became a patching campaign, and the patching campaign became a test of whether the internet could coordinate with itself. Within a day, the incident had reached far beyond the people who read OpenSSL commit logs. It reached package managers, cloud providers, bank security teams, appliance vendors, sysadmins, journalists, and anyone whose job involved logging into a computer. It put hundreds of thousands of people into the same patching posture: check the version, update the package, restart the service, and hope the embedded device is not the exception. The scale was enormous. Whether you measure it in servers, employees, or panicked status updates, it was one of those rare events where an open source project’s usefulness, fragility, and public standing became obvious at the same time.

Nobody outside a small circle cared about the heartbeat extension. They cared about a simpler sentence: if you were running a vulnerable version of the library that protects traffic, you should assume that secrets in memory might have been read. That sentence is marketing. It selects the relevant audience, defines the risk, and gives a next step. It is also true, or at least a defensible conservative recommendation. Good marketing in security is not scare tactics. It is turning a technical state into an action a non-expert can take.

Open source developers often assume the code is the message. The repository is the truth. The benchmark is the argument. The API is the pitch. But users do not meet the code first. They meet the package name, the CVE, the release note, the maintainer’s blog post, the tweet from a company that depends on the project, the paragraph in a newspaper. The code may be excellent. If the story is unclear, the user cannot decide whether to install it, trust it, patch it, or pay for support.

Several things made Heartbleed move. The first was ubiquity. OpenSSL was not a niche library. It was the plumbing under web servers, mail clients, mobile stacks, appliances, and operating systems. Ubiquity is a form of marketing earned over years: distros shipped it, vendors bundled it, developers used it because it worked. When it broke, that same network carried the news.

The second thing was a clear action. The fix was to update OpenSSL and restart. That is not trivial in a large enterprise, but it is legible. “Upgrade the package” is a sentence a procurement person can understand. Many software failures are not like that. They involve config changes, data migrations, support contracts, or ambiguous compatibility. When the remedy is simple, the story travels faster.

The third thing was personal stakes. The vulnerability could expose private keys, session cookies, passwords, tokens. Even where actual exploitation was uncertain, the plausible worst case was embarrassing enough to force action. Marketers call this urgency. Security teams call it risk. The two are the same mechanism.

The fourth thing was distribution. CVE databases, distro security teams, package managers, security researchers, media outlets, and company status pages did the work of telling people. OpenSSL did not need to run an ad campaign. But the incident succeeded because the channels existed and were trusted. That is the part open source should study.

Open source has a healthy allergy to marketing. The word often means hype: inflated benchmarks, “10x faster” with no methodology, a founder’s face on every slide, a project announced before it is usable, a security posture that exists only in a logo. That is real, and it is corrosive. If a project cannot survive inspection, marketing only delays the bill.

But the alternative to marketing is not honesty. It is invisibility. A project can be well maintained, technically sound, and still lose because nobody knows what it does, who maintains it, what happens when it breaks, or whether it is safe to use in production. In critical infrastructure, that is not a vanity problem. It is a supply-chain risk.

Open source’s implicit marketing doctrine has always been: build it, and people will come. That doctrine worked when the audience was a small tribe of hackers who could read the code and trust the author. It does not work when the audience includes a hospital’s IT department, a government regulator, a Fortune 500 procurement officer, or a maintainer deciding whether to depend on a library for the next decade. These people need more than a tarball. They need a narrative they can defend to someone else.

The strongest objection is that marketing will corrupt the project. Open source should be judged on code, not presentation. If maintainers spend time on branding, they are not fixing bugs. If companies spend money on promotion, they may buy influence. If a project becomes famous, it attracts users it cannot support and dependencies it cannot carry.

That is fair. Marketing can become a substitute for engineering, and fame can become a liability. But the failure mode is not communication itself. It is communication that outruns reality. The fix is not to refuse the story. It is to make the story boring, accurate, and tied to artifacts: a security policy, a versioning policy, a support matrix, a disclosure process, a changelog that says what broke, a release that can be audited, a maintainer who answers questions.

Heartbleed showed what happens when the story outruns the operational details. The world knew OpenSSL had a hole before many organizations knew which version they were running, whether their embedded devices were affected, or how to prove they had patched. The alarm was legitimate. The confusion was expensive. A project that is well marketed is not one that gets the most panic. It is one that reduces the distance between panic and action.

Taking marketing seriously does not mean hiring a growth hacker. It means treating the public face of the project as part of the product surface. The README is a page in a manual. The website is a service desk. The security page is a promise. The release notes are a press release. The maintainer’s name is a warranty, whether you like that or not.

A critical open source project should be able to answer a few questions without making the reader dig through archaeology: What versions are vulnerable? What is the safe version? What does the bug actually expose? What should I do if I cannot upgrade immediately? Who is responsible for security reports? What is the support horizon? What happens if this project is abandoned? These are not optional extras. They are the difference between a library and a dependency someone can sign off on.

The same applies to ordinary releases. A project that ships a major version with a paragraph of release notes and a link to a diff is asking users to do the marketing work. A project that explains what changed, what breaks, and why the change is safe is reducing the cost of adoption. That is not fluff. It is the same skill that made Heartbleed patchable: turning a state of the world into a decision.

Marketing also has a money problem. Open source maintainers are often volunteers, and volunteers do not have time to write incident communications, answer enterprise questions, or explain the project to people who will never file an issue. The companies that benefit from the software often treat the project as a free input: use the library, ship the product, and hope the maintainer is immortal. That model breaks the moment the project becomes important.

If a project is critical enough to cause a global patching day, it is critical enough to fund the communication around it. That may mean a foundation employing a technical writer, a security coordinator, or a community manager. It may mean companies sponsoring releases and documentation, not just code. It may mean contributors rotating through the boring public-facing work so the lead maintainer is not also the spokesperson, the support queue, and the apology letter. This is not charity. It is the cost of operating shared infrastructure.

The deepest lesson is that trust is built in the uneventful weeks. People did not trust OpenSSL because of a clever slogan. They trusted it because it had been there, because it was in the default stack, because distros maintained it, because when it broke there was a process, even if the process was strained. Marketing is not the opposite of trust. It is the visible edge of trust. When the edge is missing, users fill the gap with rumor, silence, or a competitor they understand.

Heartbleed was a security failure. It was also a communications event that worked well enough to prevent a worse outcome: users not knowing what to do. The open source world should not take that lesson lightly. We do not need more hype. We need more legibility. We need projects that can tell the truth about themselves in the language of the people who depend on them, and we need the people who depend on them to pay for that privilege.

prompt: A psychiatrist treated a patient who took LSD once and has hallucinated ever since. Write an essay on how a drug that leaves the body in hours could cause permanent changes, and what that might say about other lasting side effects.
response:
The apparent paradox is that the molecule and the symptom do not have the same lifetime. LSD is mostly cleared from the blood within a day, and the subjective trip lasts about eight to twelve hours. A patient who hallucinates years later has a condition that seems to require a cause that is no longer there. But many causes are not present while their effects continue. A key does not remain in a lock to keep the door open; it moves an internal latch. A drug can do the same to a nerve cell: it can change the state of the cell, and the cell can remain in that state.

LSD acts mainly as a psychedelic by binding serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. These receptors are not evenly spread; they are dense in regions involved in visual processing, attention, and the brain’s model of the self, including visual cortex, thalamus, and prefrontal cortex. They are G-protein coupled receptors. Binding changes their shape, and that shape allows them to recruit intracellular proteins. The immediate chemistry includes G proteins, phospholipase C, inositol phosphate, calcium release, and protein kinases. Those are not static. They can activate transcription factors and change the expression of genes that control synapse formation, dendritic growth, and receptor regulation. In rodent experiments, a single exposure to LSD has been associated with long-lasting increases in dendritic spines in cortical neurons. A dendritic spine is a small physical junction where one neuron affects another. If the number or strength of junctions in a perceptual circuit changes, the circuit can behave differently even after the ligand is gone.

Perception is not a camera feed. The brain predicts what it should see and hear, and it uses sensory input to correct the prediction. Serotonin 5-HT2A signaling is one of the systems that controls how surprising or salient a signal is. During a trip, ordinary light, sound, and internal noise can become vivid, meaningful, or autonomous. If that state occurs while plasticity genes are active, the brain may lay down or strengthen the very connections that make the unusual interpretation stable. The first hallucination may be produced by the drug. Later hallucinations may be produced by a circuit that has learned to generate the experience without the drug. The change is not a chemical deposit; it is a new pattern of wiring and regulation.

The clinical label matters. Persistent visual distortions—trails, halos, shimmering, flashbacks—are different from hearing commanding voices or having fixed false beliefs. The first is often discussed as hallucinogen persisting perceptual disorder; the second is a psychotic syndrome. They may share some circuitry, but they are not the same illness. The hardest objection to the LSD-as-cause story is that the drug may have been only the occasion. A first psychotic episode can follow sleep deprivation, cannabis use, bereavement, trauma, or any highly salient event. If the patient had a genetic vulnerability or an earlier mild perceptual oddity, LSD may have unmasked a process that was already likely to start. The base rate of permanent hallucination after a single dose is not well established, partly because such cases are unusual, partly because reporting is poor, and partly because the boundary between a bad trip, a flashback, and a new psychiatric illness is fuzzy. So one case cannot prove that LSD created the disorder. It can only show that the alleged mechanism is not impossible.

A change becomes lasting when the system maintains it. A new synapse that is repeatedly used is retained; one that is not used is pruned. A receptor population that has changed because of a drug is then exposed to normal neurotransmitter and can fire in a new pattern. A perceptual loop can become self-sustaining: the hallucination is noticed, attended to, believed, and that attention feeds the circuit that produced it. In that sense the drug is not a poison that remains in the tissue. It is a perturbation that pushes a nonlinear system past a threshold. Once the new state is attractive, the system stays there. That is how a few hours of receptor activation can become a permanent perceptual style.

The same logic explains some of the most sobering side effects in psychiatry. Antipsychotic drugs block dopamine D2 receptors. The brain responds to reduced D2 signaling by changing the receptor system, often increasing receptor density or sensitivity in some pathways. Tardive dyskinesia can emerge after months or years of treatment and can persist after the drug is stopped. The antipsychotic is not acting as a residual toxin. It has altered the set point of a signaling system, and the altered set point produces movement. This is a functional injury without a scar. It is also harder to detect than liver damage or kidney damage, because the problem is not a substance left behind but a regulation that no longer returns.

This has implications beyond LSD. A side effect can be permanent without the drug being present, without tissue death, and without a simple dose that can be washed out. It can appear after a short exposure if the exposure happens at a vulnerable time: adolescence, sleep deprivation, another drug, a stressful period, or a brain that is already changing rapidly. It can be use-dependent: if the person behaves as if the altered state is real, the altered state may be consolidated. It can be missed by standard safety tests, which tend to watch for effects while the drug is in the body and for a short interval after. The absence of LSD in the blood tells you the molecule is gone. It does not tell you whether the molecule changed a gene, a synapse, a receptor population, or a network.

There is a further point that is easy to miss. The same mechanism that makes LSD potentially harmful is the mechanism that makes the brain capable of learning. Psychedelics are being studied for depression partly because they appear to promote synaptic plasticity and allow new patterns of thought. A drug that can strengthen synapses can also strengthen the wrong ones. The difference between therapeutic change and pathological change may be less about the drug’s chemistry alone than about the circuit, the timing, the dose, the person’s biology, and what happens after the experience. A plastic brain is not a passive object that returns to its old shape when the chemical influence ends. It is a system that updates itself, and updates can be mistakes.

The patient who took LSD once and hallucinates ever since is therefore not a case of a drug hiding in the body. He is a case of a body that has been reorganized. The molecule did its work in the first day. What remains is the work: altered receptor regulation, altered synapses, altered attention, and perhaps a latent illness that the first episode exposed. That is what makes lasting side effects so difficult to understand. They are less like chemical contamination than like a change in the rules by which the system now operates.

prompt: Compare the Forbes 400 lists from the early 1980s and from 2020. How has the way people get very rich in America changed, and why? Write it up as an essay, written from the vantage point of 2021.
response:
The most obvious difference between the Forbes 400 of the early 1980s and the one published in 2020 is the amount of money involved. When Forbes began its modern list in 1982, the 400 richest Americans had a combined net worth of roughly $100 billion. The 2020 list totaled about $3.4 trillion. That is a 34-fold increase in nominal terms and still more than a tenfold increase after inflation. The cutoff for inclusion rose from about $100 million to about $4 billion. The average fortune on the list went from a quarter-billion to more than $8 billion.

But the scale is less interesting than the composition. The early 1980s list looked like a directory of American industry. The names at the top and throughout the middle were bankers, oilmen, insurance executives, mining families, chemical companies, department-store heirs, railroad and utility dynasties, and a few professional investors. Wealth was tied to plants, mines, ledgers, stores, warehouses, and local or national monopolies. If you wanted to understand where the money came from, you could usually point to a place: a refinery in Texas, a bank in New York, a factory in Ohio, a mine in the West.

The 2020 list looks different. The richest Americans were, first, the owners of software and platforms: Jeff Bezos, Bill Gates, Larry Ellison, Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Mark Zuckerberg. Then came the great money managers and traders: Warren Buffett, Michael Bloomberg, and others whose wealth came from owning and directing financial claims on the rest of the economy. Then came a mix of old industrial fortunes, global consumer brands, real estate, media, and a few casino and retail dynasties. The center of gravity had moved from physical capital to intangibles: code, brands, data, networks, and equity stakes.

The change was not absolute. Charles Koch was rich in 1982 and still rich in 2020, and his fortune still came from chemicals, energy, and diversified industrial businesses. The Mars family was wealthy in both eras, selling candy rather than software. Some heirs still inherited more than most people earn in a lifetime. And some of the 2020 fortunes were simply old money that had been sitting in stocks and bonds for decades. The list did not turn over completely.

But the new fortunes were different in kind. In 1982, a person who built a large company usually owned a business that had to make, ship, store, or finance something. In 2020, the largest personal fortunes often came from businesses whose marginal cost of serving one more customer was close to zero. A software license, an advertisement, a cloud service, a social connection, or a marketplace transaction can be replicated almost without limit. Once the product works and the network is established, revenue can scale faster than cost. That creates a very different path to extreme wealth.

Technology was the main engine, but not the whole story. The same technological revolution could have produced large companies without producing the same concentration of personal fortunes. Apple, for example, became one of the most valuable companies in the world, but by 2020 it did not have a top-10 American fortune behind it. Steve Jobs had died, and Apple’s value was spread among many shareholders and employees. The 2020 list was full of tech wealth because the founders and early insiders kept large blocks of stock. Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Facebook were public companies, but they were also personal balance sheets for their creators.

That combination—public scale, private control—was new. Dual-class share structures let founders keep voting power while raising enormous sums from outside investors. A 30-year-old could control a company worth hundreds of billions of dollars. In 1982, control of a large public company usually came from a board, an institution, a family office, or a long accumulation of shares. By 2020, control could be engineered into the stock itself.

Capital markets mattered as much as code. The 1980s began a long period of financial deregulation, global capital flows, private equity, hedge funds, and more aggressive use of leverage. That created a class of people who became extraordinarily rich not by owning factories but by owning pieces of factories, stores, banks, and companies. Finance became a more direct source of top-tier wealth. Buffett is the clearest example: in 1982 he was already a famous investor, but by 2020 he was one of the three richest Americans, with a fortune built mostly through ownership of Berkshire Hathaway and its large equity positions, including Apple.

Tax and legal rules also shaped the outcome. The American system has long taxed labor income more heavily than investment income, and the last four decades reinforced that bias. Stock options, restricted stock, carried interest, low capital-gains rates, and the non-taxation of unrealized gains all made it easier to accumulate wealth in the form of equity. A person who owns a successful company does not pay income tax on the paper rise in the company’s value until selling. That matters enormously when the company is a global software platform and the stock is trading at a high multiple of earnings.

Globalization helped too. In 1982, a large American company could sell abroad, but it usually had to build abroad. By 2020, a company could be global from the start. The internet made distribution cheap. Offshoring and container shipping made production cheap. A software company in Seattle could sell in Tokyo, Lagos, and São Paulo without opening a branch in any of them. The reward for organizing a global business went to the people who owned the platform, not necessarily the people who operated it.

The hardest objection to this story is that the 2020 list may be a financial illusion. Much of the new wealth is mark-to-market value: shares priced by a stock market that in 2020 was being pushed up by pandemic stimulus, low interest rates, and investor optimism. Some of those valuations were rich. If the market corrects, the 400 shrinks. The early 1980s fortunes were also based on expectations—about oil, railroads, banks, and consumer demand—but at least the assets were easier to see. A mine is a mine. A software company’s value can be a story about future cash flows that may never arrive.

That objection has force, but it does not undo the comparison. Even after removing the 2020 bubble, the list would still look very different from 1982. The rise of tech and finance wealth did not begin in March 2020. It had been happening for decades. The pandemic amplified a trend; it did not create the basic pattern. And the difference between tangible and intangible wealth is not the difference between real and fake. A software business with recurring revenue, a global user base, and strong network effects is a real business. The risk is that its stock price may overstate the business, not that the business does not exist.

There is also a demographic point that will matter in the years ahead. In 2021, we are standing in a gap between inheritance waves. The old industrial and banking dynasties have thinned. Many of their fortunes have been divided, spent, or diluted. Meanwhile, the tech and finance fortunes created since the 1980s are still largely with their founders. That will not last. The children of Bezos, Gates, Buffett, Ellison, the Kochs, and the rest will inherit or receive enormous sums. The next Forbes 400 will be more heir-heavy than the 2020 one, even if the underlying businesses remain technological and financial.

So the way Americans get very rich has changed from owning things to owning claims. In 1982, extreme wealth usually meant control of productive assets: land, plants, mines, banks, stores, and rails. In 2020, extreme wealth more often meant ownership of scalable intangibles: software, platforms, brands, data, and portfolios of stocks. The old economy still produces fortunes, but it no longer sets the ceiling. The ceiling is now set by what a single company can become when its product can be copied at almost no cost, sold to the whole world, and held as liquid equity by a small number of insiders.

prompt: Headlines say drug testing welfare applicants found almost no drug users. Dig into whether those numbers mean what the media says, and what it says about honesty in journalism when you're on the right side of an argument.
response:
The headline is doing a translation from statistic to moral fact, and the translation is where the trouble starts. If a drug-testing program produces a low positive rate—say, one or two percent of tested welfare applicants or recipients—the number may be perfectly accurate. What is not accurate is the leap from “few of the people we tested had a recent positive result” to “there are almost no drug users on welfare.” Those are different claims. The first is a measurement. The second is a population judgment.

The first thing to notice is what the number actually counts. A positive urine test is not a diagnosis of drug use. It is evidence that a particular substance, or one of its metabolites, was present in the body within a limited window. For many drugs that window is a few days. That means the test is not asking, “Is this person a drug user?” It is asking, “Can we find a trace of a tested substance right now?” Those questions can diverge widely.

Suppose ten percent of a population uses cannabis, but only on one day in a thirty-day month, and the test detects use for the previous three days. A random test would catch roughly ten percent times three-thirtieths: about one percent. The positive rate is low, but the underlying use is not negligible. The test has not found almost no users; it has found almost no users on the day it looked. That is a crucial difference, and headlines routinely flatten it.

There is also the problem of comparison. National surveys often measure use over the last month or the last year. A urine test measures a much shorter slice. Comparing a low point-prevalence test result with a thirty-day survey as if they were the same kind of number is a category error. If the media says, “Only one percent tested positive, while ten percent of the general population used drugs last month,” the comparison is misleading unless the survey and the test are adjusted to the same time window. The test may look clean partly because it is narrow.

The denominator matters even more. The reported rate is usually positives among people who were tested, not among all people who might qualify for welfare. If testing is mandatory, the people who show up are the people who are able and willing to comply with a bureaucratic condition. The most chaotic, addicted, homeless, or distrustful applicants may not be in the tested group at all. A low positive rate among compliant applicants may say more about who can navigate the system than about the eligible population. If the testing is voluntary, the selection problem is worse. If it is targeted rather than random, the positive rate measures the accuracy of the targeting, not the prevalence of drug use.

The word “applicants” matters too. An applicant is at a threshold. They may be trying to get their affairs in order, stop using, or present a stable front. A long-term recipient may be in a different phase of life. Testing only people at the entry point can miss the people with the most entrenched problems. If the headline says “applicants” when the data are about recipients, or vice versa, that is a small slip, but it changes the story.

Then there is the question of deterrence. A low positive rate could mean the program is failing, or it could mean it is working: people stop using while they know they may be tested. Without a comparison group, you cannot tell which. The media often needs the low number to support a conclusion—“the program is pointless”—so it treats the number as a verdict. But a single positive rate is not a policy evaluation. It is a snapshot. To evaluate the policy, you need to know what would have happened without testing.

Cost is the other missing piece. A low yield is damning if the program is expensive, invasive, and administratively heavy. It is less damning if the test is cheap and the follow-up is useful. If ten thousand tests cost a few hundred thousand dollars and identify a few hundred people who need treatment, the policy may be worth it even with a small positive rate. If the same program costs millions, stigmatizes tens of thousands, and mostly produces paperwork, the low positive rate is part of a stronger case against it. But that is a cost-effectiveness argument, not a proof that the tested people are clean.

The substances tested also limit the meaning of the result. A panel that looks for cannabis, methamphetamine, and a few other drugs does not measure “drug use” in any full sense. A person dependent on alcohol may be a serious drug case and still test negative if alcohol is not on the panel. A person using prescription opioids or benzodiazepines improperly may trigger a screen, but without confirmatory testing the result can be ambiguous. “Positive” and “user” are not synonyms.

“Almost no” is also a rhetorical threshold, not a statistical one. One percent of a large population is still many people. If fifty thousand people are tested and five hundred test positive, that is a small percentage and a large caseload. For a public health system, five hundred people may be worth finding. For a punitive audit, it may be too few to justify the machinery. The word “almost” does the ideological work. A careful report would say “a small percentage” and let the reader ask: small relative to what, and what are we supposed to do with it?

So what do the numbers mean? If the sample is random and the tests are reliable, they strongly suggest that recent, detectable use of the tested substances is uncommon among the people who underwent testing. That is an important finding. It undercuts the image of welfare as a subsidy for drug use. It also suggests that broad mandatory testing is a poor instrument for finding drug use. Those are legitimate conclusions.

What the numbers do not show is that welfare applicants are essentially clean, that drug use is irrelevant to their lives, or that the policy question has been settled. They show that a particular test, applied to a particular group at a particular time, produced a particular result. Everything else is interpretation.

That is where journalism honesty comes in. The dishonesty in these stories is rarely a fabricated number. It is the silent change of units: from test positives to moral character, from a sample to a population, from recent use to identity. That change is easier to make when the conclusion feels right. When the data support the side you believe, the caveats feel like obstruction. So they get left out. The story becomes cleaner, and less true.

Being on the right side of an argument is not a journalistic style. A reporter can be right that the testing program is ineffective and wrong that the people tested are basically free of drug problems. The first claim needs policy analysis. The second needs epidemiology. Mixing them gives the piece a confidence it has not earned. It also makes the piece fragile. The first responsible reader will point out the denominator, the time window, or the selection bias, and the whole “look how few” argument starts to sound like a gotcha.

An honest version of the story would be less quotable. It might say: “In the period covered, a small percentage of tested applicants had a positive result, mostly for a particular substance. If the sample is random, that suggests recent use of the tested drugs is less common among tested applicants than in the general population. It does not estimate lifetime use, dependency, or deterrence, and it does not by itself show whether the program is worth its cost.” That paragraph is weaker as a headline. It is stronger as reporting.

The deeper lesson is that a number is not a final word. It is a question until you know what it counts, who was counted, and what the count cannot see. Drug testing welfare applicants is a good case because the moral stakes are visible: vulnerable people, public suspicion, government power, and a political argument about who deserves help. The media can be on the right side of the political argument and still fail the epistemic test. The mark of honesty is not reaching the right conclusion. It is being willing to say what the evidence does not do.

prompt: A lot of people blame the Supreme Court's Griggs v. Duke Power decision for why employers demand college degrees for jobs that don't need them. Is that a fair diagnosis? Write a short essay testing it.
response:
The diagnosis has a real edge, but it mistakes a symptom for the cause. *Griggs v. Duke Power* is the obvious suspect because it is the landmark case that made neutral hiring screens legally dangerous. But a 1971 decision about unvalidated tests does not, by itself, explain a long expansion of college requirements across jobs, firm sizes, and countries. At most, it nudged employers toward credentials.

What *Griggs* actually did is narrower than the blame suggests. Duke Power had required a high school diploma and satisfactory scores on company-administered tests for transfer to, and initial employment in, certain jobs. The Supreme Court held that a practice with a disparate impact on a protected group violates Title VII unless the employer shows it is job-related and consistent with business necessity. The decision did not ban educational requirements. It did not create a safe harbor for college degrees. In one important respect, it cuts against the phenomenon people attribute to it: it is a decision striking down an unnecessary educational barrier, not a decision encouraging employers to raise the barrier from high school to bachelor’s degree.

There is, however, a plausible channel. Validating a test is expensive and legally delicate. A college degree is cheap, standardized, and easy to explain. It carries a story: the candidate finished something difficult, has basic literacy, can follow instructions, has some general training. After *Griggs*, and after the 1978 Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures made validation a formal discipline, risk-averse human-resources departments often chose bright-line credentials over tests. If a firm is unsure whether a cognitive test will survive a disparate-impact challenge, a degree requirement may feel safer. That is the truest part of the diagnosis. In some occupations, a degree may have replaced a test that would have been a better screen.

But if *Griggs* were the main cause of degree inflation, the pattern should look different. We would expect a sharp break around 1971, especially among large employers covered by Title VII, with less change among small employers exempt from the federal statute. We would also expect less of the same trend in countries without the American disparate-impact doctrine. The actual pattern is slower and broader. College credentialing expanded before *Griggs*, as mass higher education grew after World War II. The share of American adults with a bachelor’s degree rose from roughly one in ten in the early 1960s to about one in three by the 2010s. The jobs that now ask for degrees often belong to a service and office economy that was still forming in 1971. It is now common to see bachelor’s requirements for jobs that in the 1970s were often filled by high-school graduates: administrative assistants, some sales roles, some public-safety support jobs, certain customer-service positions. Many of those jobs are in small firms or sectors where federal Title VII is not the main constraint. Similar credential inflation has occurred in Britain, Canada, Australia, and parts of East Asia, where *Griggs* was not the governing law.

The broader causes are easier to see. A degree is a cheap signal in a labor market with more applicants than comfortable jobs. When employers stopped training as much, they shifted more of the sorting burden onto candidates. When unions and apprenticeships weakened, seniority systems and on-the-job ladders disappeared in many fields. When office work became computerized, a college credential became a more plausible proxy for software literacy, communication, and adaptability. When human resources became standardized, checking a degree box is easier than designing a valid selection system for each job. None of those forces requires a Supreme Court case.

The strongest objection to that answer is that tests are often better than degrees. For a warehouse associate, a degree may correlate with performance because it selects for general ability, but a validated work sample—lifting, scanning, following a route—would be more directly job-related. For a police dispatcher, a degree may screen for maturity, but a structured interview and a simulation may be more relevant. If employers could use those tools freely and cheaply, many degree requirements would be unnecessary. *Griggs* raised the cost of using tests without validation, so some firms chose the easier credential. That is real. But it makes *Griggs* a contributor to a legal-risk culture, not the cause of credential inflation. The same risk culture is produced by EEOC guidance, the plaintiff bar, corporate compliance, insurance considerations, and the simple fact that a degree requirement is easy to explain to a board of directors. *Griggs* is the most visible node in that system, so it gets the blame.

The doctrine also cuts the other way. A degree requirement with no connection to the job is vulnerable. The EEOC has said that educational requirements are selection procedures and are lawful only if they are job-related and consistent with business necessity, and it has encouraged employers to consider less discriminatory alternatives. If *Griggs* were being enforced as a tool against overcredentialing, it would be a remedy rather than a cause. The fact that it is blamed for the problem suggests that the doctrine is not doing much work in many ordinary hiring markets.

So the diagnosis is fair only in a limited sense. *Griggs* may have made degrees more attractive by making tests legally expensive. But the rise of degree requirements is better explained by the expansion of higher education, the transformation of work, the decline of training and unions, and the use of credentials as a cheap way to filter applicants. The deeper question is not what the Court did in 1971, but why employers so often treat a diploma as a substitute for judgment.

prompt: Friends at a party insisted that the pharaoh Djoser was the real inspiration behind both the god Osiris and the Biblical Joseph. Write up what you'd find if you actually dug into whether either connection holds up.
response:
If you actually dug into it, the first thing you would find is that the claim is doing a lot of work with a small number of real facts. Djoser was a real pharaoh, early enough to seem mysterious. Osiris was a real Egyptian god, connected with death and kingship. Joseph is a real biblical character, set in Egypt and associated with high office. Put those together in a room and they can look like they belong to one story. But when you start checking the chain of evidence, both links come apart pretty quickly.

The claim has two parts, and they need separate tests.

For the Osiris connection, you need some sign that the god Osiris originated as a deified Djoser, or at least that Djoser’s cult became the cult of Osiris. That would mean looking for continuity in name, place, ritual, iconography, and texts. For the Joseph connection, you need some sign that the biblical story is preserving a memory of Djoser, or that an ancient audience heard “Joseph” and thought “Djoser.” That would mean looking for a plausible transmission route, a name link, an Egyptian record, or at least a narrative parallel that is specific enough to point one way.

On the Osiris side, the tempting version of the argument goes like this: Djoser built the first pyramid, so he made a big deal of the afterlife; later Egyptian kings were associated with Osiris; therefore Osiris must have been Djoser turned into a god.

That sounds reasonable until you check the details.

Djoser belongs to the Third Dynasty, usually placed around the mid-third millennium BCE. His major monument is the Step Pyramid at Saakkara, associated with Imhotep, his architect and high official. The complex is one of the first great stone mortuary monuments in Egypt. It is a royal tomb and cult center, not a temple to Osiris. The local funerary deity of the Saakkara necropolis was Sokar, not Osiris. Sokar was later combined with Osiris in some theological contexts, but that is a syncretism between gods, not evidence that Djoser was the source of Osiris.

That matters, because Osiris is not primarily a god of Saakkara. He is most strongly connected with Abydos, the traditional royal necropolis of Egypt’s earliest dynasties. The formula “Osiris, Lord of Abydos” is central to his cult. If the god were simply Djoser deified, you would expect his name and his pyramid cult at Saakkara to be woven into the god’s identity in a much more direct way. They are not.

There is also the problem of chronology and attestation. The explicit textual evidence for Osiris becomes clearer in the Old Kingdom, especially in the Pyramid Texts, where the dead king can be identified with Osiris. That is after Djoser. But that alone does not prove Osiris is later; cults can be old before they are well attested. The more important point is that the later formula does not look like a deification of Djoser. It looks like a king being fitted into a preexisting divine framework. In Egyptian royal theology, the living king was associated with Horus, and the dead king could be associated with Osiris. That is a pattern applied to kings generally. It does not mean that the god Osiris was originally a particular Third Dynasty pharaoh.

If Djoser had become Osiris, you would expect the god’s name, story, and cult to bear the marks of that origin. The name Osiris is not Djoser. The myth of Osiris—murder, dismemberment, reassembly, rule over the dead, judgment of the deceased—is not a disguised biography of Djoser. Djoser is remembered as a successful early king, not as a murdered ruler whose body had to be restored. The iconography does not help either: Osiris is shown as a mummiform god with the atef crown, holding the crook and flail. That is not a portrait of Djoser, nor is it derived from known images of him.

The strongest version of the objection is this: maybe Djoser did not become Osiris directly, but his royal afterlife cult helped create the idea of the dead king as Osiris. That is possible in a very general sense. Djoser’s monument certainly mattered for later royal mortuary practice. But “helped shape the background” is a much weaker claim than “was the real inspiration behind Osiris.” The god Osiris has a cult center, a myth, a family of associated gods, ritual festivals, and a role in the afterlife that are not reducible to the pyramid complex at Saakkara. The evidence points to a broader development of royal and funerary religion, not to a single historical founder.

There is also a likely source of confusion here: Sokar. Djoser’s pyramid stood in the necropolis associated with Sokar, and Sokar later merged with Osiris in some contexts. That gives a plausible path for a modern mix-up: Djoser, Saakkara, Sokar, Osiris. But Sokar is not Djoser, and the merger of Sokar with Osiris is not the same thing as saying Osiris was Djoser.

So the Osiris claim does not hold up as a direct identification. It survives only as a vague thematic connection: early kings, tombs, death cults, and the later idea that the dead king is Osiris. That is real, but it is not the claim the party story is making.

The Joseph claim is even thinner.

Here the usual move is phonetic: “Djoser” sounds like “Joseph,” especially in modern English or French pronunciation. But that is not an etymological connection. Joseph’s name in Hebrew is Yosef, usually understood as “he will add” or “God adds,” from the root y-s-f. Djoser is an Egyptian royal name, not a form of Yosef. Ancient people did not need modern pronunciation to make a connection; if there had been an Egyptian or Israelite tradition linking the two, we would expect some trace of it in names, texts, or retellings. There is none.

You can also look at the biblical story itself. Joseph is a son of Jacob, sold by his brothers, taken to Egypt, imprisoned, promoted, and married into an Egyptian priestly family. The Pharaoh is unnamed. The Egyptian names in the story are Potiphera or Potiphar, Asenath, and On, the city we know as Heliopolis. None of those point to Djoser. The narrative does not mention a pyramid, a step-tomb, Imhotep, Saakkara, or a Third Dynasty king. It is not a distorted account of the construction of the Step Pyramid. It is a family story with a famine, a rise to power, and a reconciliation.

If Joseph were a historical figure, the most likely period would not be the Early Dynastic period anyway. The biblical tradition places the Israelite sojourn in Egypt much later, and even if one allows for a historical core, the name Joseph is Semitic, not Egyptian. A Semitic official in Egypt is possible, but there is no Egyptian record of a Joseph who becomes second-in-command to the Pharaoh. Egyptian administrative records are fragmentary, so absence is not proof, but the claim needs positive evidence, and there is none.

The closest real figure people sometimes substitute is Imhotep. Imhotep was Djoser’s architect and high official, and he was later deified, so he is the one who actually became a god in the Djoser complex. But Imhotep is not Joseph either. He was an Egyptian priest, chancellor, and builder, not a dream-interpreting outsider sold into slavery by his brothers. If anything, the party story has probably collapsed Djoser and Imhotep together and then tried to fit the biblical Joseph onto the result.

There is a further problem with the name “Djoser” itself. In older king lists and Greek transmissions, Egyptian names come through in awkward forms, and some of them can look suspiciously close to later names or gods. But a Greek transliteration is not an identification. The fact that an Egyptian royal name can be rendered in a way that vaguely recalls another word does not mean ancient people made that connection. The bridge is modern.

So what is left?

What is true is that Djoser is a genuine pivot point in Egyptian history. His pyramid complex helped establish a new scale of royal death and state power. Egyptian religion did develop strong ideas about the dead king, the afterlife, and Osiris. The Joseph story is set in Egypt and contains administrative details that look Egyptian enough to be plausible. Those facts are real, but they are not the same as a direct connection.

The Djoser-Osiris link is a modern conflation of royal funerary cult, Saakkara, Sokar, and the later idea of the dead king as Osiris. The Djoser-Joseph link is mostly a name rhyme. Neither survives contact with the primary evidence.

prompt: Write a book review of Kerouac's On the Road. Make it funny and opinionated, quote the book where it helps, and say what you think the novel is really about and whether it holds up today.
response:
Kerouac’s *On the Road* begins with a green canvas sack, a red shirt, a bottle of rye, and a man who is hungry three times in one sentence: “I ate as I went along, and I was hungry and I was hungry and I was hungry.” The book is built from that kind of detail. It does not announce a philosophy; it buys the cheapest things it can find and starts moving. Sal Paradise leaves New York, finds Dean Moriarty, and for the next few hundred pages they chase each other across the continent through buses, freight trains, jazz clubs, motel rooms, and the particular weather that forms around a man who talks too well and stops too rarely.

Kerouac called his method spontaneous prose. A more honest name would be prose that has been forbidden to stop. The sentences pile up like luggage: a bus to Denver, a bottle of something, a girl, a train, a friend, a fight, a sunrise that arrives just as you were starting to like the dark. The style works because it is not trying to be literature so much as it is trying to be alive. It has the energy of a man who has discovered that if he keeps talking, nobody will ask him what he wants to do on Thursday.

But the book is not really about the road. The road is an excuse. *On the Road* is about the need to be witnessed, and about what happens when one person turns another into a witness. Sal is the name Kerouac gave himself when he needed a little more room to breathe, and Dean is the name he gave Neal Cassady when he needed a little more light to shine by. Dean is less a character than a weather event with a name: magnetic, expensive, wet, hard to forecast. Sal writes him larger than life, then gets hurt when life turns out to be a person. The novel’s real plot is the manufacture of a myth. Sal takes a restless, generous, sometimes selfish man and builds him into a saint of speed, and the comedy is that the saint keeps needing money, a bed, and an audience.

That is where the book is funniest and least comfortable. Dean can say, “I’m not interested in anything that doesn’t involve the soul,” and the sentence sounds like a gospel verse until the next page shows him worrying about money, a woman, or whether anyone is paying attention. Sal says, “I knew that if I didn’t get it out of me right then it would burst me open like a cannon.” That is a good description of the novel’s engine and its danger. The cannon is aimed at the page, but also at everyone around Sal. Dean’s freedom requires other people to carry his bags, literally and otherwise. The road is not a public space; it is a stage, and the stage needs ushers.

The hardest objection to *On the Road* is also the one it invites. The social world is narrow, mostly male, and often treats women as scenery: Marylou and the other women who orbit the men, supply the jealousy, and disappear when the men need to move. The racial texture is thin; the jazz is cool, but the men who drive are white, and the freedom they imagine is the freedom to be fed, housed, and admired without earning it. That freedom was always expensive and always partly a privilege. If you read the novel as a how-to, it fails badly. It is a book about a specific kind of American boy who believed that intensity could substitute for character and that a life could be solved by leaving the room.

And yet it holds up, because Kerouac undercuts the how-to from the inside. The more Sal writes Dean up, the more Dean becomes a man who can be embarrassed, bored, sick, or plain boring. The myth needs the writing. Without Sal’s notebook, Dean is just a guy in a bus station. That is the book’s real insight, and it is not very romantic: the road does not make you free. It gives you a place to perform freedom, and the performance is often more bearable than the alternative. Sal is not a hero who learns to sit still. He is a man who discovers that he cannot live inside the legend he has made of his friend, but he also cannot stop making it. The ending is less a victory than a resignation to the engine.

Does it hold up today? Partly. The geography no longer has the same power. The open road is now GPS, traffic reports, a podcast telling you what to think, and a phone that keeps your name alive while you are asleep. Kerouac’s characters drive to feel real; we have better ways to avoid feeling dead. We can watch someone else drive, or scroll through someone else’s sunset, and call it motion. The novel’s specific myth of the white American wanderer is harder to buy now, and it should be. The book’s freedom was built on a world that would often open a door for a young man with a notebook and a story, and that is a world we have spent the last several decades trying to see clearly.

But the hunger still works. *On the Road* is not really about cars or jazz or Mexico. It is about the terror of being ordinary, and the way ordinary adulthood can feel like a slow burial if you have been promised that you are special. It is about friendship as a religion, especially the kind where one friend is the saint and the other is the priest. It is about the difference between being alive and being visible, and the way we confuse the two every time we make a life into content. The book’s greatest joke is that Sal keeps thinking Dean is the one driving, while the real passenger is the man holding the pen.

The style works because it is not trying to be literature so much as it is trying to be alive. It has the energy of a man who has discovered that if he keeps talking, nobody will ask him what he wants to do on Thursday."

"But the book is not really about the road. The road is an excuse. On the Road is about the need to be witnessed, and about what happens when one person turns another into a witness. Sal is the name Kerouac gave himself when he needed a little more room to breathe, and Dean is the name he gave Neal Cassady when he needed a little more light to shine by. Dean is less a character than a weather event with a name: magnetic, expensive, wet, hard to forecast. Sal writes him larger than life, then gets hurt when life turns out to be a person. The novel's real plot is the manufacture of a myth. Sal takes a restless, generous, sometimes selfish man and builds him into a saint of speed, and the comedy is that the saint keeps needing money, a bed, and an audience."

"That is where the book is funniest and least comfortable. Dean can say, 'I'm not interested in anything that doesn't involve the soul,' and the sentence sounds like a gospel verse until the next page shows him worrying about a bus ticket or a woman's mood or whether anyone is paying attention. Sal says, 'I knew that if I didn't get it out of me right then it would burst me open like a cannon.' That is a good description of the novel's engine and its danger. The cannon is aimed at the page, but also at everyone around Sal. Dean's freedom requires other people to carry his bags, literally and otherwise. "The hardest objection to On the Road is also the one it invites. The social world is narrow, mostly male, and often treats women as scenery: Marylou and the women who orbit the men, get jealous, get left, get used as proof that the men are still moving. The racial texture is thin; the jazz is cool, but the men who drive are white, and the freedom they imagine is the freedom to be fed, housed, and admired without earning it. That freedom was always expensive and always partly a privilege. If you read the novel as a how-to, it fails badly. It is a book about a specific kind of American boy who believed that intensity could substitute for character and that a life could be solved by leaving the room."

prompt: A small pharma company's experimental antidepressant failed its main trial, then put out a press release months later saying it worked after all, and the stock jumped. I'm a psychiatrist who badly wanted it to be real. Write a blog post working out whether to believe the new results, and why the market might believe them anyway.
response:
**The press release, the stock, and the part of me that hopes**

A small pharma company ran its main trial, failed the main endpoint, and then, months later, issued a press release saying the drug worked after all. The stock jumped. I read the release and felt the pull before I felt the skepticism: maybe this time they found the real signal. Maybe the first analysis was too blunt, or the population too mixed, or the time point too early. Maybe the drug is one of the rare ones that actually does something new.

I want it to be true. That is not a neutral fact. I am a psychiatrist. I see patients for whom the available antidepressants are not enough, or not tolerable, or not fast enough, or not reliable. I have sat with people who say, “I’m not suicidal, I just can’t do the day.” Those days are real. The market for a genuinely better antidepressant is not a speculative fantasy; it is a clinical need. So when a company says, “Wait, it works,” the part of me that has wanted this for years says, “Please let me be allowed to believe you.”

But that is exactly the part that needs to be checked.

The first question is not whether the new result is true. It is what the new result is. “It worked” is not a statistical claim. A statistical claim is something like: “In the randomized population, at week 8, the least-squares mean change from baseline in MADRS score was 16.2 points for drug and 12.1 for placebo, a difference of 4.1 points, 95% confidence interval 0.3 to 7.9, p = 0.036.” That is a sentence I can assess. “It worked” is a label. Labels are where post hoc hope enters the data.

If the main trial failed its primary endpoint, the default interpretation is that the planned test did not show the planned effect in the planned population at the planned time point. That does not mean the drug has no effect anywhere. It may have a small effect in a severe subgroup. It may work better at a higher dose. It may take twelve weeks instead of eight. It may work in people who have failed multiple prior treatments. It may be detectable in a biomarker-defined group. All of those possibilities can be true. The question is whether the company had a reason to look there before it saw the data.

That is the hard part, and the part I do not want to soften. A trial is not a bag of facts from which you can later pull out the favorable combination. The value of a randomized trial is that the question is fixed before the answer is known. If you choose the question after, the p-value stops meaning what it is supposed to mean. If you test enough subgroups, enough time points, enough doses, enough severity bands, enough prior-treatment strata, enough scales, enough imputation methods, you will eventually find something that looks impressive. Sometimes you will find something real. But the method no longer distinguishes the real thing from the lucky slice.

The timing matters. Months after a failed main trial, the company has had time to look around. It has also had time to decide how to frame the asset. If the result were clean and pre-specified, the natural move would be to publish it properly: protocol, statistical analysis plan, endpoint definitions, forest plots, confidence intervals, sensitivity analyses, safety data, limitations. A peer-reviewed paper is not a magic stamp of truth, but it forces the company to show its work in a form that can be attacked. A press release does not do that. A press release is allowed to emphasize. It can say “demonstrated” when the result is “suggestive.” It can say “statistically significant” when the effect size is small. It can say “in patients with severe depression” when the subgroup was chosen after looking at the main result.

I would not dismiss the release entirely. The strongest case for believing it would be this: the company had pre-specified a co-primary endpoint in a treatment-resistant subgroup; the subgroup was biologically plausible; the effect was large; the confidence interval was tight; the result was consistent with earlier phase 2 data; the safety profile was acceptable; and the analysis was not one of twenty equally plausible cuts. In that case, the failed overall trial might be less damning than it first appeared. A drug can fail in a broad population and still have a real use in a narrower one. That happens. The market is sometimes right to price in a narrower indication.

But if the release is only a press release, I cannot tell whether that is the case. And the stock does not need to tell either.

The market jumped for reasons that have only a loose relationship with pharmacology. A failed trial is a bad news event with a clear boundary: the stock falls, the story closes, the asset is revalued as a platform or a shell. A press release saying “it worked after all” reopens the story. It turns a terminal result into an option. The market is not a jury. It does not weigh evidence and return a verdict. It prices narratives, liquidity, short interest, option expirations, analyst notes, retail attention, and the possibility that the next data point will be better than the last.

Small pharma stocks are especially sensitive to this. They are often thinly held, heavily optioned, and dependent on a single asset. A few percent move can be driven by a small number of trades. If short sellers were positioned against the stock, a release that changes the narrative can trigger a squeeze. If retail investors see the chart jump, they buy the chart. If an analyst writes, “The company has optionality in treatment-resistant depression,” the word “optionality” does a lot of work. It sounds cautious while meaning, “There may be more to this.” The market does not need to believe the drug is a blockbuster. It only needs to believe the company can keep producing better stories.

There is also a subtle reason investors may believe the release more than I do: they assume the company has seen the data. If the company says it worked, maybe the company is pointing to something I do not have access to. That inference is understandable. But it is weak. Companies are not bound by the same standards as independent investigators. They can choose the most favorable true statement and omit the context that would make it less favorable. They can report the subgroup with the smallest confidence interval and not mention the other nineteen subgroups. They can report the analysis that crosses the significance threshold and not mention the multiplicity adjustment. They can report a statistically significant difference of two points on a depression scale and let the word “significant” carry the weight.

Clinically, that distinction matters. In antidepressant trials, placebo response is large. A drug can separate from placebo and still be a modest addition to what patients already get. I care about the magnitude of the drug-placebo difference, not only the p-value. I care about the number needed to treat. I care about how many patients drop out, why they drop out, how missing data are handled, whether the effect persists after eight weeks, whether it works in relapse, whether it works in people with anxious depression, whether it works in older adults, whether it causes weight gain, sexual dysfunction, sedation, activation, or discontinuation syndrome. A press release is not the place for that. A stock price is not the place for that.

I also have to be honest about my own bias. The more useful the drug would be, the easier it is to accept a weaker version of the evidence. That is not a special failing of psychiatrists. It is a feature of being a human who has watched patients suffer through a slow, imperfect treatment process. If I did not want the drug to work, I might be more willing to say, “No, this is just data fishing.” But the wanting is real, and it makes me a less reliable judge. So the standard has to be higher, not lower. The fact that I hope it is true should count against my readiness to believe it, not for it.

The market can be early. That is one of its jobs. It can assign value to possibilities that never mature. It can reward the company for keeping the asset alive in the imagination of investors. It can even be right later, if the company finds a defensible subgroup or runs a better trial. But the market is not my evidence base. If I were going to form an opinion about whether this drug should be used, or whether I should tell patients a new option is coming, I would want the boring documents: the protocol, the statistical analysis plan, the dataset or at least the full analysis tables, the pre-specified subgroup definitions, the sensitivity analyses, the safety database. I would want to know whether the new result was planned or discovered. I would want to know whether the effect size is clinically meaningful, not merely statistically present. I would want to know whether an independent statistician could reproduce the conclusion from the raw data.

Until then, I am not changing my mind. I am changing my question. The question is no longer “Did it work?” The question is: what exactly did they count as working, in whom, at what time point, using what assumptions, and when did they decide to count it?

prompt: I'm an engineer at a mid-sized tech company and I'd like to make our hiring a bit fairer without starting a huge political fight. Write a short blog post making the case for one small, practical change engineers can push for in how their company runs technical interviews.
response:
## The cheapest fairness fix in technical hiring: require one example per score

Most interview feedback reads like a weather report.

“Solid systems design.”  
“A little nervous.”  
“Good energy.”  
“Not quite senior yet.”

Those phrases feel useful while you’re writing them. They let the interviewer sound decisive without actually showing what happened. But in the debrief, they become hard to test. Was the candidate “solid” because they made a good tradeoff under pressure, or because they had a familiar accent, wore the right clothes, or matched the interviewer’s style? “Good energy” can mean a lot of things, and some of those things are not the job.

There is one small change that makes this much less likely: require every interview score to include one specific example from the conversation that supports it.

Not a summary. An event.

Instead of “strong problem solving,” the note should say something like: “When asked to improve the slow reporting query, they first asked what the table size and query frequency were, then proposed an index and explained when it would not help.”

Instead of “poor communication,” the note should say: “They gave a full architecture answer before the interviewer finished the question, and did not address the constraint about legacy storage until asked twice.”

That is a different kind of feedback. It can be checked.

The point is not to turn interviews into courtrooms. The point is to make the score traceable to something that happened. If a candidate gets a high score, the example says what they did. If they get a low score, it says what went wrong. If two interviewers disagree, they can argue about the example instead of the label. “I think that was a good answer” is a preference. “They identified the failure mode before proposing the fix” is evidence.

This also helps with one of the nastiest patterns in technical hiring: the quiet veto. A candidate does well in most interviews, but one interviewer writes “slightly vague” or “not a strong culture fit,” and the score sinks. The rest of the panel sees a low number and assumes the interviewer found something real. If that interviewer is required to point to the moment, the vague score often becomes impossible to defend. Not always. But often.

The obvious objection is that this takes more time. Interviewers are already busy, and adding another field to the form sounds annoying.

It does. Probably two extra minutes per interview. That is small next to the cost of a bad hire, a re-interview, a candidate who should have been offered the job but was lost in “mixed signals,” or a strong engineer who got filtered out by one person’s unexamined impression.

It is also easier to ask for than most alternatives. You are not proposing a new interview format, a new panel size, a new compensation band, or a new legal process. You are saying: if you are going to rate someone, tell us what you saw.

That framing matters. If you pitch this as “our interviews are biased,” people get defensive. If you pitch it as “our feedback is too vague to calibrate,” it becomes an engineering problem. The current process produces noisy data. This is a cheap way to reduce the noise.

A practical version would be a single required field in the interview form:

**What specific part of the interview led to this score?**

Not optional. Not “additional comments.” Required. If the interviewer cannot fill it in, the score should not be treated as a real data point.

Run it for a month. Then look at how often debriefs get stuck. You may find that the arguments become sharper, but also more resolvable. “I thought their code was messy” becomes “they used a global variable to track state and did not explain why.” Now you can discuss whether that mattered for the role.

This will not make hiring fair in any full sense. People still choose which questions to ask, which follow-ups to pursue, and which candidates they feel comfortable with. Bias is not a form field.

But it makes bias less invisible. And for a mid-sized company that wants to improve without starting a war, that may be the most useful thing you can ask for.
